It wasn’t clear if there was any demand for a publication about software engineering, written by a software engineer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I soon found out there was demand that surpassed </span><em><span>all</span></em><span> my expectations – and then some! Fast forward to today; the newsletter has more than 1.1M readers, tens of thousands of paid subscribers, a podcast, and more than 500,000 YouTube subscribers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>But the numbers aren’t the most validating thing for me; that would be the feedback sent in by readers. </span></strong><span>Via email, in DMs, or in-person at events, it’s great to hear how an article or a podcast we published helped someone try a new approach, or to gain confidence that theirs was the right one, or that an article helped convince a team to change things. It also means a lot to learn that The Pragmatic Engineer helps people feel more confident about keeping up in this fast-changing industry.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Thanks again for your support! </span></em><span>It’s the reason why The Pragmatic Engineer is a viable business and a growing publication, and means we can “scale up” our coverage to deliver ever-more detail about how software gets built, today.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today’s issue covers:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Diving deeper, year after year. </span></strong><span>The evolution of the Pragmatic Engineer’s coverage over five years, getting in through the “front door” instead of the “back door” for deepdives, launching the podcast, The Pragmatic Summit, and growing our team.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>What’s next? </span></strong><span>What we’re excited about, the second Pragmatic Summit, and how you can expect us to stay focused on how building software is changing, and the ways that successful engineers, teams, and companies adapt.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Cash-prize writing contest: </span></strong><span>Software is changing faster than ever. Send us your essay about how things are changing for you, for the chance to win cash prizes worth up to $10,000. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/35a2a2e1-5efa-47ed-a0af-2015bf1ecd66?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Read more on how to take part</span></a><span>.</span></p></li></ol><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>1. Diving deeper, year after year</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Pragmatic Engineer was 15 years in the making and not an overnight success; I </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f663af13-6f5e-4b39-ae42-a90f355b2366?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>started</span></a><span> to write a blog in 2007 about software development, which was “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/65c76e2b-7847-4b7b-a23f-03b7579b125d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>rebooted</span></a><span>” as “The Pragmatic Engineer Blog” in 2015. At the time, it was read by almost nobody! </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b7867433-c79d-478b-a629-fc4d351b0c47?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>In 2019</span></a><span>, I launched an email digest (“v0” of the newsletter), and a year later, I decided to focus on the newsletter fulltime after quitting Uber as a manager following job cuts in 2020, when a quarter of my team was laid off and the rest were disbanded due to the pandemic. I took an employment break, planning to finish </span><em><span>‘</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ce26b6d4-2b75-4cbc-ab40-612f58cee120?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>The Software Engineer’s Guidebook</span></a><span>’</span></em><span> in six months and then start a VC-funded startup. In the end, finishing the book took another two years, and I didn’t kick off that VC-funded startup! Instead, I decided to go all-in on writing a newsletter targeted exclusively at software engineers and engineering leaders.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: I’ll share details in the coming weeks; we’re in the middle of putting this event together now!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>2026: Growing the team in order to dive deeper</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Predictably, the most time-consuming task in The Pragmatic Engineer is working on deepdives. We often spend up to two months on a single deepdive, educating ourselves on the topic being covered, talking with expert engineers, and generally getting deep into a topic in order to deliver a deepdive worth reading.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I say “us” because this year, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3c375114-17fe-4bd6-aedd-24843d9fdfba?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Jessica Salmon</span></a><span> and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/97f2d4d7-7fb1-466f-98d4-12706ad3d672?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Ivan Klaric</span></a><span> joined the team. Both are software engineers with startup and Big Tech experience, who enjoy spending time getting to understand topics and contributing to longform articles.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>2. What’s next?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With a larger team than before, we’ve continued to produce deepdives for readers. A few recent ones:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a underline;"><span>Why Ramp built its own in-house coding agent, Inspect</span></a></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3a526402-8d8b-4e7c-8200-7580c7d903bb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Software engineering at a proprietary trading company: Optiver</span></a></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b6574b4a-1c32-49ba-aa9e-566372648f53?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: href="https://substack.com/redirect/9be45588-7d9f-4f51-a92b-b7dd1acb2fce?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>State of the software engineering job market in 2026</span></a></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>I’ve found there are no shortcuts for producing an in-depth article on a relevant topic for readers. You simply have to put the time and effort into it. </span></strong><span>This involves spending a lot of time on thinking and understanding things, going directly to engineers who build what we want to learn about, and then spending even more time on organizing research material into a lengthy article that’s informative and hopefully not dull to read.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Needless to say, we’ve experimented with the analytical powers of AI tools in parts of the research process. The technology is good at gathering publicly-available sources and does a decent job of summarizing them, but that’s been more or less the limits of AI’s usefulness for our purposes to date – except as a spelling and grammar checking tool after a full draft is written by a person.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If anything, AI can easily lead you down the wrong track by theorizing about non-existent connections and confidently espousing theories which some basic critical thinking could easily debunk!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Aside from research and correcting (most) typos, we don’t use AI in this publication. That’s because we are writing for a readership of humans and believe in the value of human voices. What you read, hear, and see in The Pragmatic Engineer comes from me and other engineers, and plenty of thought goes into each sentence.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>What comes next?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As a company that doesn’t have any venture funding, we can be ambitious without chasing any “growth goals.” In the near future, our goal is to keep doing what we do, and do it better. This means:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>More ambitious deepdives. </span></strong><span>We’ll keep bringing you deepdives from inside companies and teams building cutting-edge, fascinating software; how do they do it, what is working for them, and why? The more you understand about why engineering approaches work in certain places and situations, the more likely you’ll be able to effectively apply them in your own setting.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>In-person events. </span></strong><span>The Pragmatic Summit returns to San Francisco in February 2027. It’s my long-term goal to have a second summit in Europe, as well. Meanwhile, I’ll keep attending in-person events, like the upcoming shows in New York City with </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2a9ec1cd-9ca3-4e7e-bd96-d1f256d977db?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>turbopuffer</span></a><span> and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3275cd00-ac77-440e-a9ba-44cb45bac642?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>WorkOS</span></a><span>, and let you know in the newsletter when these happen.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Interesting podcast conversations. </span></strong><span>Recording conversations with software professionals and leaders is something that keeps filling my bucket. Expect more great conversations coming your way.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Keeping up with </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f0d211d4-86dd-4ad3-b652-9f0843ca9314?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>The Pulse.</span></a><span> </span></strong><span>I spend most of the week talking with engineers on various channels and at companies as part of my efforts to check ‘the pulse’ of the tech business: what’s happening and what’s changing. Writing The Pulse on Thursdays remains a personal highlight of my week.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Building more of our own software stack – on the side. </span></strong><span>One thing that AI has made easier is context switching between writing and building software. In the past six months, I’ve found myself building more parts of The Pragmatic Engineer backend stack, such as landing pages, through to API endpoints used for group subscriptions, refunds, and more. This year, I’ve probably built more software scratching my own itch at the publication than in previous years combined! </span><em><span>Of course, our software stack is not our top focus, but it’s a welcome distraction to work on.</span></em></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>A big theme for the rest of 2026 is how software engineering is changing: </span></strong><span>tools used for decades like IDEs are falling out of style, and processes long considered as best practices, like code reviews, are becoming optional. Of course, the biggest change is that we’re spending little to no time on typing out the code, which has never been the case since computing existed. Even before computer keyboards, programmers were writing programs on punch cards!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The good news is that we see that fundamentals still matter: many software engineers who were considered standout devs before seem to be even more in demand than ever, while picking up AI engineering appears to be easier than learning a new programming language.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Nonetheless, this change is destabilizing, fast-paced, and no one has figured out the “right” way to build software with AI. We’ll keep reporting on cases of teams and individuals that adapt well, while also paying attention to those things that don’t change, such as how teams, as a “core” unit of a business, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fbda43e6-b5fc-469e-8817-04a0058251d5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>seem to be just as important</span></a><span> at leading AI labs as they were pre-AI.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>3. How software engineering is changing: essay challenge</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To finish, we’re delighted to announce an essay challenge on the prescient topic of how software engineering is changing for professionals.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As mentioned, the pace of change in software engineering is only accelerating, with rapid industry-wide adoption of LLMs, AI tooling, and AI infrastructure. At The Pragmatic Engineer, we aim to cover much of what’s going on, and as part of that, we’d love to pull in more perspectives than what our team can cover alone.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Send us an article no more than 10,000 words long on how you see things changing at your startup or tech company. We’ll award $10,000 for the best essay we read, </span></strong><span>and other leading entries can win smaller prizes. Articles sent to us will be eligible for publication in future editions of the Pragmatic Engineer. </span><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/35a2a2e1-5efa-47ed-a0af-2015bf1ecd66?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>See more details here.</span></a></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So, tell us what’s new, different, better, or worse in your part of the tech industry since AI has been in your workflow.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Submissions close 4 October at midnight (PST). </span></strong><span>Read all </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/35a2a2e1-5efa-47ed-a0af-2015bf1ecd66?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>details of the challenge here,</span></a><span> and we look forward to reading your article about interesting and consequential changes in your part of the industry.</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Thank you for being a reader of The Pragmatic Engineer; we value your attention and support, and never take it for granted. With that, onwards to the next five, exciting years!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>– Gergely and The Pragmatic Engineer Team</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>Thanks for subscribing to </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIxMzczMzA1MSwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3ODgyODMyMTIsImV4cCI6MjEwMzg1OTIxMiwiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.aY0YAGvVQSji07wxjiF5VmJSeprkeGVqaYV5BsxTIOE?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">What Makes a Language Model Intelligent?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Large language models like ChatGPT are quite different from normal software programs. They don’t depend on typical if-else statements to decide what should happen next.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A large language model is essentially a very big pile of numbers called parameters or weights. These weights are the foundation of a language model’s intelligence. For reference, a model with 70 billion parameters means 70 billion numbers or weights. Each weight is normally stored in 16 bits, which is two bytes. Two bytes multiplied by 70 billion comes to 140 GB, which is basically considered the size of the model.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The weights are arranged into matrices. A single weight matrix is a grid, often something like 4096 by 4096. This comes to roughly 16.7 million numbers in a matrix. A 70 billion parameter model has hundreds of these matrices stacked across 80 or so layers.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Of course, weights in themselves aren’t the whole story behind a model’s capability. Multiple components work together to make a model intelligent. For example, the model needs an architecture like the Transformer to route data and perform attention. It also needs a context window that holds the prompt and everything generated during the conversation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">However, the architecture is made up of a few hundred lines of code. The prompt may be a few kilobytes. In contrast, the weights form the bulk of the language model. Without the proper weights, a language model cannot work as intended. The weights perform a bunch of tasks:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">They store patterns such as grammar, facts, and reasoning shortcuts.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Once the training is finished, the weights freeze into an immutable network of numerical values.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The weights decide how strongly one simulated neuron influences the next.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Running the model means pushing the input through these weight matrices until the next word comes out of the other end.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">One thing to keep in mind over here is that no single weight means anything on its own. If you opened a model file and looked at weight number N, you might see something like 0.0293. On either side of this number may be other numbers such as -0.0117, 0.004, -0.0862. On their own, each of these numbers hardly makes sense. The ability of the model is hidden in the relationships between the various weights. Think of it like a photograph where every pixel comes together to show something recognizable. Even if we modify every pixel’s brightness slightly, we can still make out the things in the picture. This is because the information isn’t sitting in one single place.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Following on from all this information, it is quite easy to figure out that to shrink a model, we’ve to somehow deal with these weights. And this is exactly where the techniques come into the picture. However, a couple of points can help us make better sense of the techniques to shrink a model:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Firstly, not all weights matter equally. Most of the weight values are close to zero and barely impact the final output. However, a small handful are large and produce a bigger impact.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Second, we can only judge a model based on its behaviour, not its internals.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Let us now look at the techniques.</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Three Techniques to Shrink the Model</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The techniques to shrink a model revolve around using fewer bits to store a weight or using fewer weights. There are three main techniques:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Storing Each Weight in Less Detail (Quantization): </strong><span>In this approach, we keep all the weights, but describe each one in a less precise manner. For example, two bytes become half a byte.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Removing Irrelevant Weights (Pruning): </strong><span>This approach involves finding the weights that contribute nothing and deleting them.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Building a Smaller Model to Mimic the Larger One (Knowledge Distillation): </strong><span>In this approach, we don’t touch the original model, but train a new, smaller model to behave in a similar way.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Going back to our photograph example, we can think of quantization as taking a picture with a cheaper camera that has a slightly lower resolution. Pruning is more like cutting away the blank edges of the photograph that might not be adding any value to the picture. Distillation can be thought of as paying a skilled painter to reproduce the picture at a quarter of the size.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The great part about all these techniques is that they can be stacked. For example, a model can be distilled by the lab that made it. It can be pruned by a research team. Lastly, it can be quantized by the user before it is loaded on a specific machine. In other words, stacking can make it possible to run a high-end large language model on normal consumer hardware.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Let us now look at each of these techniques in more detail.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Shrinking a Model by Packing Fewer Details</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The first technique to shrink a model is to pack fewer details for every weight. This technique is known as quantization.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Let’s say a particular weight might be stored as 0.02934517. This takes a lot of space, but in a 70 billion parameter model, it just happens to be one single weight. Whether it is stored as 0.02934517 or 0.029 makes almost no difference to the model’s output. In other words, a lot of storage is spent on precision that might not even be important.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Quantization is a technique that takes away this precision.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The first bit of quantization happens even before the model is shipped. During training, model weights are normally stored as 32-bit (4 bytes) floating-point numbers. This is also known as the FP32 format. Since training involves making millions of tiny adjustments to each weight, high precision is needed. But when the model is distributed, the precision is usually brought down to 16-bit float format, which is also known as FP16 or BF16.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">However, we can bring the precision down even further. To understand how, we need to first be clear about how a float value is actually built.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A floating-point number splits the bits into three parts: a sign, an exponent, and a mantissa. FP32 gives 1 bit to the sign, 8 bits to the exponent, and 23 bits to the mantissa. BF16, on the other hand, keeps all exponent bits and cuts the mantissa down to seven. This is basically the same range as FP32, but with less detail. For clarity, BF16 is slightly different from FP16, which gives the exponent only 5 bits and keeps more bits for the mantissa. BF16 has largely replaced FP16 in practice.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">An integer has an even greater difference. An 8-bit integer is a whole number from -128 to 127. A 4-bit integer is a whole number from -8 to 7. There is no exponent and no scale. In other words, converting a float into an integer not only causes a loss of precision, but also removes each weight’s scale.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);">1 - Mapping Ranges</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In the first step, we find out the minimum and maximum values of a data set and divide the total span into a fixed number of steps.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">To be clear, “the data set” is not the entire model. It’s just a small group of neighbouring weights. We can call it a block, and it should ideally be pretty small.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">For example, consider these eight weights: 0.021, -0.017, 0.004, -0.048, 0.011, 0.033, -0.006, 0.070. They span from -0.048 to 0.070. The largest value in either direction is 0.070. With 4 bits as our target precision, we can write whole numbers from -7 to 7. In other words, seven steps in each direction. Therefore, one step can be calculated as 0.070/7, which comes to 0.010.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);">2 - Rounding Values</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Instead of keeping a long decimal, each original number is rounded to the closest available step. To do so, we divide each weight by the step size and round it to the nearest whole number.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The table below auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">As you can see in the table, the right-hand column values are the ones that go into the model weights file eventually. Every entry here is a whole number between -7 and 7.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The original weights were floating-point numbers. Since a float carries its own scale, rounding off to engineers removes the precision as well as the scale of every weight. This scale has to be stored somewhere.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);">3 - Using a Scale Factor</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We need to keep track of the scale factor so that the compressed numbers can roughly reconstruct the original values when the model needs to read them.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In our example, the scale factor is the step size (0.010). It is stored once for the entire block. To recover a weight, we can multiply the stored integer by the scale factor.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So, for example, the stored weight of 2 is multiplied by 0.010 to arrive at the value 0.020. Of course, it is still different from the original value of 0.021, but the error is much less now. In other words, the model is still quite unchanged. We still have the same weights (with some error), the same matrices, and the same layers. However, it takes a lot less storage.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Shrinking the Model by Removing Unused Weights</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The second technique takes the opposite approach. Instead of trying to store each weight in less space, we delete some of them. This approach is known as pruning.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Pruning works because not all weights matter equally. Most of them have a value close to zero, such as 0.00004, -0.0011, and so on. These values are so small that they don’t impact the output in a meaningful manner. However, billions of such weights are produced during training. They are useful during the training phase, when the model is taking its original shape. You could think of them as driveways and service roads that are never used but still shown on a city map. Even if you remove them, they won’t have any impact on the people who are using this map to commute through the city.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The key decision with pruning is which weights to remove. The easiest approach uses the size. We sort the weights by how far they are from zero in either direction and delete the smallest ones. For example, if this approach helps prune 20% of the weights, it comes to around removing 14 billion weights from a 70 billion model.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">However, there is a flaw in this approach. The influence of a weight also depends on the pathway on which it sits. A better method runs a few hundred sample texts through the model first. It then monitors how large the typical inputs are to each weight. Based on this, each weight is assigned a final score.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There is another factor that should be considered when it comes to pruning. It is related to the mechanism of removing weights. There are two main approaches:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Setting to Zero: </strong><span>The first approach is to set the chosen weights to zero. This does minimal damage. But we end up with a matrix that is full of zeros in no particular pattern. The GPU still has to run the calculations with those entries.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Removing Structural Pieces: </strong><span>The second way is to remove the structural pieces such as an entire neuron, an attention head, or even a complete layer. This helps shrink the matrix. But this is also a coarser approach. Removing one neuron might mean removing every weight attached to it. Some of these weights may be important, but they are also deleted. In other words, the overall damage to the model is greater in this approach.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">See the diagram below that shows the two approaches:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table rarely a complete solution. It is much better to use pruning in combination with some other techniques.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Shrinking the Model by Mimicking Behaviour</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The third technique to shrink the model creates a new smaller model.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In this technique, we take the big model. It is called the teacher model. Next, we build a new model from scratch using the same architecture. However, it has fewer layers and smaller matrices. For example, a model with 7 billion weights instead of 70 billion. We call this new model the student model.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The student model starts its life with random weights that are meaningless. This model goes through the training process, but we don’t use the raw text from other sources on the internet. Instead, the student model is trained on the teacher’s behaviour. This involves feeding both the student and the teacher the same input and pushing the student model towards producing output closer to what the teacher model produced.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This technique is known as knowledge distillation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This type of approach might appear counterintuitive. But it works because of how the model works internally.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When a model predicts the next word, it doesn’t just produce a single word. It produces a probability score for every word in its vocabulary. For example, given the sentence “the cat sat on the…”, the teacher model might say “mat 41%”, “floor 12%”, “couch 9%”, and so on. In an ordinary training approach, the student model only receives the correct answer. But during distillation, the student model receives the whole distribution of probable answers. In other words, the student model learns that “couch” was also a pretty sensible guess, but maybe the word “purple” was quite absurd.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">See the diagram below:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Think of knowledge distillation like a teacher evaluating a paper, but instead of just putting ticks and crosses, the teacher writes in the margins to give a better idea to the student about the mistakes they might have made. The second approach helps the student learn faster</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Of course, distillation involves training at scale. A huge teacher model runs over enormous amounts of data, which requires datacentre-level resources. For a developer, it involves downloading the smaller student model that can run on less demanding hardware.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Does Shrinking Damage the Model’s Intelligence?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Shrinking a model definitely reduces its overall intelligence, but usually only a tiny bit. Think of it like a trade-off between the model’s physical size and its mental sharpness.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Each of these techniques has an impact on the model’s intelligence:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Quantization: </strong><span>It makes the weights less precise. The model can lose its ability to understand extreme nuance. It might forget highly specific facts, or its tone might sound slightly less natural. Many of the changes depend on how far you go on the quantization scale. For example, shifting from 32-bit to 8-bit causes almost no noticeable change in intelligence. But pushing down to 4-bit or even lower might have a huge impact.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Pruning: </strong><span>It reduces the model’s ability to handle complex, multi-step logic. However, only trimming the idle pathways does not have a big negative impact on intelligence. Only when we aggressively prune the deeper pathways do we end up making the model dumb.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Knowledge Distillation: </strong><span>The smaller student model may lack original problem-solving skills. It can perfectly mimic the big teacher model’s style, but a completely new logical puzzle might throw it off if the same wasn’t explicitly taught by the teacher model.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Conclusion</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In this article, we’ve looked at the various techniques of shrinking a large language model in detail.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Shrinking a language model without any plan can cause a loss of intelligence. Therefore, various techniques follow different approaches to ensure that the model takes less space without losing its original capabilities drastically. Here are the key points to remember:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Quantization involves storing each weight in fewer bits.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Pruning deletes the weights and pathways that contribute the least.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Distillation does not modify the original model, but involves a large teacher model training a smaller student model.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Ultimately, choosing a technique or combination of them depends on the overall goals that the language model needs to fulfill.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>References:</strong></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><li item.title: Coaching Questions That Work
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.content:encoded:
Coaching Questions That Work

Dan Rockwell

Some questions focus on situations. What happened? What’s wrong? What do you want? Begin with situations, but don’t park there. Coaching questions turn attention to the person. (1) What did you notice about yourself in that meeting? (2) What was going on for you when she said that? (3) What do you make of your reaction?

#Management Coaching Tips
item.description: Coaching Questions That Work

item.title: Modern Engineering Values
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.content:encoded:
Modern Engineering Values

Christoph Nakazawa

“I’ve been trying to wrap my head around engineering values and principles that matter for 2026 and beyond that will help individuals and organizations move faster. Looking at my engineering workflow it feels like on one hand everything changed, and on the other, not that much."

#Management AI
item.description: Modern Engineering Values

item.title: How To Figure Out Your Next Career Move
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.content:encoded:
How To Figure Out Your Next Career Move

Cliff Maxwell

“In this post, I’ll help you answer six fundamental questions that will instill confidence and focus anytime you are navigating a transition at work. Each question comes with exercises and tools to help you build understanding.”

#CareerGrowth Guide
item.description: How To Figure Out Your Next Career Move

item.title: Responsibility Is Taken Before It Is Given
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.content:encoded:
Responsibility Is Taken Before It Is Given

Lalit Maganti

“To get promoted as a software engineer in Big Tech, you generally need to show “ownership” of a product or area. This means being responsible for it and deciding what should happen over time.”

#Staff+ CareerGrowth
item.description: Responsibility Is Taken Before It Is Given

item.title: Bug Blindness
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.content:encoded:
Bug Blindness

Dan Luu

“I used to wonder why I see so many more bugs than most people. I easily observe hundreds to thousands of bugs per week and nothing seems to work, but most people I talk to don't see anything like this. For a long time, I thought this had something to do with how I use computers but, over time, I've realized that it's mostly that people are hitting the same bugs and don't notice.”

#CodeQuality Debugging
item.description: Bug Blindness

item.title: Three Mistakes Of New AI Teams
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.content:encoded:
Three Mistakes Of New AI Teams

Doug Turnbull

“A surprising amount of the pain I see on AI teams looks very much like what budding search teams in the 2010s went through. Admittedly this gives me a biased perspective, but perhaps a useful one.”

#Management AI
item.description: Three Mistakes Of New AI Teams

item.title: How To Write An Effective Software Design Document
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.content:encoded:
How To Write An Effective Software Design Document

Michael Lynch

“I’ve written design docs as a developer at Google, Microsoft, and within my own companies. The specifics vary, but the underlying principles remain the same. A design doc should articulate the hard problems you’re solving and help your teammates give you feedback. Below, I share my approach to creating effective design docs and explain what belongs in a design doc and what does not.”

#KnowledgeManagement Guide
item.description: How To Write An Effective Software Design Document

rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When you type a follow-up question into an AI chat and press Enter, nothing happens for a second or two. Then the answer appears in a quick succession of words. It appears much faster than what the initial pause indicated.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This pause is not dead time. In a typical LLM, a single message passes through roughly a dozen distinct stages before a reply starts to appear. Two very different kinds of computing work happen in the background to make this possible. Some key points about this journey are as follows:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The model never receives the message as it was typed.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It has no memory of the conversation. The history on screen is rebuilt from scratch every turn.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It shares a machine with strangers, and the group it lands in can affect the reply.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Once a word has been sent, the model cannot take it back.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we are going to look at this entire journey in detail. Here’s what we will cover:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How is the input to the model assembled?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Why is every input message to the model independent?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Performing safety checks on the input</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How does the model understand the words?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 across multiple conversations?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: guardrails</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>How the Input to the Model is Assembled?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The first key point to understand is that the sentence typed into the box is not the exact thing that reaches the model. What reaches the model is a document assembled around that sentence before the request is sent.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This document contains several ingredients, which are as follows:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A system prompt, which is a block of instructions written by the LLM provider. These instructions tell the model how to behave during the conversation.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Definitions of any available tools, describing what each one does and what inputs it accepts.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Anything stored as memory from earlier sessions.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Documents pulled from a knowledge base in cases where retrieval is the key.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The full conversation so far.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Finally, the new message.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The process of deciding what goes into this document in what order, and what gets left out, is a discipline in its own right known as context engineering. It is not a simple matter of filling a container. Models have a finite attention budget, and every token added draws it down.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Accuracy degrades as input grows longer, even on tasks that are quite simple. The decline is gradual. A longer prompt does not break anything outright, but the underlying precision falls away.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The approach used towards this discipline of context engineering leads to scenarios where two products built on the same underlying model, given word-for-word the same question, return different answers. The model might be identical, but the document wrapped around the question is not.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Different providers also differ in when they gather the material for the document. Some retrieve everything up front. Others hand the model lightweight references, file paths, or stored queries, and let it pull in what it needs while working. The first is faster, and the second wastes fewer tokens on material that might be irrelevant.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Why is Every Input Message to the Model Independent?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The models are stateless by design, meaning they retain nothing between messages. Each request arrives with no recollection of what came before. In other words, the conversation that we see on screen is reconstructed and resent in full every single time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The maths related to this gets quite uncomfortable. Consider a product with a thousand-token system prompt, where each message and each reply runs about a hundred tokens.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Turn one processes about 1,100 tokens.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Turn two processes about 1,300.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>By turn three, we have about 1,500.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>By turn twenty, we might have closer to 4,900.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Though output tokens cost more than input tokens, input volume compounds on every turn while output stays roughly constant. This is why input usually dominates the total spend in any conversational product despite being the cheaper of the two.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The naive approach is to resend everything, but it works well only for short exchanges. Once the conversation outgrows the context window, it stops being viable. There are a few refinements that can help:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The simplest one drops the oldest turns. This doesn’t cost much in latency and loses whatever was dropped.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A more careful version summarises the conversation and restarts with the summary. This helps preserve decisions and open questions while discarding things like raw tool output that nobody needs to see twice.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The third one stores material outside the context window entirely and retrieves it when it becomes relevant.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Long chats get slower and more expensive because every turn has to reprocess everything that came before it. The assistant eventually loses details because some details get trimmed or condensed. Also, editing an earlier message rewrites what the model treats as having happened.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Performing Safety Checks on the Input</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Before the generation of the answer starts, the assembled document passes through a separate, smaller model trained to judge whether the request should proceed. Think of it like a safety layer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The key point to note here is the separation in the design. This safety layer is a distinct system from the assistant, which means that it can be retrained, tuned, and monitored on its own schedule without any impact on the main model. It can also do more than permit or block. It can route a request elsewhere, log it, or escalate it for review.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This separation costs time, which is evident in the pause that precedes the answer. Published figures from one production system put an earlier generation of these classifiers at roughly a 24 percent increase in compute, alongside a 0.38 percentage point rise in refusals of harmless requests. Both numbers were high enough to limit how widely the approach could be deployed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The replacement uses a cascade, where a very cheap validation is used to screen all traffic. Only flagged conversations are sent to the expensive classifier. This brings the overhead down to around one percent and refusals of harmless queries to 0.05 percent.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>How the Model Understands the Words?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the next step, the document gets converted into the units the model works with. These units are known as tokens, which are chunks of text that are generally smaller than a word but larger than a letter. Common words are often represented as a single piece, while rarer ones break into fragments.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most modern systems build these chunks starting from raw bytes rather than characters, which guarantees that text in any writing system can be represented. As a working figure, one token averages around three-quarters of an English word.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are two consequences due to this:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The first is that cost and capacity vary by language. Research presented at a major machine learning conference measured the same text across translations and found token counts differing by as much as fifteen times. This is not just a matter of billing. Higher token counts also mean higher cost, slower processing, and less content fitting inside the same context window. Therefore, speakers of some languages get materially less usable space for an identical document.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The second is that character-level questions can get awkward. Counting how many times a specific letter appears in a word means looking inside the chunks.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>How the Model is Shared Across Multiple Conversations</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>No model sits idle waiting for a request to arrive. In a typical setup, the token sequence joins a queue, and then a batch of other people’s requests running on the same hardware.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why the need for this batching?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is because while modern accelerators have enormous computing capacity, a great deal of their memory bandwidth is spent on loading model parameters rather than performing useful work on any single request. Loading those parameters once and applying them across many requests simultaneously is what makes serving affordable.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The naive version of batching collects a group of requests, runs them together, and waits for the entire group to finish before starting the next. This works when every response is a similar length. However, chat responses are not of similar length. Some might finish in ten words while others can run for a thousand. Therefore, the hardware might be partly idle waiting on the longest one.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A better approach schedules a request at the level of individual generation steps. As soon as one response finishes, a new request takes its slot rather than waiting for the group to clear. Benchmarks have demonstrated throughput improvements of up to 23 times over the naive method. Also, this approach improved median response times as well.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There is another strange consequence of sharing resources to generate answers. Identical requests can return different answers even with randomness switched off. This happens because the numerical operations involved are sensitive to the number of requests being processed together. In other words, sending the same prompt a thousand times to a large model might end up with 80 distinct completions.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Prefill And Decode</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is the point where the pause and the typing separate.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Producing a reply happens in two phases with opposite characteristics</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The first reads the entire assembled document in one pass. Every input token is processed alongside every other. Therefore, this work runs in parallel and pushes the hardware on raw computation. This phase is the pause.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The second phase produces output one token at a time. Each token depends on the one before it, so none of it can be parallelised. The limiting factor here is memory speed rather than computation, since every step reads back everything that has been computed so far. This phase is the steady typing.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The first phase scales with input length. This means a conversation twenty turns deep takes measurably longer to begin than the same question asked in a fresh window. The second phase runs at roughly the same rate regardless. In other words, the pause time increases as a chat continues, but the typing speed barely changes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These two halves are measured separately:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Time to first token covers everything up to the first visible output, including the queue wait time.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Time per output token covers the gap between each token after that.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Total response time is calculated as approximately the first plus the second multiplied by the length of the reply.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A single very long input can delay generation for every other request in the batch. Splitting that long input into chunks and interleaving them with ongoing generation keeps everyone else’s output flowing. The trade-off is a slightly longer wait for the request that was split.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure
