Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Caching the Existing Calculations</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why is the second phase quick at all, given that every token has to account for everything before it?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is because that work is not repeated. The calculations produced while reading the input are stored and reused at each subsequent step.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This stored state is large. For a model in the 70-billion-parameter range holding an 8000-token conversation, it can run to a few gigabytes per request. A bunch of concurrent conversations can exceed the memory of an entire high-end accelerator before the model weights are even accounted for. In other words, the number of users a machine can serve is usually limited by this conversation state rather than by the model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Early serving systems reserved one contiguous block of memory sized for the longest response a request might produce. A widely cited systems paper measured that cost and found sixty to eighty percent of the memory going unused. The fix involved a technique that operating systems have used for decades. This technique is to split the storage into small fixed-size blocks provided on demand. In this case, the wastage dropped below 4% and throughput improved by 2-4 times.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The same idea extends across turns. Since every message resends the same opening block, the computed prefix can be kept stored and reused instead of recalculated. Providers price this explicitly, with cached portions of a prompt often costing around a tenth of the normal input rate. Cache entries typically expire after a few minutes unless they are refreshed due to continued use.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is why prompt structure follows a rule that stable content belongs at the top and changing content at the bottom. This is because a prefix that changes on every request cannot be reused effectively.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Streaming And Guardrails</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are two things that happen during the response phase of the conversation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Text appears word by word because it is sent as it is produced instead of being held until finished. This improves the perceived speed. Ordinary reading runs at something like six tokens per second, and production systems generate comfortably faster than that. Streaming lets reading start almost immediately instead of after a blank wait.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The second part is around safety checks. Many products run a safety check on output as well as input. A check of that kind has to read the finished response before it can judge it. By that point, the response is already on screen, and it is not possible to retract a word that has been displayed. Holding the response back until the check completes removes the benefit of streaming entirely.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There is no settled answer to this yet. Some systems use guards designed to evaluate output as it streams, token by token. Others read the model’s internal state during generation rather than waiting for finished text, which is cheap enough to apply.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>How Tools Are Run?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Everything so far describes a straight line from pressing Enter to the response. Once tools are involved, this straight line turns into a loop.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A model does not search the web, read a file, or query a database. It produces text requesting that one of those things happen, using the tool definitions included in the assembled document. The surrounding application recognises the request, carries it out, and puts the result back into the context.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The result is new input, which means the entire sequence runs again from the beginning. It is reassembled, checked, tokenized, queued, and run through both generation phases again. For example, a reply that involved three web searches made several complete round trips through everything described here. This accounts for why those replies take noticeably longer than ordinary ones.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The cost compounds sharply. Across a session of twenty calls with growing context, the earliest messages are paid for twenty times over. A two-thousand-token instruction block sent across two hundred calls accounts for four hundred thousand input tokens on its own, before any of the actual work.</span></p><div rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The two seconds of delay now have a clear picture that we can understand.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A fraction went to network travel and authentication.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A larger fraction went to assembling the document and gathering whatever memory and reference material the product uses.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A small fraction went to the input safety check, which cascaded designs now keep near one percent of compute.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Tokenization was negligible.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Some unknown portion of the delay went to queueing, depending entirely on concurrency.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>In a long conversation, the largest fraction goes to reading the input, which is the reason for the initial pause growing as the chat continues.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Everything after that was the second phase, running at a rate that had barely changed since the first message.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The model receives a constructed document in which the typed message is the smallest component. It has no memory, so the conversation is rebuilt from scratch. This is why long chats slow down, cost more, and lose details.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>References:</span></p><ul item.title: Git at any scale
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Git at any scale

Vicent Martí

26 minutes by Vicent Martí Git hosting is hard because Git was designed for distributed use, but most teams rely on a central server. Early approaches like distributed filesystems failed due to Git's random read patterns across packfiles. GitHub's Spokes system improved things with consistent replication using three-phase commit, but struggles with large monorepos and scale.
item.description: Git at any scale

item.title: Regressive JPEGs
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Regressive JPEGs

Maurycyz

4 minutes by Maurycyz JPEG files can store image data across multiple scans, loading low-quality previews first and refining them over time. By stripping out certain markers and combining multiple images into one file, each scan can overwrite the previous image data, creating a crude animation. Browsers stop rendering after around 90 scans, so each frame must use a minimal single DC-only scan. The result is a working video packed into one image file, with playback speed controlled entirely by network delay.
item.description: Regressive JPEGs

item.title: How Cloudflare saved 100 terabytes of memory
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How Cloudflare saved 100 terabytes of memory

Sebastiaan Neuteboom

12 minutes by Sebastiaan Neuteboom Cloudflare's DNS platform stores over 250 billion cache entries, so even single-byte savings matter at scale. Five memory optimizations cut the per-entry footprint by 56%, freeing around 100 terabytes of RAM across the fleet. Changes included dropping unused capacity fields, storing record data as raw bytes in one contiguous buffer, and inferring repeated domain names instead of storing them. Beyond saving memory, insert throughput rose 43% and lookup latency fell 19%.
item.description: How Cloudflare saved 100 terabytes of memory

item.title: A quick look at zero-knowledge proofs
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
A quick look at zero-knowledge proofs

Max Bernstein

12 minutes by Max Bernstein Zero-knowledge proofs let one party convince another that it has solved a hard problem, without revealing the solution itself. Graph 3-coloring is a classic example: the prover shuffles colors, locks them in hashed boxes, and lets the verifier check one random edge per round. Repeating this many times makes cheating statistically very unlikely. The same idea extends to other hard problems like Sudoku, or anything reducible to a known NP-complete problem.
item.description: A quick look at zero-knowledge proofs

item.title: Agentic code quality
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Agentic code quality

Addy Osmani

9 minutes by Addy Osmani AI agents can write massive amounts of code, making traditional human code review impossible to scale. Quality now depends on automated constraints like unit tests, security scans, and complexity checks that act as gatekeepers throughout the pipeline. These constraints create back-pressure, catching bad output early before it reaches production. The key is placing tight constraints where quality matters most, while relaxing them elsewhere to keep delivery fast. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: Agentic code quality

item.title: How fast is .NET 11 Runtime Async?
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How fast is .NET 11 Runtime Async?

Kai Sawano

Runtime Async is a new asynchronous execution model arriving in .NET 11. Instead of having the C# compiler eagerly turn every async method into a state machine, it preserves the original asynchronous control flow until runtime, where the JIT can process and optimize it directly.
item.description: How fast is .NET 11 Runtime Async?

item.title: Garbage collection fundamentals in .NET
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Garbage collection fundamentals in .NET

Abdul Rahman

.NET developers never manually free memory. The runtime's Garbage Collector handles it automatically by tracking which objects are still in use and reclaiming the rest. It does this through three steps: marking live objects, sweeping dead ones, and compacting survivors to close memory gaps. Knowing how the stack, heap, and GC work together helps you write code that uses less memory and puts less pressure on the runtime.
item.description: Garbage collection fundamentals in .NET

item.title: Eventual consistency explained
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Eventual consistency explained

Irina Scurtu

Distributed systems often show stale data briefly after an update. This is not a bug but a deliberate trade-off called eventual consistency, where systems prioritize staying available over guaranteeing every node agrees instantly. DNS, CDNs, and read replicas all work this way already. The real risk is not choosing this trade-off, but failing to design for it and discovering the gap when users notice their data has vanished.
item.description: Eventual consistency explained

item.title: What's new with CoreCLR GC handles
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
What's new with CoreCLR GC handles

Austin Wise

.NET 9 and 10 brought major updates to GC handles in CoreCLR. Four new generic handle types were added as public APIs, offering better type safety, cleaner code, and a modest performance boost over the old GCHandle struct. Two new internal handle types were also introduced. Weak interior pointer handles track object locations across GC moves, while cross-reference handles solve a tricky problem of coordinating object lifetimes between the .NET and Java garbage collectors when running MAUI apps on Android.
item.description: What's new with CoreCLR GC handles

item.title: Finding the total number of processors on a machine with .NET
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Finding the total number of processors on a machine with .NET

Andrew Lock

Modern .NET has no built-in way to get the total CPU count of a host machine. Environment.ProcessorCount returns processor count available to the process, not the host total. The only solution is to call native system APIs on Windows and macOS, and read a system file on Linux. Each platform needs its own code, then a shared helper ties them together based on the current OS. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: Finding the total number of processors on a machine with .NET

item.title: How Much Can You Hold Before It Breaks?
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How Much Can You Hold Before It Breaks?

Steve Huynh

“My optimal approach for a person has two parts, and each one addresses one of those problems. First, we want to pick a single piece of high-priority, high-impact work and protect it, so that whatever else happens, the thing that matters gets done. Second, we want to cut the number of things in flight down to as few as we can stand, so the switching costs are minimized. We want one thing at the top, and as little as possible underneath it.”

#Management Productivity

item.title: How We Saved 100 Terabytes Of Memory By Optimizing 1.1.1.1’s DNS Cache
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How We Saved 100 Terabytes Of Memory By Optimizing 1.1.1.1’s DNS Cache

Sebastiaan Neuteboom

“Five successive changes to how cache entries are stored in memory cut the per-entry footprint by over 50%. Across our fleet, these changes freed up roughly 100 terabytes of memory, equivalent to the amount of RAM in 130 of our Gen 13 servers. The cache also got faster. Insert throughput rose 43% and lookup latency dropped 19%, as fewer allocations and better memory locality meant we did not trade speed for space.”

#CaseStudy Scale Performance

Symbol';font-weight: 400;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em><span>The Pulse is a series covering events, insights, and trends within Big Tech and startups.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today, we cover:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Did Meta really decide to reduce team sizes by 60% because of AI? </span></strong><span>An in-depth report by Reuters details how Meta’s leadership decided to slash team sizes by 60%, hatching plans in January to execute the social media giant’s largest-ever layoffs. But Mark Zuckerberg changed his mind at the last second, and now the company is stuck with all-time low morale, a wave of resignations, and its prized culture turning mercenary. Analysis.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>More thoughts on Ramp’s in-house AI infra. </span></strong><span>Building AI tools in-house is akin to an “internal bootcamp” for AI engineering, which probably justifies the exercise at most tech companies.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Industry Pulse. </span></strong><span>GitHub’s load increase is speeding up, Stripe acquires OpenRouter, Ramp launches Ramp Router in public, a career “double boomerang”, App Store revenue drops for the first time ever at Apple – and what is a bug?</span></p></li></ol><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>1. Did Meta really decide to reduce team sizes by 60% because of AI?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Two months ago, I asked </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c59fa734-2c08-44e5-804e-4d8248990a27?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>why Meta appeared intent on destroying its engineering organization</span></a><span>, at a time when the social media giant was reporting record revenue and profits. The question was raised after the company did two unexpected things:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Laid off 10% of staff. </span></strong><span>Executed large layoffs in May, with circa 10% of engineers shown the door.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Moved 20-30% of engineers to AI training. </span></strong><span>At around the same time, infra and product teams lost a further 20-30% of their engineers, who were reassigned to data labeling work for AI training.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The outcome of that period was low morale and a string of embarrassing outages, including </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c6bd27ae-ebc6-4f23-9986-416bf82bbd25?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>a “zero auth password reset” outage on Instagram</span></a><span>, where anyone’s account – including that of former US president Barack Obama – could be taken over just by asking the AI bot to replace Obama’s email with a different one.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now, thanks to reporting by Reuters, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b72af0c2-0078-4c14-a01b-8b2f4c0ca6d9?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>new details</span></a><span> have emerged about a plan for much larger layoffs, which eventually did not go ahead. The news report is pretty damning, and I want to get into what the planned AI job cuts reveal about Meta at this point in its history, what Zuckerberg might have been thinking, and what it could mean for other tech companies.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Making Meta “AI-native:” Project Organization Transformation</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The plan was formed in January of this year. As </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b72af0c2-0078-4c14-a01b-8b2f4c0ca6d9?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>per Reuters:</span></a></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“In January, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his top lieutenants gathered for their annual leadership retreat at his Hawaii compound. There they hatched a radical plan to reimagine work at the social-media giant in the age of artificial intelligence.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Code-named Project OT – short for Organization Transformation – the plan envisioned an “AI native” future for the owner of Facebook and Instagram. AI would take over much of the daily work performed by thousands of human employees. Virtual workers would be overseen inside Meta by smaller, “talent-dense” cadres of human staffers, according to one internal planning document reviewed by Reuters and three people familiar with the project.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The idea was that many existing teams could be reduced by 60% in their size through layoffs and reallocation of workers to other parts of the business. Underpinning this was the assumption that AI would enable these smaller teams to operate as well as before. HR at the social media giant projected that the project would involve a bigger layoff than happened in 2022-2023, when 25% of staff were let go. The new plan was to do one layoff+restructuring in May, and another in November.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>I suspect a 30-40% company-wide layoff was planned.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But at the last minute, something changed. From </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b72af0c2-0078-4c14-a01b-8b2f4c0ca6d9?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Reuters</span></a><span> (emphasis mine):</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“But on the night of May 19, just hours before the first layoff wave, Zuckerberg blinked. Meta laid off 10% of its employees the next day, but it called off planning for the November cuts, according to one internal document reviewed by Reuters.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>By then, Meta employees were in open revolt, convinced that the company’s AI transformation initiatives were partly aimed at replacing them</span></strong><span>.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Reuters report shows those employees were right: Meta’s AI initiatives were indeed aimed at laying off as many of them as possible, without changing overall productivity!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Even though these 60% cuts did not happen, some teams had 30-40% cuts and struggled to cope with their workloads. It also didn’t help that I talked with teams whose key engineers got reassigned to AI labeling: those were devs with critical domain knowledge that was lost after they left.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Why did Meta want 60% smaller teams?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You must assume that a company like Meta acts rationally overall, and on that basis it’s worth figuring out what the rationale might be in the case of ‘Project OT’. The article offers a hint: executives at the company had been captivated by “AI-native” businesses in Asia, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b72af0c2-0078-4c14-a01b-8b2f4c0ca6d9?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Reuters</span></a><span> claimed:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Meta executives, including Chief Data Officer Alex Schultz and Head of Product Naomi Gleit, visited Asia last year and admired how startups there had built their organizational charts around AI, according to three people familiar with the trips. Meta executives also commissioned their own research into how AI startups were organized and set up pilot projects to determine what being “AI native” would mean at the company, according to one source familiar with the research and internal documents describing the pilots.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And indeed, in February Meta experimented with “AI-native pods” as </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9651d467-949b-4917-b28b-33b1712f6f4b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>reported in The Pulse</span></a><span> at the time. The presentation obtained by Reuters shows leadership intended to achieve 60% reductions in team size with small, 3-5 person, “AI-native” teams doing the work of what had been between 10 and 20 people:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td href="https://substack.com/redirect/3a5019f7-d8b3-413b-a361-e825f555bdfc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/4101a302-8ebd-44c4-906e-367d8be75b59_1242x892.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":892,"width":1242,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="image-caption" style="box-sizing: content-box;color: rgb(119,119,119);font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>Internal presentation at Meta about “traditional” vs “AI-native” teams. Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b72af0c2-0078-4c14-a01b-8b2f4c0ca6d9?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>Reuters</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And Meta is probably on the money that engineering teams are becoming a lot smaller at startups – and “AI-native companies” are also getting smaller, by size. But those are companies that are </span><em><span>growing </span></em><span>slower, without ever having done mass layoffs. Meanwhile, Meta seems to have wanted to become smaller not organically, and over time, but with a brutal layoff and sudden reassignments, in the span of a year, ignoring the impact such a sudden change would have on the company, teams, and employees.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Downsides of tiny teams</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In theory, a smaller team could work better with less communication overhead and quicker decision-making, so there are cases where the upsides of a small team outweigh the downsides. For example, if there’s a small team of very senior folks with sound judgment skills, outstanding domain knowledge, and who don’t care about growing professionally anymore. However, such expected gains would come with several real costs, mostly associated with losing so much experience and skill:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Domain knowledge:</span></strong><span> A lot of personal domain knowledge is suddenly gone.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Redundancy</span></strong><span>: what if someone is on vacation, another is sick, and the other has an urgent appointment that cannot be moved? In a 10-20 person team, it would mean business pretty much as usual. But in a 3-5 person team, you’re down to two people doing everything!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Capacity for oncall:</span></strong><span> a healthy oncall schedule needs 6+ engineers if every alert is to be taken </span><em><span>seriously</span></em><span> by an engineer whose main focus is oncall and systems stability.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Lack of “slack time”: </span></strong><span>Innovation often comes from having time to focus on other work, instead of putting out fires. A bigger team naturally creates more “slack time” that can be used for other things, like university recruiting events, writing engineering blog posts, working with other teams on building things together, etc. In contrast, one that’s stretched thin with a maximum of 5 people or less gets almost zero slack time.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Professional growth: </span></strong><span> engineers pair with more devs and get more feedback on larger teams. There’s more discussion and generally more opportunities to learn.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Judgment</span></strong><span>: For honing one’s skills, there’s more experience and mentoring to be gained in larger teams than on small, “AI-native” ones where engineers spend the most time with AI. How good is AI’s judgment, anyway?</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Is Zuckerberg’s worst fear being out-executed by a startup?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With Meta’s business posting record revenue and profits, and facing zero pressure to radically change how the social media giant operates, it’s worth asking why the social media giant was in a rush to get to 60% smaller teams. It would be a significant challenge for the 75,000-strong company, unlike for some small startups with under 100 people.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>My hunch is that Mark Zuckerberg is paranoid about a startup which executes better and that could “destroy” Meta at some point. After all, this is exactly what Facebook did, back in the day. In 2008, Myspace was the king of social networks and Facebook was only a small player – yet three years later, Myspace’s usership had collapsed. The Huffington Post </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3056e398-db8b-45ee-be08-8db5a55844af?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>analyzed the collapse</span></a><span> (emphasis mine) at the time:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Just over three years ago, in the spring of 2008, Myspace was top dog. That April, the upstart Facebook grabbed the lead and never looked back. In those three years, Myspace has lost over forty million unique visitors per month, lost both co-founders, laid off the vast majority of its staff and more generally, has diminished to a cluttered afterthought of the power it once was.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span><span>In an interview with Businessweek, former founder Chris DeWolfe blamed Myspace’s overenthusiasm and underexecution on the product side for many of the site’s problems.</span><br><br><span>“We tried to create every feature in the world and said, ‘okay, we can do it, why should we let a third party do it?’” said DeWolfe. “We should have picked five to ten key features that we totally focused on and let other people innovate on everything else.”</span></span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Instead, Myspace unleashed a slew of products that were buggy and dysfunctional and confusing and alienating to users, and which couldn’t keep pace with Facebook’s own progress.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“[Myspace failed] to execute the product development,”</span></strong><span> former Facebook president, Sean Parker, said in a recent interview. “</span><strong><span>They weren’t successful in iterating and evolving the product enough</span></strong><span>, it was basically this junk heap of bad design that persisted for many, many years. There was a period of time where, if they had just copied Facebook rapidly, I think they would have been Facebook. The network effects, the scale effects were enormous. There was so much power there.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ironically, Myspace’s desperate attempts to recoup its former success came in the form of imitating Facebook, a site it’d once tried to set itself apart from. It adopted the news feed Facebook had popularized, and neatened up the site itself in a way that also suggested it was taking visual cues from Zuckerberg’s page. In November 2010, the site integrated with Facebook Connect, calling it “Mashup with Facebook.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Myspace had twice as many employees as Facebook (around 800 at the time), and grew faster than Facebook in 2003-2007. But Facebook out-executed Myspace by being more nimble and more focused. Zuck’s business has seemed to try and be like a startup in its nimbleness of execution since then, not wanting to give anyone the chance to disrupt it like it did to Myspace.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>If so, is Zuckerberg being paranoid about a similar threat to Meta today? </span></strong><span>Myspace was far from being the decades-old company that Meta has become! It was only founded six months before Facebook and got more traction in its early years, but fumbled execution as it grew. In contrast, Meta is today the tenth largest publicly traded company by market capitalization in the world, with a $1.4T valuation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Then again, maybe there’s cause for Zuckerberg to be paranoid: Anthropic, only five years old, with one twentieth of the workforce Meta has, and might be going public at a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c18e8651-568c-4fed-b9b3-a1ffec853143?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>close to $2T valuation</span></a><span> as soon as October. Anthropic is not a direct competitor to Meta – it’s not a social media company – but Zuckerberg clearly sees AI companies as a form of competition to Meta’s business model. After all, every minute a person spends chatting with an AI chatbot like ChatGPT, they’re not spending it on Instagram, Facebook or WhatsApp.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Maybe this is one reason for the forced reallocation of 20-30% of software engineers to do data labeling and other training tasks on Meta’s AI model. To Meta’s credit, Muse Spark is a pretty capable model, and while it is behind the likes of GPT-5.6 and Opus 5, it’s already ahead of Google’s AI models – no small feat!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Most valuable assets: people or GPUs?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let’s consider how Zuckerberg might respond if he perceives these things:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Smaller teams execute better with AI</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>These smaller teams can out-execute Meta: like Anthropic has done with AI model development</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>There’s a danger that Anthropic and OpenAI could do with Meta, like Facebook did with Myspace</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One approach would be to lay off 20-40% of the workforce, but there are consequences:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Workers reject being treated like “cattle”. </span></strong><span>Meta’s “Project Organization Transformation” assumed that productivity would go up if teams greatly shrank and used AI tools. But would this happen? When people realize 60% of their colleagues were reassigned or let go because of AI, they might look further ahead: will another 60% be laid off at some point for the same reasons? Work could start to resemble the “Hunger Games”, where people have job security only until the next model release.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Engineering is officially a cost center, not a profit center. </span></strong><span>We previously covered how most tech companies </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/339786df-1d28-44dc-a163-92571278544f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>treat engineering as a “profit center</span></a><span>” that generates revenue, and is therefore worth investing in. At such companies, engineers are treated well; not just financially, but in how leadership treats them as a key part of the business. At Meta, software engineering became a cost center pretty much overnight!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Mission, what mission? </span></strong><span>People often join a company and stay motivated over time due to a mission they personally believe in. What if next year’s mission is to lay off as many people as possible, or to survive future culls? That doesn’t seem like a very inspiring mission.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>What makes Meta worth its $1.4T valuation, anyway? </span></strong><span>Meta generates $228B annual revenue, and $68B profit (net income). The company is valued 6x its annual revenue and 20x its annual profit because investors bet its revenue and profits will continue to rise. But how does this happen? It’s via advertising, innovation, and launching new products.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>How do you promote and enable the innovation which creates the products of tomorrow? “AI-pilled” folks might look to the technology as it gets more capable. But AI-native companies which can innovate will achieve results faster, putting Meta behind the likes of Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceX.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Or you develop a smaller workforce full of entrepreneurs and innovators, who will invent these new approaches and products. Basically, the best employees need to be motivated to stick around longer term.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>That’s the problem with large layoffs; they prompt </span></strong><em><strong><span>precisely</span></strong></em><strong><span> the best employees to quit to join competitors, or launch their own businesses. </span></strong><span>This happened with Meta’s previous layoffs, as covered two weeks ago in ‘</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ce61326d-18e7-4ed1-9d87-4b6c40d084e1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Meta’s self-inflicted resignation wave’.</span></a><span> When leadership declares the ‘bottom’ 20-40% of the workforce is redundant, then very few people feel safe, and key members of Meta’s engineering organization will get offers from AI labs and Big Tech rivals. This is the “resignation wave” in action, all started by May’s layoffs and forced reassignments.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" layoffs and even larger forced reassignments</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Knowingly or not, Meta creates an internal “mercenary” culture, where more of the people who stay are in it for the money and little else. Everyone knows they could well be laid off at any time the AI becomes good enough to replace them. People cannot control whether they end up on a list of positions to be cut, so it’s sensible to just make as much money as possible while awaiting the seemingly inevitable. </span><em><span>That sounds like a pretty miserable place to work.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It could also lead to a situation where the workforce becomes more populated by those with no better options, who are not in demand from other companies.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Do social impacts matter to Meta?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A final element of the planned drastic job cuts, as revealed in the Reuters report, that I want to touch on is the potential wider, external impacts. Honestly, I’m surprised that none of Meta’s leadership seems to have considered this angle.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>By executing massive layoffs for the sake of AI, Meta could have invited more regulation of the emerging AI sector. </span></strong><span>Meta is one of the largest tech employers in the US, and the CEOs of Anthropic and OpenAI are on record for predicting mass unemployment, and calling on governmental intervention should it happen. In fairness, other tech companies have also held major AI-related layoffs; Block let go 40% of its workforce, about 4,000 people in February.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But Meta is not just another tech company: it’s the world’s leading social media company, and just </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3c64024e-625d-44ca-8535-727f29c54e6a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>lost a major US lawsuit</span></a><span> alleging that its platforms harm children and faces an $18B fine. As a result, it has committed to make its platforms less addictive. If the planned cuts had happened at Meta and all those staff became unemployed, how would it have dealt with complying with the court’s ruling to make its products safer for children? Could AI be relied on to deliver this with much less human input?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In light of the recent legal defeat, it wouldn’t be a good look for Zuckerberg’s company to blatantly put profits ahead of people by dismissing a load more workers. The combined effect of the two events would create terrible optics. In response, the government could decide that Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s CEOs were right about the threat to society of mass job losses and roll out things like:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Stricter employee protection, specifically around AI-related layoffs.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Higher taxation on profits of companies that “replace” staff with AI, and channel the revenue to deal with widespread whitecollar unemployment</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Start taxing AI at source whenever tokens are sold, and use the surplus to counter the social ills of unemployment</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Or the government could do nothing and leave it to the market to deal with unemployed whitecollar workers by creating enough new companies to employ highly-skilled software engineers, PMs, designers and other folks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Overall, the canceled plan to cut thousands more jobs in this climate just adds to the feeling that there are no adults running Meta. </span></strong><span>Since Sheryl Sandberg quit in 2022 as Chief Operating Officer and Zuckerberg’s “right hand”, Meta has acted irrationally, irresponsibly, and unpredictably:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>2022-2023: laying off 25% of staff</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>2024-2025: immediately rehired even more people so that 2025’s headcount returned to 2022 levels, raising the question of what the point of layoffs even was</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>2026: on track to overtake Google as #1 in advertising revenue this year</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>May 2026: conducted sudden layoffs and forced reassignments of engineers, while aiming to replace as many devs with AI as possible for no obvious reasons like external pressure or competitive threats.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’ve long had a generally positive view of Meta’s engineering culture, but with the company’s leadership seemingly worshiping AI and holding their colleagues in disdain, you have to wonder which software engineer would choose to work at Meta if other options are available. There are many tech companies that value their human software engineers, understand that great teams make for great companies, and that AI is a tool and not a replacement for human energy, motivation, and thoughtfulness. But Meta is clearly not among them.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>2. More thoughts on Ramp’s in-house AI infra</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Thanks for all the feedback on </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ddee51b1-838e-424d-8378-b79f4a4a9839?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>this week’s issue</span></a><span> on how and why Ramp built its in-house coding agent. A few additional notes:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Building AI tools in-house is like an “internal bootcamp” for AI Engineering. </span></strong><span>I asked Inspect co-creator Zach Bruggeman, if they had access to a similar system from a vendor, would they have built Inspect? He told me they would because they learned so much and developed a lot of AI infrastructure “muscle.” Plus, it was a lot less effort than a similar project would have been in the past.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Building in-house AI infra allowed Ramp to quickly launch </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3ff4a790-0b90-42c5-bb55-d28aad7efb4b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Router.com</span></a></strong><span>. Stripe made a strategic move by acquiring LLM gateway OpenRouter. Having built something similar internally, Ramp made their Ramp Router infra publicly available within a few days of the Stripe announcement. It’s rare to see a fintech company launch AI infrastructure, but Ramp evidently has enough “AI infra muscle” in-house to do so.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Building internal, dev-facing AI infra feels like a low-risk, high-reward investment. </span></strong><span>What’s the worst that can happen when a few engineers inside a company build out AI infra? They get hands-on with AI engineering, spend some money on AI infra providers, and create a product that could work better than what AI vendors offer out of the box. And there’s less to worry about in terms of vendors accessing sensitive data. In the best case, you’ve built infra that competitors don’t have, and can potentially attract AI engineers more easily than rivals. Meanwhile, current engineers there who want to get into AI Engineering don’t leave for AI startups as they can do this kind of work in-house.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>It’s not just Ramp that is building AI infra; many 100+ person companies are also doing it. </span></strong><span>Reader Nick Pleatsikas shared that at his 200-person company, they built AI coding infra to pipe company-specific context to the models without worrying about vendors logging sensitive information. Other similarly-sized businesses are doing the same.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The effort to build this kind of coding agent is relatively minor compared to the potential upside. Plus, it’s interesting and challenging to do. </span><em><span>The question isn’t necessarily “why” to do it, but rather, “why not?”</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>3. Industry Pulse</span></h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>GitHub’s load increase speeds up</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In April, after a large GitHub outage, we</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/21ae857e-53ea-464c-8cc0-89fb3c8671e8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span> looked into</span></a><span> how much its load had increased over the past three years. It was an average load increase of 3.5x; high, but not impossible to plan ahead for. Last week, new details about the increased load became available after GitHub suffered another lengthy eight-hour outage. The company’s post showed that load had nearly doubled since April, to stand 5-6x higher than three years ago:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: If so, that will create some interesting challenges for us software engineers to solve!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Stripe acquires OpenRouter</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In June, we covered the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fa3b8ca7-4130-4acf-ae66-8a7a8ae15b4c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>trend of “smart model routing:”</span></a><span> automatically selecting the right AI model for the right task as a way to reduce AI token spend. OpenRouter is the leading LLM gateway, with routing built in. A week ago, Stripe </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dc6244c2-6106-4acc-8ee8-421ff0a521ce?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>announced</span></a><span> it will acquire OpenRouter for $7.5B, an incredible exit for a startup founded in 2023!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why would Stripe spend so much on an AI infra company? A few possible reasons:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Business model: </span></strong><span>OpenRouter charges a 5.5% fee when users buy credits through its interface. This is a very similar business model to Stripe’s of charging 2.9% on top of a transaction.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Growth of AI token usage. </span></strong><span>AI token usage is increasing exponentially across the tech industry, and surely so is OpenRouter’s business. It generates $140M in revenue from its fees (</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6b6f5d12-4192-4be3-be1a-c76ce784c85f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>per The Information</span></a><span>). If dramatic growth continues, OpenRouter would be on course to generate billions in revenue per year.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Becoming an AI payments infra company? </span></strong><span>The cost of AI lies with the price of tokens, and if Stripe becomes a provider of tokens, it would basically become a payments infra company; all without having to develop state-of-the-art AI models!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Stripe’s upcoming IPO. </span></strong><span>Stripe is likely to go public at some point, and being seen as an AI infra company could attract a higher valuation in the current climate than “just” being a payments company.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This acquisition looks like a smart move by Stripe.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Ramp launches Ramp Router in public</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A week after Stripe announced acquiring OpenRouter, fintech competitor Ramp launched a very similar offering. The company bought the domain </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3ff4a790-0b90-42c5-bb55-d28aad7efb4b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Router.com</span></a><span> and launched a service that’s near-identical to OpenRouter. Under the hood, it’s powered by Ramp Router and promises to cut AI costs by 40% on average.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One reservation I have about Router.com is its data retention policy: unlike OpenRouter that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0e25cc53-0335-4ff7-b945-6036d5b12801?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>offers</span></a><span> Zero Data Retention (ZDR), Router.com only offers ZDR to select US-hosted models. Additionally, Ramp’s Router “stores model inputs, outputs, and metadata and uses this data to improve the service.” Basically, Ramp Router by default stores potentially sensitive data sent to the service: a red flag in any serious usage!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Such data retention is hardly a good use case for a company, and suggests that Ramp may be targeting the hobbyist crowd with this offering – at least until they get more serious about data privacy.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That Ramp felt the need to launch </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3ff4a790-0b90-42c5-bb55-d28aad7efb4b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Router.com</span></a><span> suggests to me that Stripe’s move to buy OpenRouter probably caught them by surprise, and they are not ready to let Stripe become the leading LLM gateway without a fight.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe RevenueCat is the leading in-app purchase SDK, and CEO Jacob Eiting </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4ad7a3d7-28f1-40fd-997d-ce491d66cd3b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>explained</span></a><span> how they see it:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Gaming revenue down 4.5% year-on-year (YoY); the majority of the decrease</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Non-gaming revenue (apps) up 14.6% YoY</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Web payments share rose from 20% last year to 26% this year.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So, it’s a mix of people spending less on games IAPs, and more companies bypassing Apple’s in-app-purchase flows (where Apple levies the 30% “Apple Tax”) in favor of web checkout. A 2025 court ruling </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bdf6a291-0a5d-477d-83fe-05b3a606842c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>forcing</span></a><span> the iPhone maker to allow web payment links on iOS is also likely to be a factor.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>What’s a bug, anyway?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’m a big fan of Claude Code creator Boris Cherny, but must part ways with his definition of ‘bug’, as per a recent post from him. It came after a Claude Code user </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7f4297e5-707a-4617-a735-b02813e5bff9?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>complained</span></a><span> on X that the agent could not be hot reloaded. Boris looked into it and declared it was a “UX issue” and not a bug. As the Community note helpfully pointed out, that is also known as a bug:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>Consider what can happen when someone uploads a profile photo to a web application.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Depending on the use case, the application may resize the image into different sizes. It might run the image through a content check process. It can also push the resized images to a content delivery network for faster access. Lastly, it will also update the user record with the latest metadata. Now, imagine if all of these operations take place during the same picture upload request path. As all of these functionalities are carried out, the user sees a spinning button for several seconds, wondering whether the photo has been uploaded successfully. Needless to say, it would be a pretty poor user experience.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If we move all of that extra work outside the request path, the upload can more or less respond immediately as soon as the image file is stored in an object storage. The image still gets resized, scanned, and distributed, just not in the same flow. This is known as background work, and here are some examples of why it is needed:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A user action may have triggered it. For example, someone signs up, and a welcome email goes out.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The clock may have triggered it. For example, nightly reports, monthly invoices, hourly cache refreshes.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Another system could have triggered it. For example, a webhook arrives, or a file is stored in object storage.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Perhaps the sheer volume of work made it worthwhile. For example, some work is naturally cheaper or safer done a thousand items at a time.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most of the time, teams start with a single scheduled script on a single machine. It can handle a great amount of background work. However, as the system gets bigger and more complex, the amount of background work requires different strategies. In this article, we will look at various such strategies to perform background work in detail.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin:
