style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The fourth vector is prompt injection. Long agentic runs are expensive to repeat. Therefore, it makes sense to resume a published run. Encrypted blocks make that possible.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A block containing an instruction can be planted in a shared trace. When the session resumes, that block is processed as prior context. In one demonstration, a block carrying an instruction to upload PowerPoint files to an external address was ported into a conversation with GPT-5.6 Sol and paired with an unrelated slide-editing request. The resulting script added the requested slide and uploaded the presentation.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Field Observations</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Recovering traces at this scale brought out findings unrelated to the vulnerability itself.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Summaries and traces sometimes diverge. On an AIME 2025 mathematics problem, the summary returned by the API described methodical work through the geometry using the law of cosines. The recovered trace opened by stating the answer from memory and then working backward toward a justification, with several wrong guesses along the way. The researchers did not measure how often this occurs. However, they note that a smaller model summarising a larger one will compress the original.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Recovered GPT traces are frequently not fluent English. They are made up of compressed telegraphic notes with articles dropped and grammar abandoned. This carries a direct consequence for oversight, because trace monitoring depends on traces being legible.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Proposed Mitigations</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The research paper ultimately makes one strong point, which is the cause of the overall problem. The envelope we talked about earlier authenticates the content of a reasoning block, but it does not authenticate the context in which that block was produced or replayed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The cheapest fix for this problem should address cross-user replay. This involves embedding an account identifier inside the authenticated data at issuance, allowing the API to compare it against the authenticated caller and reject any mismatch. This closes the attack vector entirely without the need for server-side storage.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Cross-session binding is harder, because some genuine features depend on the same portability. Users can fork conversations, compact old turns out of long sessions, and downgrade models mid-conversation. Binding each block to the complete transcript would break all three. The proposal is a hash chain tying each block to its session and to the fingerprint of its predecessor, combined with a Merkle tree that retains only root fingerprints once older blocks are pruned. This approach preserves ordering cheaply while still allowing integrity checks over any surviving stretch.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Blocks already published present a separate problem, since they were signed under a key encoding neither user nor session. The only retroactive remedy is to rotate those keys and refuse to decode anything signed under a retired key identifier. This also invalidates legitimate continuations of old sessions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Other measures include moving to server-side storage entirely, configuring API gateways to reject envelopes from a different model version than the one queried, and training models to decline transcription requests regardless of framing.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We’ve now understood the key points in the research paper. Here are some of the main takeaways:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>This wasn’t a failure of cryptographic techniques. The guarantee made by the envelope remained throughout the flow. The missing piece was a binding between a block and the context that produced it, which is a decision about which fields go into the authenticated portion.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The summary displayed alongside an answer is a separate artifact from the trace it describes, and the two can diverge.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Sanitising a session log reaches the plaintext only. Encrypted blocks have to be removed rather than cleaned, since the person publishing them cannot inspect what they contain.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The security of a model family depends on its least protected member. Anti-distillation training on a flagship model provides limited benefits while a cheaper sibling model accepts the same blocks.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>References:</span></strong></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a Symbol';font-weight: 400;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>At a select few tech companies, they write most of their code with their own, custom-built, internal AI coding agents. This is different from most of the industry which uses AI coding agents and harnesses like Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, GitHub Copilot, etc. At Ramp, their own version is called </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a1c314f8-a18c-4bac-a5c5-a50f872da7f7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Inspect</span></a><span>, while at Block it’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bf77ea8c-5b68-40d7-99f3-d50c14fa7c8c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Goose</span></a><span> (open source), at Stripe it’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f0afa727-d401-4f8e-af60-d2a594a77b8f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Minions</span></a><span>, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f0c115fb-869b-4689-baec-3d10c4f31124?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>River</span></a><span> at Shopify.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But why not just use what frontier labs and coding harness AI startups already offer; why take the time and effort?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We reached out to Ramp, a fintech company big on building its internal AI infrastructure, and sat down with the founding team of Inspect and engineering leadership. We talked with CTO </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5bf890e3-6c13-4e66-93e8-5585da38dace?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Rahul Sengottuvelu</span></a><span>, head of engineering </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/528d6458-ecbb-4807-9a61-93f939472064?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Hamid Dadkhah</span></a><span>, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/28546ff0-0a20-44f7-8deb-ea9b1de26b36?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Zach Bruggeman</span></a><span>, principal engineer and founding engineer of Inspect.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today, we cover:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>What is Inspect? </span></strong><span>Imagine an AI coding agent running on remote sandboxes with access to most internal data sources, and verifying all backend and frontend changes on the remote machine.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Why build your own background coding agent?</span></strong><span> Engineers and designers at Ramp were dissatisfied with third-party harnesses: they wanted to run more than a few agents in parallel – which local machines don’t support – to have better frontend tooling, and also faced demand for remote development environments.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>How Ramp uses Inspect:</span></strong><span> coding, bugfixing in Slack, debugging, and building internal agents like code review and incident management on top of the Inspect platform</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Tech stack and architecture: </span></strong><span>React/Vite, Cloudflare Durable Objects, SQLite, Cloudflare Agents SDK, Modal sandboxes.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>What makes Inspect so popular?</span></strong><span> The machine in the cloud is a developer machine, plus it has access to numerous internal integrations via API and MCP.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Inside the sandbox. </span></strong><span>OpenCode, services for development (e.g. Postgres, Redis, RabbitMQ, Temporal), Chromium, and VS Code Server. Plus, we check out smart tricks to make sandboxes spin up in five seconds or less(!!)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Collaboration & feedback. </span></strong><span>All Inspect sessions are public and open to collaboration, with no opt-outs allowed. More than 150 people at Ramp have contributed to the project.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If you’re like us, you might wonder what the point would be of building your own harness and investing the time and resources in it, given all the choices already out there. This article sets out to answer that question, to understand why other places chose a similar path, and how a non-AI frontier lab can build more efficient tooling than what the frontier AI labs offer. It looks like the “buy, don’t build” tooling convention might not apply to AI tools!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let’s get Ramp</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A couple of things make Inspect different from coding agents like Claude Code and Cursor:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Remote sandboxes: </span></strong><span>Inspect spins up a sandboxed remote development environment which unlocks unlimited session concurrency, centralized setup configuration, and cross-functional session collaboration.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Internal integrations: </span></strong><span>Inspect is integrated across the org with the same tools and context that a Ramp engineer has; the only constraint on agents’ ability is model intelligence, not missing tools or access.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Inspect verifies all its changes. </span></strong><span>As a remote development environment with full tooling access, it can “close the loop” and confirm the changes it makes work:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Backend verification:</span></strong><span> Inspect runs tests, reviews telemetry and queries feature flags</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Frontend work verification</span></strong><span>: Inspect visually verifies its own work by providing screenshots and live previews to users.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At present, most third-party AI harnesses cannot do these kinds of verifications ‘out of the box’ because they lack internal integrations with things like telemetry and feature flag systems. Also, almost a year ago, Ramp built screenshot verification before it was supported by third-party vendors. Things like this placed Ramp months ahead of nearly all AI coding harnesses, and they could also build a far better feedback loop in their own harness.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Rapid adoption when background agent released</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The v1 of Inspect was a Chrome extension for designers to prompt AI to make minor website changes. A few months later, the v2 version with background agents followed.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure 1);"><span>2. Why build your own background coding agent?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are a few reasons why Ramp decided to turn down tried-and-tested products and create their own:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Local machines are limited in how many agents they can run. </span></strong><span>Ramp found third-party products below expectations; they liked Claude Code on day 1, but were constrained by only being able to run one or two sessions on local machines.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Better frontend tooling. </span></strong><span>The web engineering team wanted to improve their frontend tooling so designers could make small UI tweaks. There was an opportunity to use AI to automate themselves out of that loop.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Need for remote dev environments. </span></strong><span>As Ramp scaled, so did the complexity, and with it there was more work at the intersection of systems, like debugging backward compatibility, and broken API contracts. The solution was to create remote dev environments.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Inspect started as a designer’s frontend tool, and a good part of its team were frontend engineers with interests in UX and speedy performance. The v1 was a Chrome extension for visual edits, where a user could highlight an area and tell the AI what minor website changes to make, like copy edits and button placements. The task of building a tool for making UI edits with AI was given to two frontend engineers, Zach Bruggeman and Jason Quense, who aside from their frontend domain knowledge, brought a welcome adversarial perspective, as they were less than fully convinced by AI at that time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>People liked v1 but it wasn’t adopted because engineers already knew how to go to a file and edit a single line of code, so didn’t have a reason to use it, and it also required setting up a local development environment, making it too complicated for non-devs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For the current iteration of Inspect (released November 2025) the team pivoted. They built Inspect v2 as a remote development environment with a coding agent on top. Setting it up as a remote environment that they could configure centrally removed the need for local setup on each machine. They were also encouraged by seeing that OpenCode, the open-source coding agent which serves as Inspect’s harness, exposed an HTTP API which made it straightforward to set up, and was open-source, good enough, and importantly, offered model agnosticism.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Check out the episode of The Pragmatic Engineer podcast </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/13ecd18f-2c37-4d86-a4e7-c000e68ee9f7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>with OpenCode creator, Dax Raad</span></a><span>.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>After pivoting, adoption skyrocketed to where it is today:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure How Ramp uses Inspect</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Having built it, Ramp uses Inspect for a few things:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Coding</span></strong><span>: obvious use case; engineers prompt Inspect with small and medium-sized coding tasks that can often be one-shot passes. 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In detail:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>React / Vite: </span></strong><span>the frontend for the web interface; a React application that uses </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6eb4f5b2-7ba8-4739-b5e4-e58a6dfe6b57?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Vite</span></a><span> as its development server and build tool.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Cloudflare Durable Objects</span></strong><span>: manages sessions for Inspect and is responsible for synchronizing state across all clients. This enables users to even kick off a session from their phone as and when they have an idea, and later, to pick up the PR or jump into the Inspect session on their computer.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>SQLite</span></strong><span>: the database attached to the Durable Object. Stores all events that take place within an Inspect session, so that when another user joins, they can see the entire backlog of events. This enables ‘multiplayer’: two devs can work in the same session, or a PM can review the work inside a dev-started session.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Cloudflare Agents SDK</span></strong><span>: a layer over the WebSockets Hibernation API that handles real-time streaming between the sandbox, API, and attached clients. Allows keeping sockets open without incurring compute costs when the connection is idle, which makes Inspect sessions economical.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Modal Sandbox</span></strong><span>: the sandboxing technology used to run each session in isolation.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Fireworks and Modal</span></strong><span>: used as inference infrastructure and for fine-tuning to serve open-source models and their own fine-tuned models.</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Interacting with GitHub</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>How Inspect interacts with GitHub is interesting:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Push a new branch. </span></strong><span>The Inspect sandbox pushes the branch it works on to GitHub. It also sends an event to the API with the branch name, and the session ID.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>API layer opens a pull request (PR) as the user. </span></strong><span>The API layer opens a pull request using the user’s token to tie the PR authorship to the user, which makes it impossible for the user to approve their own pull request, if it’s in a project that requires additional approvers.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>API listens to GitHub for PR status changes. </span></strong><span>The API listens to a GitHub webhook, which fires when the status of the PR is changed: e.g. when it’s updated, merged, or closed.</span></p></li></ol><p marketplace.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Inspect has an ‘automations marketplace’.</span></strong><span> 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Sentry error 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>TODO/FIXME burndown:</span></strong><span> search the code for TODO or FIXME comments, and resolve them</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>… and many more!</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ramp’s automations marketplace reminds me a little bit of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/64e3d633-6868-4c62-9c18-0fea7b0d6e93?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Uber’s Agent Builder</span></a><span>, which is a collection of reusable agents. Except my sense is that while Uber’s Agent Builder was more geared for non-engineers, this automations marketplace is heavily used by engineers as well.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>5. </span><span>What makes Inspect so popular?</span><span> </span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Every Inspect session runs a sandbox that’s near-identical to a fully set up local development environment. This means Inspect sandboxes can be used throughout the entire development environment: from ideas and prototyping, to review and shipping:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Ideas stage</span></strong><span>: Inspect can be part of the collaboration while a feature is being discussed in tools like Slack and Linear.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Prototyping</span></strong><span>: show off a web-based prototype for feedback by sharing the URL of the web server Inspect spun up.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Development</span></strong><span>: while building a feature, other engineers can connect directly to the sandbox to check out the work and give feedback – including to the agent.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Code review</span></strong><span>: The ReviewBuddy agent runs quality gates (linters and tests) invoking the Testo subagent, adds its own review, and decides who might be the best reviewer based on previous contributions and availability.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Running in prod & operations</span></strong><span>: when errors are raised with Sentry, anomalies are detected in monitoring with Datadog, or if incidents are raised in prod in incident.io, the OncallAssistant subagent is kicked off. This agent attempts to reproduce the issue in the sandbox. If it succeeds, it also proposes a fix. By the time the on-call engineer connects to the Slack thread, all the context is there and perhaps a fix is ready to review, as well.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The “secret sauce” of Inspect’s usefulness is the work put into the sandbox itself. </span></strong><span>When I hear about a company building its own AI agent harness, I usually focus on the </span><em><span>harness </span></em><span>itself. But in the case of Ramp, the harness is very basic; just OpenCode! The reason why adoption is high is because the agent runs a full-on development environment.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is also why third-party coding harnesses like Codex or Claude Code are less used at Ramp: they don’t have access to all the capabilities an Inspect sandbox has.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Integrations with internal & external tools</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On top of local tools running on the sandbox, an Inspect session also gets access to internal and external tools that Ramp engineers use, as previously mentioned:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Integrated via API:</span></strong><span> Slack (chat), Linear (ticketing), LaunchDarkly (feature flags), Buildkite (CI/CD), GitHub (version control)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Via MCP</span></strong><span>: Datadog (observability), Sentry (application monitoring), and Langfuse (agent observability). MCP access is seen as exploratory, and is offered only for low-risk tools that don’t handle sensitive data</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Inspect has read-only, sanitized access to the prod database that no third-party tool could have. </span></strong><span>One benefit of Ramp having its own, internal coding agent is that it gives read-only access to a sanitized version of their production database. A group of security engineers and backend engineers built a sanitization layer through which Inspect can query the production database for things like masking or redacting personally identifiable information (PII), stripping data that should not leave the boundary, and other sensible optimizations.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With all this access, Inspect is also capable of things like planning and running a database migration under supervision. CTO Rahul Sengottuvelu told us:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Inspect already has every major piece of context that is necessary for how to run a database migration. Does it have access to Datadog? Does it know how to use Datadog? Does it have access to Linear and Sentry? And GitHub and Notion? Does it know where it is in Notion? Does it know what the different repos are? It does, to all of these, and so it can plan complex things well, like a database migration.”</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>6. Inside the sandbox</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For building with Inspect, Ramp has set the following constraints:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Startup time</span></strong><span>: sandboxes need to start quickly, and Ramp has a 5-second budget to start a sandbox.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Session speed:</span></strong><span> this should be as fast as the model provider’s time-to-first token. Basically, the sandbox environment should not add to token streaming latency.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Fast restore</span></strong><span>: Idle sandboxes should be frozen and restored later. </span><em><span>One reason Ramp went with Modal’s sandbox implementation is because it uses filesystem snapshots to freeze and restore state.</span></em></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Achieving 5-second sandbox startup time</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ramp got to a five-second sandbox startup time by using a few tactical optimizations:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>1. Regenerate repo snapshots every 30 minutes.</span></strong><span> Ramp sets up the environment once per repo, snapshots the finished state and stores it every half hour. The work includes:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Cloning the repo</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Installing dependencies</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Running setup and build commands</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Running the test suite once, so cached files exist</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Since the images are rebuilt every 30 minutes, there are only ever up to half an hour’s worth of changes to sync after a snapshot is created. Syncing is not a blocking operation. While syncing with the latest branch, Ramp allows the agent to </span><em><span>read </span></em><span>files using an OpenCode plugin to block file edits and writes. In a large enough repository, it is unlikely that an incoming prompt is going to modify a file changed in the last 30 minutes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ramp has 150+ repositories inside the company, which means 150+ snapshots to be rebuilt twice per hour. There’s an overhead aspect to this, but it’s the tradeoff to make for a snappy developer experience!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>2. Warming up when starting to type. </span></strong><span>As soon as an engineer starts typing their prompt in the web interface, Inspect starts warming up the associated sandbox. It boots it up from the stored snapshot and catches up on changes since the snapshot was created. In practice, by the time you’ve finished typing, the environment is set up and ready to go!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>3. High-volume repos have a warm pool. </span></strong><span>For high-volume repos, Ramp keeps a “warm pool” of sandboxes. Snapshots reduce boot time, but you still need to wait for the sandbox to boot from the snapshot and sync recent changes, which takes a few seconds.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For popular repos, Ramp keeps a warm pool of sandboxes already booted and ready. When starting an Inspect session, users pick up an already-running sandbox. The warmed pool expires and is remade in sync with the 30-minute base image refresh.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s notable that the team which built Inspect was frontend engineer-heavy and this performance focus seems more than coincidental.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: server</span></strong><span>: runs to allow engineers to make manual edits</span></p></li></ul><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>Agent harness</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ramp decided to use </span><strong><span>OpenCode</span></strong><span> as the harness, which gives Ramp devs the option to choose their model provider. The LLM gateway routes to the selected model. Below are some reasons why Ramp likes OpenCode:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>OpenCode is an HTTP API at its core.</span></strong><span> It is a server first and foremost which enables Ramp to run many different clients (command line interfaces, CLIs, etc)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Avoids vendor lock-in. </span></strong><span>OpenCode is model-agnostic and so makes it easy to use the best model and model provider for a job, and to avoid vendor lock-in. Ramp currently defaults to GPT-5.6, and experiments with Fable as a model for planning complex tasks.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Open source. </span></strong><span>LLMs can read OpenCode’s own code to understand its behavior, and this minimizes hallucinations about its capabilities.</span></p></li></ol><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>7. Collaboration & feedback</span></h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>All sessions are collaborative with no opt-outs</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An Inspect session is collaborative by default and opt-outs aren’t available; the session is open for others to join and both the work and the prompting history are exposed. This “multiplayer-first” approach is deliberate, and has probably contributed to Inspect spreading as fast as it did. Interestingly, early on, the goal was just to be able to share sessions, and not to collaborate: this was a beneficial by-product.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are benefits to collaborative features being always-on:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>More context during code review. </span></strong><span>It’s helpful if a reviewer can see the thought process that went into the PR, and they may have to ask fewer questions about why you made a decision, as a result.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Easy to jump in when needed.</span></strong><span> Need to step away from work? Send your session to a coworker and they can take over and finish it.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Helpful during performance reviews.</span></strong><span> You can just attach sessions to your performance review documents and the manager can look at them to see the work you’ve done. They should be able to write a fairer performance review based on several of your sessions.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Cross-disciplinary collaboration</span></strong><span>. Engineers, PMs, and designers can work together better, especially when collaboration starts on Slack, where the Inspect bot is. And because Inspect also does visual verification, showing screenshots or usable web demos means that designers/PMs/engineers can stay aligned during development.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An original author of Inspect, Zach, told us he feels that Inspect helped build a “system of trust” with AI tooling, which helped increase AI adoption at the company. In his words:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Inspect is not just a coding agent: it’s a system of trust.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There’s been this sentiment in the AI industry along the lines of ‘if you’re not using AI, if you’re not ahead, and you’re cooked, bro.’ What a horrible way to try and bring people on board to a very new paradigm of working!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With Inspect being out in the open</span><em><span>, </span></em><span>it has increased adoption of AI at Ramp because</span><em><span> </span></em><span>all you need to do is just go look at one of your teammates using it. The open part was not even a design goal at the start, it just happened to be something we really leaned into.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This network effect became super important. It brings this system of trust which means people learn to trust the AI to work properly.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>You </span></strong><em><strong><span>trust</span></strong></em><strong><span> your teammates more because you see </span></strong><em><strong><span>their thought processes</span></strong></em><strong><span> and how they approach and break up a problem. </span></strong><span>You probably learn something about how to solve a problem from other people!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Companies of scale are all about building trust in each other, and I think Inspect in this paradigm has kind of shifted the bar.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Gathering feedback on Inspect</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Inspect team has two main Slack channels: one </span><strong><span>#project-ramp-inspect </span></strong><span>(for announcements) and </span><strong><span>#feedback-ramp-inspect </span></strong><span>(for positive and negative feedback).</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>They try to avoid the “we’ll get back to you” style of support; when someone reports a bug or makes a feature request, the Inspect team tags Inspect and starts working and iterating on it in public. And – of course – they share their session!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Inspect team also doesn’t dictate which features Inspect should/shouldn’t have. As Zach told us:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The things we hold precious are Inspect’s performance stability and slick UX. Other than those, we’re very open to adding a feature and then just making sure it fits in the ethos of the product.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Obviously, if a feature doesn’t get used we’ll remove it and let people know. In those cases, most people just go like ‘oh well, that makes sense’.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We’re not trying to act like we think we know the direction of the product better than others. We tend to have the ‘let’s see what people ask for, then go from there’ type of approach.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Inspect team encourages others to contribute to the product. To date, about 150 engineers have contributed to Inspect. As a fun fact, in the past 30 days, ~90% of pull requests merged into the Inspect repo came from a Ramp Inspect session.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Takeaways</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we’ve heard from folks at Ramp about why they elected to build their own, home-grown AI coding agent, and it comes down to a few things.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>I have a feeling of deja vu with Cloud Development Environments (CDEs). </span></strong><span>A trend, pre-AI going mainstream for development, in 2023, was the popularity of Cloud Development Environments, which we covered </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/82049e90-3ef0-424d-90d2-851ec0006081?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>in a deepdive.</span></a><span> Companies like Uber, Slack, and Pipedrive figured out that their engineers would be a lot more productive if they could do development on a cloud machine, set up with source code checked out, tools installed, all ready to code and debug on. Those cloud machines were bigger than local ones, and devs could work on more than one problem and debugging sessions:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>Reasons why CDEs were taking off in 2023. See </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/82049e90-3ef0-424d-90d2-851ec0006081?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>the full article</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It was Developer Experience (DevEx) teams at mid-sized and large companies who were building CDEs, until around the end of 2023, when DevEx teams shifted focus to AI tooling, and CDE projects were frozen.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But Ramp shows that AI agents get a lot more productive when they can run on a remote machine set up like a dev’s machine: basically, like a CDE! And so, CDEs are back – but this time as an infrastructure component for background agents.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Context + data + remote agents beats leading coding harnesses. </span></strong><span>For its coding harness, Ramp uses OpenCode, a well-built product that the likes of Claude Code and Codex aim to out-execute. Despite that, Ramp’s Inspect is far more popular internally than any coding harness built by leading AI labs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Inspect out-executes the likes of Claude Code, Codex and Cursor because it has access to more internal systems and data at Ramp, including read-only access to their sanitized production database.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Honestly, the “forced collaboration” choice is very smart. </span></strong><span>Devs can easily collaborate remotely on the same Inspect session, while any dev at the company can view or join Inspect sessions. It’s not just devs: because Inspect also works in Slack, it means designers and PMs can “involve” an Inspect bot during discussions, giving it more instructions to work with.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But I do wonder if it could backfire if people start to assume this agent will just “get” what needs to be done from bits and bobs of information. It’s also possible that PMs, devs, and designers will have almost no reason to write down their plan or make a spec if Inspect is integrated everywhere. Is this good, or could it have unexpected side effects?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Ramp and Inspect show us the next wave of developer / agent productivity improvements: agents running on CDEs in the cloud. </span></strong><span>It’s not just Ramp, other in-house coding agents at the likes of Stripe, Uber, Block, and others are more productive thanks to integrations, and because the companies have background agents running on their own versions of CDEs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If there’s one thing that AI labs want to avoid, it’s for tech companies to move off their coding harnesses onto another setup that’s more productive for them! After all, once they move off their coding harness, a logical next step is to start using other AI models – including open ones – with custom harnesses. And should this trend spread of building bespoke, custom coding agents for better productivity, then it would be bad for business for frontier labs!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>OpenAI’s acquisition of Gitpod/Ona now makes so much more sense. </span></strong><span>In 2023, Gitpod </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b7f1660c-466f-4907-9f38-79e01d858ea0?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>was the clear leader</span></a><span> among CDE vendors. In 2025, the company rebranded to Ona, and in June of this year, OpenAI acquired Ona, so that this technology could give Codex “a persistent place to work.” Basically, the Ona team is building cloud development environments that agents will be able to use.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Don’t forget the principle of staying ahead of the competition. </span></strong><span>A tempting argument might be to say that sure, Ramp has somewhat more productivity by building Inspect, but the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor and others surely will offer an off-the-shelf cloud coding agent and CDE product within months, so why build custom infra?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But this misses a few things:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Being very good at building AI is a valuable skill in itself.</span></strong><span> Even if Ramp only built an AI coding agent that matched the cutting edge, it could already be worth it in terms of a platform team getting hands-on experience of building AI infra! Building internal tools is a low risk approach to “upskilling” in AI engineering. Every company should want to upskill its engineers, so they are comfortable building with and on top of LLMs.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Outperform competitors with better tools and by being more productive. </span></strong><span>Let’s take a competitor to Ramp that doesn’t have a tool like Inspect. Engineers there will spend more time fixing frontend issues (where Inspect helps out), spend more time debugging (which Inspect also helps with), and could ship more bugs in production (Inspect runs validation loops). So, that company could well ship slower or less frequently with the same number of engineers. For startups, such things matter!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>To attract and retain top engineering talent, being on the cutting edge matters. </span></strong><span>At the end of the day, Ramp is a fintech company and there are plenty of those. But how many of them are a few steps ahead of leading AI labs in areas like coding agents? By building cool and innovative stuff like this, Ramp could hire more easily, and engineers there might become harder for rival companies to poach if those engineers don’t want to move somewhere with inferior AI coding tooling, that doesn’t try to challenge the status quo by building something better than what already exists.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Can we take a moment to consider just how much development is changing, with agents working on developer machines in the cloud? </span></strong><span>If you said to me two years ago that we’d have AI agents fixing frontend bugs, running on a cloud machine which is like a developer machine – while taking screenshots to make sure a bug is fixed – I would not have believed it, and yet, here we are. The tooling is not widespread (as yet), but it is live at a company like Ramp, and will surely be at more companies in the near future.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>If your workplace does not yet use the concept of CDEs running in the cloud, then I hope this deepdive offers pointers on how it could be built, in order to help decide whether the tradeoff might be worth the investment. The prevailing wisdom of the “build vs buy” question is usually that it’s worth buying from a vendor instead of building infra yourself. But AI coding tools could be on course to change the calculus.</span></p></div></div><div class="post-contributor-footer" style="margin-top: 16px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div item.title: Adapting To AI: Leadership
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Adapting To AI: Leadership

Colin Breck

“Leaders are usually rewarded for being decisive, having a plan, and acting with certitude. One of the most difficult things a leader must do is sit with uncertainty. This capacity must be balanced with clear direction, a bias for action, a sense of urgency, and strong execution - otherwise it slides into indecision.“

#Leadership AI ChangeManagement
item.description: Adapting To AI: Leadership

item.title: Seeing Like A State
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Seeing Like A State

Mike Fisher

“This week, pick the single dashboard, metric, or report you rely on most, and go find the territory behind it. Sit with the people whose work becomes that number. Find the resident holder of metis and ask them what the report always gets wrong. Then come back and look at your tidy rows of data with new eyes.”

#Leadership Management Metrics
item.description: Seeing Like A State

item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Three Important Steps In My Maturation Process

Thomas Dullien

So perhaps it is natural that I am reflecting on “what were the important realizations that I made since my early 20s that had a profound impact on the way I think about the world?” This post tries to list them.

#CareerGrowth
item.description: Three Important Steps In My Maturation Process

item.title: You Should Never Be Angry At Work
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
You Should Never Be Angry At Work

Sean Goedecke

“Healthy workplaces route around anger in the same way that networks route around damage. Emotionally unreliable engineers will get left out of conversations that might cause them to blow up. Decision-making will get done around them in backchannels. I’ve seen this become a self-reinforcing cycle: angry engineers aren’t consulted on key decisions, which makes them angrier, which pushes them even further away from the spaces where decisions get made, and so on.”

#TeamHealth CareerGrowth
item.description: You Should Never Be Angry At Work

item.title: Your Executable Is A SQLite Database
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Your Executable Is A SQLite Database

Farid Zakaria

“I have been probably obsessed with two things in the last few years: Nix as a tool to explore innovative ideas that require the capability to rebuild the world and replacing ELF with SQLite as an executable format. You might have noticed that these two ideas are well suited to each other.”

#SQL DeepDive
item.description: Your Executable Is A SQLite Database

item.title: How To Report A Bug So It Actually Gets Fixed
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How To Report A Bug So It Actually Gets Fixed

Oscar Molnar

I wanted to make a blog post like this for a long time, because it’s something that I wish I could find more of myself. I think one of the things that helps us most in our careers as software engineers is knowing how to debug problems, how to reproduce them, and how to report them.

#Communication Debugging

A hijacked agent session is a live process you can kill.</span></p><p class="button-wrapper" data-attrs="{"url":"https://go.bytebytego.com/WorkOS_082426CTA","text":"Learn how it works →","action":null,"class":null}" data-component-name="ButtonCreateButton" style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: center;cursor: pointer;border-radius: 4px;"><a class="button primary" href="https://substack.com/redirect/9de8cc24-2e7d-4de2-8dbf-c0da80dc65db?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="font-family: system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';display: inline-block;box-sizing: border-box;cursor: pointer;border: none;border-radius: 8px;font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 600;text-align: center;margin: 0;opacity: 1;outline: none;white-space: nowrap;color: #ffffff !important;text-decoration: none !important;background-color: #7756e3;padding: 12px 20px;height: auto;"><span style="color: #ffffff;text-decoration: none;">Learn how it works →</span></a></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The gap between code that executes fine and code that is actually safe to trust is growing wider pretty fast. For many years, writing code was the slow, expensive step, whereas reviewing it was a smaller task at the end. With the rise of AI-assisted coding, this balance is shifting.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>AI tools can now create a working function in seconds and a full feature in minutes. Teams are able to write more machine-generated code every month. In other words, producing code is now fast and relatively easy, whereas code verification is the harder part. A reviewer still has to read the change, understand it, and decide whether it belongs in production. In fact, more code written simply means more code that should be verified.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>We recently got a chance to speak with </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2ad4e287-cbec-4b9e-8a8b-f9778e7a5f20?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;"><span>Andrea Malagodi</span></a><span>, the CTO of Sonar (the company that has built some of the most used code verification software). He provided deep insights into code verification, especially in the context of AI and how Sonar is adapting to the recent changes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In this article, we will look at how code verification works, why the rise of AI-generated code puts more pressure on it, along with the extremely useful insights from Andrea on what the future may look like.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px
