The trend has not stopped, and many – if not most – companies have increased the number of reports each engineering manager has, while reducing the number of layers in their organization.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>7. Fractional CTO work preferred over fulltime positions</span></h2><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Standout engineering leaders who have built strong reputations and are based in tech hubs like New York, San Francisco, and London, are increasingly hesitant to join startups for the reasons above. An alternative is “Fractional CTO work”, which usually means working one or two days per week on a contract basis at a startup, typically for cash-only and zero equity.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For engineering leaders on a career break who don’t want to return to fulltime work just yet, a fractional role is a great way to stay in the game for lower time commitment.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Meanwhile, why would a startup hire a fractional CTO? It’s because they can start immediately, and if things don’t work out the parties can part ways quickly. It’s also useful learning material for hiring a permanent CTO later.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The fractional CTO whom I talked with in New York, said that they work with three companies, of which two wanted them to be the fulltime CTO. But this CTO is reluctant to make the move, mostly because they expect inflated expectations, they’re unclear about how viable either startup truly is, and the hours are set to be long.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>8. AI startups pay ICs more than non-AI startups pay executives</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s an open secret that compensation for very senior hires at AI labs is extremely generous, in the multi-million-dollar-per-year range, not accounting for equity appreciation. Both OpenAI and Anthropic have managed to get high-flying engineering leaders to join their ranks as a “member of technical staff”; that is, an individual contributor with no direct reports – at least, not initially.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One example: in April, Anthropic </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5f1478d4-081d-4b53-b064-48296c2e3eb7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>hired</span></a><span> Peter Bailis, Workday’s CTO (the HR software company being worth $50B) as an individual contributor. </span><em><span>In this example, Workday could be a more “traditional” company that’s not thriving in the business landscape that’s changing with AI.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>The latest news is that private equity giant Silver Lake is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1fb01789-c331-4bb0-9ecb-265f8f9d2dcf?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>in talks to buy</span></a><span> the company, suggesting Workday predicts the business and stock price will struggle to grow in the coming years.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5a68304b-036c-4ea9-baa1-11b3469e0e19?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>as per levels.fyi,</span></a><span> Anthropic </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5a68304b-036c-4ea9-baa1-11b3469e0e19?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>offers</span></a><span> a median of $1.25M per year in total compensation for staff-level software engineers. This is total compensation (base salary plus equity), and while equity is currently not liquid, Anthropic has regularly held secondary stock sales. Plus, the company is expected to go public, perhaps </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5befb985-5433-40cc-b3da-f7169827f94c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>later this year.</span></a></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And $1.25M p/a is well above what most CTOs or VP of Engineering folks earn at smaller startups, or even some mid-sized companies. If a hands-on CTO can join an AI lab, become an IC, get the best possible AI-native experience, and make more money than before, then what’s not to like?</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>9. Quitting to launch their own business</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With AI tools, it’s now easier than ever to build a prototype, a new product, or launch a startup. If you know what you want to build, then as a tech professional, you can have a working prototype within minutes and tweak it over a few days. The tricky thing about building a viable business is no longer coding: it’s identifying an unmet customer need, getting customers, and finding product-market-fit. Of course, this all takes time, while advertising and sales cost significant sums.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Experienced engineering leaders have two ways to start a business and for the process to be a lot more accessible than before:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>1. Bootstrap an existing idea, and aim to build a lifestyle business. </span></strong><span>A lifestyle business is one that’s controlled by an owner – without investors to apply pressure for fast growth – who prioritizes work-life balance over maximizing profits and steep growth goals.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Using AI tools, create a product you know there’s a need for, without needing to hire a team of engineers. Build it with AI agents, especially if you’re a hands-on leader who knows what it takes to build quality software. Use business acumen to get customers, generate revenue, potentially hire a couple of people to help with key tasks, and turn the whole thing into a small, profitable lifestyle business.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>2. Raise funding to build an AI-related startup. </span></strong><span>Today, there’s more VC money in the market than before and most is going into AI startups. As an experienced engineering leader with strong pedigree, raising seed funding for an AI startup is probably more achievable. With funding, you can hire a strong team and give your idea a proper shot. Of course, building a startup is never easy, but building an AI-native one has the benefit that you become extremely hands-on with this new way of building software, and your future employability should be boosted, even if the startup doesn’t fly.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>10. Burnout</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>AI-related burnout seems to be an issue spreading across the industry – and not just for engineering leaders – as Charity discussed in depth on last week’s Pragmatic Engineer Podcast episode:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Receiving too much AI slop (e.g. via emails, code, social media posts)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Too much AI hype</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>“Doom trolling”: a term </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d65374a4-bd4f-45bc-92d5-653467925497?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>coined</span></a><span> by Cal Newport to describe Anthropic and OpenAI’s public predictions of AI destroying jobs and creating economic hardship for society</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Scott Tolinski, cohost of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4160daad-4582-4491-aa8c-fc7844822c95?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Syntax.fm</span></a><span>, explored the topic of developer burnout in-depth in his video </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/feb1ae40-b44e-46d1-a0be-8c0a4704397f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>The true cost of AI coding</span></a><span>. In the episode, they talked with Adam Elmore, an engineer of 17 years’ experience who works at OpenCode, who went through severe periods of burnout caused by AI coding tools. He ended up sick for more than two weeks, unable to even go for a walk. His burnout was preceded by the feeling of being ridiculously productive:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“[My burnout] was preceded by very intense AI usage. So, I think I burned myself out through just late nights. I could hardly sleep; I was so excited to just get the next prompt; I didn’t want the AI ever stalling. If it wasn’t burning tokens, I felt like I was leaving something on the table.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It felt very productive: getting stuff going, having multiple things going at once, refactors, and all this stuff. That sort of led to a pretty hard crash.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the video, Scott also talked with Dr. Courtney Tolinski, analyzing what leads to burnout in AI coding, and shared details from a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2b5f0b12-81e1-4971-a84c-aafb3865997b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>burnout-related survey</span></a><span>. He summarized:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“With AI, the data definitely shows that people feel like they need to produce more now than ever.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Among the people </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2b5f0b12-81e1-4971-a84c-aafb3865997b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>who answered this survey,</span></a><span> AI was changing more than how fast software gets made; it was changing the pressure, sleep, enjoyment, and how capable people felt.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Individual limits only really come into play if the systems around you allow you to even stop working in the first place. So, before “maximum output 24/7, all the time” becomes the baseline for you, we need to figure out what healthy AI-assisted workflows actually look like in our lives.”</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>“Founder mode”: how to deal with it as an engineering leader?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/862ed13a-788f-4f3f-b8fa-08b7de8c4e78?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Uma Chingunde</span></a><span>, an experienced engineering leader believes one trend is the most significant for folks in leadership roles: ‘founder mode’. She </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/548c071f-356d-4efc-b11a-326850c6f733?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>shared</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Talking to some peers who experienced either their CEOs getting AI-pilled and/or going founder mode, [founder mode] made the job increasingly miserable, low ROI.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This type of behavior was identified two years ago in the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b46b87e6-d071-4ee8-8d2e-3b664db64b6d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>“founder mode” essay</span></a><span> by Y Combinator founder, Paul Graham. From it:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“At a Y Combinator event last week Brian Chesky gave a talk that everyone who was there will remember.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The theme of Brian’s talk was that the conventional wisdom about how to run larger companies is mistaken.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In effect, there are two different ways to run a company: founder mode and manager mode. Till now, most people even in Silicon Valley have implicitly assumed that scaling a startup meant switching to manager mode. But we can infer the existence of another mode from the dismay of founders who’ve tried it, and the success of their attempts to escape from it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Whatever founder mode consists of, it’s pretty clear that it’s going to break the principle that the CEO should engage with the company only via his or her direct reports. “Skip-level” meetings will become the norm instead of a practice so unusual that there’s a name for it. And once you abandon that constraint, there are a huge number of permutations to choose from.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Founder mode” is when the founder of a company is extremely hands-on, to the point of micromanaging anything they can or believe they should. In the case of Airbnb, this approach seems to be working. Graham </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b46b87e6-d071-4ee8-8d2e-3b664db64b6d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>stated</span></a><span> that “founder mode” is superior to “manager mode” for startups:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Founder mode will be more complicated than manager mode. But it will also work better. We already know that from the examples of individual founders groping their way toward it.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The problem for VPs, CTOs, et al, is that in “founder mode”, there’s much less room for other senior engineering leaders. </span></strong><span>When a founder overrules or steps over their CTO, VP of Engineering, or head of engineering to directly instruct reports on what to do, this often conflicts with what was agreed with the manager. The jobs of engineering leaders become frustrating, as decisions are frequently countermanded, and time is spent on communicating the confusion to employees.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Undeniably, “founder mode” seems great from the founder’s perspective. Whatever they want done</span><em><span> </span></em><span>gets done </span><em><span>now.</span></em><span> Meanwhile, an experienced engineering leader may decide they’re seen as being in the founder’s way.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>‘Founder mode’ and a great engineering leader from Big Tech are not an ideal match, and it often causes tensions. </span></strong><span>But one tech giant, Apple, operated in what might be considered “founder mode,” for a long time. Again </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b46b87e6-d071-4ee8-8d2e-3b664db64b6d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>from Paul Graham</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“For example, Steve Jobs used to run an annual retreat for what he considered the 100 most important people at Apple, and these were not the 100 people highest on the org chart. Can you imagine the force of will it would take to do this at the average company? And yet imagine how useful such a thing could be. It could make a big company feel like a startup. Steve presumably wouldn’t have kept having these retreats if they didn’t work. But I’ve never heard of another company doing this. So is it a good idea or a bad one? We still don’t know. That’s how little we know about founder mode.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So, how do you resolve tension with someone in “founder mode”? I see some pathways:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Lean into supporting “founder mode” and proactively change your role. </span></strong><span>Be someone the founder can delegate stuff which they don’t care about, and don’t take it personally when the founder overrules you. Build trust with the founder more than in the past. This is tricky, and there are no guaranteed recipes for success as everyone is different. It might be the only way to stay relatively content in your role for a longer period of time.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Sign out and be an individual contributor (IC).</span></strong><span> Give up the engineering leader title and your direct reports to instead build high-impact things at the company. As a non-manager, you don’t have to worry how the founder manages engineering. Of course, you’ll still be a senior individual contributor and should have excellent business sense and social capital internally, so you can and should get the most complex projects done, and solve pressing problems. Ideally, be a “right hand” of the founder.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Consider quitting if not aligned with the founder, when becoming so seems unlikely. </span></strong><span>You might disagree with actions by the founder that harm the business, which they might be unable or unwilling to see. Or you might disagree with their decisions. Whatever the case, you are misaligned with them, and persisting like this will make it miserable to stay put. This is surely one reason why there’s so much churn within engineering leaderships right now!</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Founder mode makes the VPE and CTO roles “low ROI” at most startups</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A knock-on effect of “founder mode” is that over the past year, VP of Engineering and CTO roles became “low-return-on-investment (ROI).” In lots of smaller and mid-sized companies, founders flipped to ‘founder mode’ and took over directing most of engineering, while existing VPE or CTO folks left after seeing the writing on the wall (they’re no longer needed), or being nudged out or simply fired.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Of course, people talk, and VPE and CTOs share their stories, including with me. It’s evident that over the course of the last decade or so, these roles have gotten pretty high risk, and many VPEs and CTOs who were pushed out of places took on heads of engineering, or Staff+ roles at other companies.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now however, founders increasingly realize the benefit of a “right hand” in the form of a VPE or CTO to run the engineering organization, and search for solid VPE and CTO folks pushed out of their previous jobs at startups. These people could do the job, but they no longer want to!</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>‘Work at companies that truly want to drive change’</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most engineering leaders I talked with found it tricky to identify a startup to join, but I did hear a success story. A year back, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7475a16f-c5ae-4792-890c-a9b7b27e43ba?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Matt Boyle</span></a><span> left Cloudflare to join Gitpod as VP of Engineering. Gitpod was originally known for cloud development environments (CDEs), but with the spread of AI-coding tools, CDEs seem in retreat. Like other non-AI vendors, Gitpod looked at pivoting from “regular” infrastructure to AI infrastructure.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A few months after Matt joined as VP Eng, the company </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c9bdb35b-0877-4c1e-b71a-acb54b95be18?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>rebranded</span></a><span> to Ona and pivoted to be a platform for background agents. This change went well, and in June, OpenAI </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/71ea1704-5390-4b73-aaeb-acc1611dcf51?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>announced</span></a><span> it would acquire Ona and integrate it as the backend for Codex.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Matt shared with us the questions he asked Gitpod while deciding whether to join:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“My best advice is to join a company that </span></strong><em><strong><span>actually</span></strong></em><strong><span> wants to drive change. </span></strong><span>Avoid joining one that is only planning to change because they </span><em><span>think</span></em><span> they need to, or because everyone around them is doing X or Y. The questions I asked Gitpod’s founders before deciding to join were:</span></p><ul style="margin-left: 20px;margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>What company are you trying to build over the next year? What about five years?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>What is your right to win?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>What advantages does Gitpod have that are durable?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>What problem are you hiring me to own, and what outcome, specifically?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Which decisions across product, engineering, organization, and customers, can I make without your approval? Where’s the line?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>If I ask others in Leadership to describe my mandate, will they say the same thing as you?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>When we disagree, who makes the final decision, and what evidence would cause you to reconsider?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>What would cause you to lose trust in me?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>What does ownership mean at Gitpod?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Where are the biggest bottlenecks preventing you from going faster?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Building Ona will require immense talent density, and the profiles we need to hire will be very in-demand. What do you think about this?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Some customers will not want Ona, they will want Gitpod. What do you think about this? When is churn okay, and where do we re-orient?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>If this role fails despite good intentions on both sides, what will be the most likely reason?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>I think the best leaders I have ever worked with stayed “hands-on” in some capacity. In an AI-first world, I believe we all need to spend some time as an IC. Do you agree with this? If so, how have you (or how will we) build it into the company culture?</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These questions helped me confirm that the existing leadership had firm beliefs, a plan for an AI-first world, and were running towards this.”</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Takeaways</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Whenever one of the highest-ranked engineering leaders leaves a company, it’s worth asking why it happened. Having talked to many people who decided to leave impressive jobs, my sense is that two factors loom large in people’s reasoning for signing out of their jobs:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The impact AI is having on the business and their role. At companies where business is doing poorly, leaders seek the exit when they know there’s little they can do to stop the ship from sinking.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>“Founder mode” sidelines them and makes the role less autonomous and relevant. Founders can be a lot more hands-on; as they (re)take responsibility, the scope of CTOs and VPEs shrinks, and opportunities become scarce.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Also, it’s worth asking about the impact on an org’s lower levels when there’s more than the usual amount of uncertainty at the top.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Getting hands-on AI experience at places that take a sensible approach to building software with LLM-based tools is table stakes for most engineering leaders to build long-term career stability. The same is true for engineers, I’d argue. If you work somewhere that’s modernizing its infrastructure, challenging how code reviews and deploys are done, how incidents are managed, etc., then that place is pretty close to the cutting edge of the industry.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s fine if that’s not where you work, but the longer you spend at places that are behind in new engineering practices, the harder it will be in the future to make the jump to startups and tech companies that integrate AI into most parts of their development workflows.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I hope this article has been interesting. If you have personal observations on this novel trend, or have experience of anything covered today, post a comment below.</span></p><p class="button-wrapper" A few interesting points made in its introduction are as follows:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Inkling has 66 layers, and each layer holds 256 experts, of which only six activate for any given token [2].</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Most layers can access only a short window of recent text, while a few can access all of it [1].</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Word positions are encoded using a method most labs moved away from years ago.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Thinking Machines, founded by Mira Murati (the ex-CTO of OpenAI), describes its mission as building AI that extends human will and judgment. The company lists four directions of work, which are training strong models, building tools that let people customise models with their own knowledge, developing interfaces that widen the communication channel between people and machines, and publishing research on how models are made [3].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Before Inkling, the company shipped Tinker, a service for fine-tuning open models [4]. Inkling is the company’s first model trained from scratch [1]. The weights sit on Hugging Face under an Apache 2.0 license [2], so anyone can download them and retrain the model on their own data.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we will work through the various choices Thinking Machines made while building Inkling. Here is what we will cover:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Mixture of Experts, and the gap between 975 billion parameters and 41 billion.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The mix of local and global attention layers behind a context window of one million tokens.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Position encoding, and the older method Thinking Machines chose over the current standard.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How images and audio enter the model without a separately pretrained encoder in front of them.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Thinking effort, a setting between 0 and 1 that adjusts how much the model reasons before answering.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><em><span>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The diagram below shows where each of these 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Groundwork</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let us first understand four key terms that are really important to make sense of the architecture:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Token: </span></strong><span>A token is a chunk of text. Models work with pieces smaller than sentences and usually a bit smaller than words. For example,  the sentence “Inkling was released in July” might become six tokens, with common words getting one token each and unusual words getting split into two or three.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Parameter: </span></strong><span>A parameter is one number stored inside the model, learned during training. When you read that a model has 975 billion parameters, it is the count of individual numbers sitting in the file. Each one started as random noise and was adjusted millions of times until the model produced sensible text.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Training: </span></strong><span> It works by showing the model text, letting it predict the next token, comparing that prediction against the token that actually came next, and then adjusting every parameter slightly in whichever direction would have made the prediction better. The size and direction of each adjustment is called a gradient, and the procedure that computes all of them at once is called backpropagation. By repeating this across trillions of tokens, the parameters settle into values that produce useful predictions.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Layer: </span></strong><span>It is one processing stage in the journey of a token. Inkling has 66 of them stacked in order [2]. A token’s representation enters layer 1, gets transformed, passes to layer 2, and so on until layer 66, after which the model predicts the next token. Every layer has the same two parts:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>An attention step that pulls in information from other tokens in the sequence.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A feed-forward step that transforms the result.</span></p></li></ul></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Sparsity</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Inkling separates the cost of storing a model from the cost of running it. This is the reason a model this large is affordable to use.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In an ordinary transformer, the feed-forward step in each layer is a single network, and every token passes through all of it. If that network holds 5 billion parameters, then every token processed involves all 5 billion.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Inkling replaces that single network with 256 smaller ones, called experts. For each token, a selection step picks six of the 256. Only those six run, and the remaining 250 sit idle for that token while handling other tokens instead [2]. This design pattern is called Mixture of Experts, and Thinking Machines states that their version largely follows the approach published by DeepSeek [1][8].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px this via a simple example:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Suppose you build a layer with 10 experts holding 1 billion parameters each, and you run 2 of them per token.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The file on disk contains all 10 billion parameters, and every one of them has to be loaded into memory before you can run the model at all.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Processing a single token involves 2 billion parameters, so each token costs about a fifth of what it would in an ordinary layer of the same total size.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Inkling does this at scale. The total across the whole model is 975 billion parameters, and the count involved in processing any single token is roughly 41 billion [1]. That is about 4 percent of the model running at a time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The hardware requirements make things clearer. A checkpoint is the saved file holding all the trained parameters. Inkling’s full-precision checkpoint needs at least 2 TB of combined GPU memory, which the model card gives as eight NVIDIA B300 cards or sixteen H200 cards [2].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Thinking Machines also talks about a quantised checkpoint. This means the same parameters are stored with less numerical precision, in roughly the way that writing 3.14 instead of 3.14159265 uses less space at the cost of some accuracy. That version needs around 600 GB and fits on four B300 cards [2].</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/da573382-bc44-4426-b7ca-619daac8a8ef?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">What Makes an FDE Role Credible? 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Routing</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Picking six experts out of 256 sounds simple, but it is not. Here’s how the selection works:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A small component called the router produces a score for every expert.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Each expert has its own list of numbers attached to it, learned during training.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The router compares the incoming token’s representation against each of those lists and gets a raw number out, higher when the two match closely.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Those raw numbers can be any size, so they get passed through a sigmoid. A sigmoid is a mathematical function that takes any number and converts it into a value between 0 and 1. For example, feed it 8, and you get back about 0.9997. Feed it 0, and you get exactly 0.5. Feed it negative 4, and you get about 0.018. Very large numbers approach 1, very negative numbers approach 0, and everything else ends up somewhere in between. Inkling’s router uses a sigmoid to produce its expert scores [1].</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>After scoring, the six highest-scoring experts run, and their outputs are combined using those same scores as weights. An expert scoring 0.9 contributes more to the result than one scoring 0.4.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This approach makes one specific type of failure more probable. To understand the failure, consider what happens across millions of training steps. Suppose, by luck, expert 47 gets picked slightly more often than average early on. It receives more tokens, so it receives more gradient updates, so it improves faster than its neighbours. Since it is better, the router scores it higher. Because it scores higher, it gets picked even more.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If we run that loop long enough, we can end up with a 256-expert layer where perhaps 20 experts handle nearly everything and the other 236 stay underdeveloped. This is called routing collapse. In other words, while we paid to store 256 experts, we got the capability of just 20. There is a second cost too. Since experts are usually spread across different machines, a machine holding four popular experts can become a bottleneck while its neighbours idle [9].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The traditional fix for this adds a penalty to the training objective that grows when expert usage is uneven. This means training the model on two things at once: predicting the next token correctly, and keeping expert usage balanced.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The trouble is that these two goals produce gradients pointing in different directions. The prediction gradient might say “increase this parameter,” while the balance penalty says “decrease it.” One of them wins, and either way the model is being pulled away from what you actually wanted. If we set the penalty strength high, the text quality degrades. If we set it too low, the experts collapse anyway [9].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Thinking Machines uses a method introduced by Wang and colleagues, which was also adopted by DeepSeek [1][8][9]. This method removes the conflict entirely by keeping a separate bias value for each expert, which is just a small number added to that expert’s score. The trick is where the bias gets applied.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td a token arriving at a layer in this setup. Consider that the router produces these sigmoid scores for four of the experts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Expert 47 has been overloaded recently, so its bias has drifted down to −0.15. This drops its selection score below expert 88’s, and expert 88 takes the slot instead. The bias changed which expert got picked. When expert 88’s output is combined into the final result, it is weighted by 0.80, its original router score, with the bias left out. In other words, the bias affects selection only. It never touches the weighting, and it is updated by a simple counting rule that runs outside backpropagation entirely. The main goal is to nudge down busy experts while giving a chance to the quieter experts.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The result is that expert usage stays balanced, and the training objective receives no competing gradient at all.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One point to note here is that two additional experts run on every single token regardless of routing [2]. These are called shared experts, and they hold the general-purpose processing that nearly every token needs. Thinking Machines states that the scores of the six selected routed experts and the two shared experts are normalised together before being used as weights [1], which means all eight are scaled to a common range and contribute proportionally. In other words, eight experts run per token in total.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Attention</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Sparsity handles the cost of the feed-forward step. The attention step carries a separate cost that grows far faster, and Inkling manages it by having most layers examine very little.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For every token, the model computes three sets of numbers:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A query, describing what kind of information this position needs.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A key, describing what kind of information this position offers.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A value, carrying the actual content this position passes along.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Every token’s query is compared against every earlier token’s key. Strong matches produce high scores, and those scores determine how much of each earlier token’s value gets pulled into the current position. This is how the word “it” in a sentence ends up connected to the noun it refers to.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Since every token compares itself against every earlier token, the number of comparisons grows with the square of the sequence length. For example:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>1,000 tokens produce roughly 1 million comparisons.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>10,000 tokens produce roughly 100 million.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>1,000,000 tokens produce roughly 1 trillion.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Inkling supports a context window of one million tokens [2], and a trillion comparisons per layer across 66 layers is far beyond what any reasonable amount of hardware can deliver.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is where a sliding-window layer restricts each token to a fixed number of recent tokens rather than everything before it. If the window is 1,000, then token number 500,000 compares itself against tokens 499,000 through 500,000 and stops there. That is 1,000 comparisons instead of 500,000, and the total for the whole sequence grows in a straight line rather than as a square.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This raises the obvious question that if every layer sees only a small window, how does information from page one of a long document ever reach page four hundred?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Inkling alternates between sliding-window layers and full-attention layers at a ratio of 5:1 [1]. Integration notes published by the vLLM project put concrete numbers on the split, describing the 66 layers as 55 sliding-window layers and 11 full-attention layers [7].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Information from far away travels through those eleven full layers. For example, picture a fact at token 200 that matters for a prediction at token 900,000. In layer 6, the first full-attention layer, the representation at position 900,000 can reach back and pick up that fact directly. From there, it rides forward within the local representations, is refreshed at layer 12, again at layer 18, and so on. The long-range path exists on roughly one layer in six, and the other five handle nearby context at a fraction of the price.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Inkling also uses 8 key-value heads [1]. Attention normally runs several times in parallel with different query, key, and value sets, and each parallel copy is called a head. Sharing a smaller number of key and value sets across many query heads reduces the memory needed while generating text.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below that tries to show this setup in a simplistic manner:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" href="https://substack.com/redirect/1261544b-ba89-48ff-b98a-fb6f4da65916?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There is one practical consequence of this approach. Long-context models often handle the general content of a large document well, but can still miss one specific detail buried in the middle.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Position</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Dealing with a million tokens brings up another question: how does the model represent where each token sits in the sequence?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Thinking Machines picked an older technique over the current standard. This is due to the lengths the model never saw during training.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The comparison between queries and keys involves no information about order. For example, both “the cat bit the man” and “the man bit the cat” contain the same five tokens, so without a position signal, the attention step produces the same comparisons for both. Something has to tell the model that “cat” came before “bit” in one case and after it in the other.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Almost every recent open model uses Rotary Position Embedding, shortened to RoPE. Each token’s query and key are treated as points that get rotated by an angle proportional to that token’s position in the sequence. Token 1 gets a small rotation, token 500 gets a much larger one, and so on.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The usefulness of this shows up when two tokens are compared. Since both were rotated by amounts tied to their own positions, the comparison between them depends on the difference between those two rotations, which tells how far apart they are.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, those rotation angles were only ever encountered at positions the model actually trained on. If training used sequences up to 32,000 tokens, then every angle the model learned to interpret came from that range. If we ask it about position 900,000, the angle involved falls outside anything it has experience with.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A whole family of techniques exists specifically to stretch RoPE into ranges beyond its training data.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Inkling uses a relative scheme in the style of Shaw and colleagues [1][10]. Rather than encoding where each token sits, this approach learns a value for each distance between two tokens and adds that value directly to the comparison score. For example, tokens at positions 5 and 9 are 4 apart. Tokens at positions 500,005 and 500,009 are also 4 apart. A relative scheme treats both pairs identically, because 4 is 4 wherever it occurs. Distances beyond some cutoff, say anything more than 128 apart, all share the same learned value, so a pair 900,000 tokens apart uses a value the model has seen countless times during training. Nothing has to be extrapolated.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The vLLM notes describe the implementation as a learned relative-position term added to the attention scores before they are converted into weights [7].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Thinking Machines states that this performed better and extrapolated better to longer sequences than RoPE in their testing [1].</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Convolutions</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Inkling adds one small operation named convolution to handle a job that attention would otherwise have to learn from scratch.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A convolution here means combining each position in the sequence with a few positions immediately before it. Inkling uses a window of four [7], so the numbers at position 100 get mixed with the numbers at positions 97, 98, and 99, using a small set of learned weights. Position 101 does the same with 98, 99, and 100. It is a cheap, fixed, strictly local operation.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td href="https://substack.com/redirect/dd038d3f-52fa-46b9-bdc0-e39356f47ade?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To understand better, consider the two tokens that make up “New York.” The second token means something quite different on its own than it does following the first. Attention can learn to make that connection, and it has to learn it, because attention starts as a general comparison mechanism with no built-in preference for nearby tokens over distant ones. A convolution supplies that local mixing directly through its structure, without any training required to discover that neighbours matter.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Thinking Machines places these convolutions at two kinds of locations:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>First, on the keys and values inside each attention layer</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Second, on the outputs of the attention and feed-forward steps before those outputs rejoin the main path through the model [1].</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The effect is that immediate context arrives pre-mixed, and attention can spend its capacity on the connections that genuinely require learning.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Multimodality</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Everything so far concerns text moving through the model. Images and audio have to get in first, and Inkling accepts both without a separately trained encoder standing in front of it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most multimodal models attach three trained components to a language model:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A vision encoder, trained on its own beforehand, converts an image into a list of numbers.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>An audio encoder does the same for sound.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Projection layers then convert both into the format the language model works with.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, in the case of Inkling, Sound arrives as a mel spectrogram, which is a standard way of representing audio as a grid of numbers. Frequency bands run down one axis, short slices of time run across the other, and each cell holds a loudness value. A three-second clip becomes a grid of a few hundred columns.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The dMel method then rounds each of those loudness values to one of a fixed set of levels, in the same way you might round 0.73 to 0.7 [1][11]. That is the entire conversion. No separate audio model needs training beforehand, because rounding numbers requires no training.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the case of images, an image is cut into square patches measuring 40 by 40 pixels [1]. A 400 by 400 pixel image therefore becomes 100 patches. Each patch passes through a small four-stage network called an hMLP stem, which combines the pixels within that patch and processes each patch independently of every other one [1][12]. The paper describing this reports that it adds under one percent to compute compared with the simplest possible alternative [12].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Both then pass through a lightweight conversion layer and join the text tokens in a single sequence, processed by the same 66 layers we have been talking about [1]. Thinking Machines states that these multimodal components were trained from scratch on general-domain data [1], meaning they learned alongside the rest of the model rather than arriving pretrained.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static"
