confusion can be that the launch announcement labels this as an encoder-free architecture [1], while the model card describes images as being encoded via a hierarchical patch encoder [2]. Both descriptions are accurate. Encoder-free here means there is no large, separately pretrained encoder network, rather than meaning there is no processing at all.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Moreover, this design predates Inkling. Thinking Machines described the same arrangement two months earlier for their real-time interaction system, using dMel for audio, 40 by 40 patches through an hMLP for images, and a lightweight conversion layer, with every component trained together from scratch [5].</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Effort</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>How long the model reasons before answering is adjustable, and it was trained into the model rather than requested through wording. This impacts the model’s benchmark numbers</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Effort is a number between 0 and 1. The documented presets run from 0 for none, through 0.1 for minimal and 0.2 for low, then 0.7 for medium, 0.9 as the default, and 0.99 at the top [6]. The spacing between those values is uneven, which is a hint that the number represents a learned response rather than a token allowance.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Mechanically, the setting arrives as text. Before the conversation begins, a system message stating the effort level is inserted ahead of everything else [6].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Reasoning models produce a stretch of working out before their final answer. This working-out phase costs tokens like everything else. Thinking Machines trained Inkling’s response to the effort setting during reinforcement learning, a training stage where the model produces complete attempts at tasks and receives a score for each attempt, then adjusts toward whatever scored well.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>During that stage, Thinking Machines varied the effort message across attempts while also adjusting the cost charged per token generated:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>An attempt labelled high effort could produce lengthy working-out without much penalty.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>An attempt labelled low effort was charged heavily for every token, so short answers scored better.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Across many attempts, the connection between the message and the profitable length was learned.</span></p><div auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here are some key points about limits:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Higher effort encourages more reasoning without guaranteeing a longer response or a better one on any single sample.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Setting effort to 0 pushes the model toward minimal reasoning without enforcing it as a hard rule.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Effort and the maximum token limit are separate settings that work independently, so a high effort setting may need a larger token limit to avoid being cut off.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Sweeping the effort setting across its range produces a curve of score against tokens generated. On the coding benchmark Terminal Bench 2.1, Inkling reaches the same score as NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Ultra while producing roughly a third as many tokens [1].</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Tradeoffs</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each of the design decisions we have looked at has trade-offs. Let us look at some of them:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Sparse routing keeps the per-token cost low and requires the entire model in memory regardless. The hardware floor stays high even though each token is cheap.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Mostly-local attention makes a million-token window affordable and leaves most layers with a narrow view of the sequence.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Relative position encoding removes the extrapolation problem and means every serving framework had to write new code for it, since the surrounding tooling was built around RoPE [7].</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Open weights covers the weights. The training data, the exact recipe, and the training code remain private, and the model card describes data provenance only in general terms [2]. The model can be modified, and reproducing or auditing it stays out of reach.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Safety behaviour is adjustable by anyone who retrains the model. The model card recommends layering external moderation tools around the model rather than relying on its own refusals, particularly for consumer-facing deployments [2].</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Thinking Machines states that other models available today, both open and closed, are stronger overall [1]. However, considering the availability for fine-tuning from day one, and the quantised checkpoint that brings the hardware requirements down, it is clear that Inkling has been built to be taken and adapted to the company’s use case.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let us look at the key ideas we’ve encountered while understanding Inkling’s design and architectural decisions:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Sparsity separates storage from compute. Total parameters tell you how much memory you need to hold the model. Active parameters tell you how much work each token requires. Inkling stores 975 billion and runs about 41 billion at a time.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Routing needs balancing, and the balancing mechanism matters. Applying a bias when selecting experts, while leaving it out when weighting their outputs, keeps usage even without adding a competing goal to training.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Long context works because most layers see little. Inkling runs 55 sliding-window layers and 11 full-attention layers, and long-range information travels through the eleven.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Position encoding is a decision about untrained lengths. Encoding the distance between tokens, rather than their absolute positions, means a pair 900,000 apart uses a value the model has seen many times.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Reasoning effort can be a trained setting. When it is, a benchmark score becomes one point on a curve rather than a fixed property of the model.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>References</span></strong></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: item.title: Beyond Senior - Creating Hope
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Beyond Senior - Creating Hope

Brandon Weaver

“This series explores what changes when engineers move past the senior level into staff and principal roles... I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about over the past 15 years, having now seen it at several companies, including how I’ve likely contributed to this problem myself. So what do we do then, when hope feels lost? That’s what I want to explore with this article, as I increasingly believe the most important responsibility we have as engineering leaders is creating hope.”

#Staff+ CareerGrowth
item.description: Beyond Senior - Creating Hope

item.title: Maximizing The Value Of Your Claude Code Sessions
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Maximizing The Value Of Your Claude Code Sessions

Lydia Hallie

“Being efficient with tokens doesn't mean using fewer of them overall. It means making sure the ones you do use go towards the thing you actually asked for. So let's look at what decides the price of a token, then what decides how many of them a session sends, and along the way, what that means for how you run a session.”

#Productivity AI CostOptimization
item.description: Maximizing The Value Of Your Claude Code Sessions

item.title: A Faster Way To Calculate The Day Of The Week
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>

A Faster Way To Calculate The Day Of The Week

Ben Joffe

“Throughout this article I will present a range of really fast functions to solve this problem, tuned for different use cases (throughput vs latency, different platforms etc.). Each outperforms existing solutions, and many have a latency of just a single multiplication plus two cycles.“

#DeepDive Performance Algo

item.title: Compression Is Prediction
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Compression Is Prediction

Annie Sexton

“I was reading about compression recently when I stumbled upon something crazy: that compressors and LLMs are, at their core, trying to solve the exact same problem. In this post, I’m going to walk us through the basics of compression to understand its deep relationship with language modeling. It’s probably going to blow your mind.”

#AI DeepDive
item.description: Compression Is Prediction

Within that second, software has to determine what is physically nearby, classify each object, estimate where those objects will move, select a path, and issue steering and braking commands.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Doing all of this quickly is something that has been largely solved. However, doing this correctly in unpredictable and distinct traffic situations is still an open problem. This is because real-world traffic produces more distinct scenarios than any team can pre-determine. For example, Waymo describes one such case, where a vehicle is on fire on the road ahead while the drivable lanes remain physically clear [3]. The geometry of such a scenario might permit driving straight through it. However, the real meaning of it calls for turning around or taking preventive action.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Waymo and Tesla, two companies investing in self-driving cars, have tried to come up with different types of answers to these questions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For reference, Waymo reports 220.6 million rider-only miles through March 2026. These are miles covered with no human in the driver’s seat, across five metro areas [5]. On the other hand, Tesla reports more than three million vehicles in the United States covering over 30 billion miles a year, with 1.28 million active Full Self-Driving subscriptions in the first quarter of 2026 [10]. Almost all of those Tesla miles involve a driver who remains responsible for the vehicle. Tesla’s driverless service is separate and much smaller, running without safety monitors in Austin, Dallas, and Houston, while the Bay Area service uses a safety driver [10].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Both approaches depend heavily on machine learning. But they differ in how much gets fixed in advance. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Sensing</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A camera records light intensity across a grid of pixels. Distance appears nowhere in that grid, so depth has to be computed from the arrangement of pixels, but that computation can be wrong. A large object far away and a small object nearby can occupy the same region of an image.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Lidar arrives at the same answer by a different route. The unit emits laser pulses, measures how long each pulse takes to return after reflecting off a surface, and converts that interval into a distance. We can think of the output of this as a point cloud, which is a three-dimensional set of measured points describing the surfaces around the vehicle [1]. The distance is no longer an estimate but a measurement.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Waymo’s sixth-generation system, which began fully autonomous operations in February 2026, carries 13 cameras, four lidar units, six radar units, and a set of external audio receivers used to detect sirens and railroad crossings [2]. Coverage overlaps in every direction and extends to 500 metres. This overlap is for help situations when rain, road grime, or ice limits what a camera captures. Lidar and radar sustain the perception capabilities in such scenarios. [2].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Tesla’s vehicles mainly rely on cameras. Instead, Tesla relies entirely on a “pure vision” approach that uses exterior cameras and artificial intelligence to navigate. For example, Tesla’s documentation describes Model 3 and Model Y as running camera-based Tesla Vision, without radar, using cameras and neural network processing [9].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 is that a direct measurement costs money while adding a component that can fail noticeably. However, a derived value may not cost much, but it can be wrong as well.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Representation</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Something has to convert millions of pixels and points into a description that the system can understand and operate on. The nature and form of that description is one of the most important architectural decisions for an autonomous driving setup.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Waymo places the Waymo Foundation Model at the centre, built from two components:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Sensor Fusion Encoder:</span></strong><span> It merges camera, lidar, and radar data over time and outputs objects, semantic attributes, and embeddings. These are compact numerical summaries that downstream components consume.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>A Driving VLM: </span></strong><span>Trained using Gemini and fine-tuned on Waymo driving data, they cover rare situations requiring background world knowledge, such as the burning vehicle example mentioned earlier.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Both feed a World Decoder that forecasts the behaviour of other road users, produces high-definition maps, generates candidate trajectories, and emits signals used to verify them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The system maintains compact structured representations, meaning explicit lists of objects, their semantic attributes, and roadgraph elements describing lanes and connections. The Waymo engineering team provides three reasons for such a setup:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Correctness and safety validation can run at inference time, while the vehicle is moving</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Simulation runs efficiently at large scale, because a compact world state is cheap to replay and modify</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Training feedback becomes verifiable, since a component evaluating driving quality has something concrete to measure</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This design provides significant benefits over pure end-to-end or modular approaches [3].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Tesla’s documentation talks about per-camera networks performing semantic segmentation, which assigns every pixel to a category, plus object detection and monocular depth estimation, meaning distance estimated from a single camera [6]. Those feed birds-eye-view networks that output road layout, static infrastructure, and three-dimensional objects in a top-down view. A full build involves 48 networks taking nearly 70,000 GPU hours to train and producing 1,000 distinct tensors per time step [6].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px occupies one end of this decision. For example, Waymo surveys a territory before operating there, recording lane markers, signs, curbs, and crosswalks. It then matches those maps against live sensor data to establish position, since GPS alone can lose signal [1]. The map is basically knowledge acquired once and reused. It saves computation on every trip, but also creates an obligation to keep it current. In contrast, Tesla’s approach skips the survey and derives equivalent information during the drive.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: that a structured representation can be inspected, logged, replayed, and checked against explicit criteria. But it limits what the system can express. On the other hand, a learned representation carries nuance no schema can anticipate.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Prediction</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Once the system holds a description of its surroundings, the next task is estimating what those objects will do. Several futures are valid at the same moment. For example, a cyclist approaching an intersection might continue straight, turn, or stop. A safe response should account for all possibilities.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Waymo describes the system as producing many possible paths for each road user rather than one, drawing on accumulated driving data and accounting for the different ways a car, a cyclist, and a pedestrian move [1].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In June 2025, Waymo published research on whether prediction quality scales predictably [4]. Using an internal dataset spanning 500,000 hours of driving, the study found that motion forecasting quality follows a power law in training compute, matching a pattern observed in language models. A power law here means each doubling of compute yields a proportional, predictable improvement. Data scaling proved critical, and increasing compute at inference time improved performance on harder scenarios.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Waymo reported the same trend in closed-loop performance, where results are measured in simulations in which the system’s own actions change what happens next. This trend suggested that real-world driving improves with more data and compute, rather than only benchmark scores.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Tesla’s describes an upgraded reinforcement learning stage in version 14.3, intended to cover long-tail edge cases, meaning rare situations that appear infrequently even across very large mileage [10].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div commits to one predicted future becomes fragile in situations where prediction matters most. However, carrying several weighted futures costs compute on every cycle, but can guard against the possibility of unusual situations.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Planning</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With a description of the surroundings and a set of likely futures, the system selects a trajectory. You can think of it as a specific path with speeds attached to it. The question is what verifies the trajectory before the vehicle executes it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Waymo trains large Teacher models to generate safe, comfortable, and compliant action sequences. It then distils them into smaller Student models sized to run onboard in real time [3]. Distillation transfers behaviour from a large model to a compact one. Output from that Student model then passes through a separate onboard validation layer, which verifies the trajectories the generative model produced [3]. This means that two independent components have to agree before the vehicle moves.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Tesla talks about building a planning and decision-making system that operates under uncertainty, with algorithms evaluated at the scale of the entire fleet, optimising for throughput, latency, correctness and determinism [6].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For Tesla vehicles on the road today, verification comes from a person. Full Self-Driving (Supervised) requires an attentive driver and leaves the vehicle slightly short of autonomous [7]. The system enforces this through a strikeout mechanism, where repeated inattention warnings disengage the feature for the remainder of a trip. Enough strikeouts suspend access for a week [7]. In the driverless service, that role belongs to safety monitors or remote supervision [10].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A validation layer catches a category of unacceptable outputs before they reach the actuators, and it can only evaluate against the defined criteria. Anything outside those criteria passes through unexamined. This is the same tradeoff as an assertion in production code, where the check is only as good as the condition behind it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Validation</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Waymo’s Safety Impact hub reports 220.6 million rider-only miles through March 2026, meaning no human occupied the driver’s seat for any of them [5]. Measured against human crash rates in the same operating areas, adjusted for where within each city the service drives, the reported reductions are 94% for serious injury or worse crashes and 82% for injury-causing crashes [5]. The methodology has been published in peer-reviewed journals, and the raw data is downloadable so third parties can reproduce the figures [5].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Tesla’s Vehicle Safety Report takes a different form. It compares Teslas with Full Self-Driving (Supervised) engaged against Teslas driven manually, using the same telemetry pipeline for both, and reports 7 times fewer major and minor collisions and 5 times fewer off-highway collisions [7][8]. A collision counts as occurring with the system engaged if it was active at any point within five seconds beforehand, a window chosen to capture cases where a driver took over shortly before impact [8]. Tesla attributes no fault in the reported data, treating that determination as too subjective to include [8].</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As you can see, the two reports answer different questions, and we can’t simply do a side-by-side comparison. The difference comes down to what each population represents:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Waymo is measuring outcomes across miles where no person was available to intervene.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Tesla is measuring whether an assistance system reduces collisions while a driver remains responsible.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Both companies also state their own limitations. Waymo states that no perfect comparison between autonomous and human data exists today, and that its operating cities see no appreciable snowfall [5]. Tesla states that its estimate of a United States average involves unavoidable assumptions that may skew the figure in either direction [8].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Waymo separates two things that are easy to conflate. Safety impact gets measured after deployment. Whether a release is acceptable to deploy at all gets determined beforehand through a Safety Framework and a Safety Case [5].</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Training</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Both systems improve between releases. However, the underlying mechanisms differ as much as the architectures.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Waymo runs three components off the same foundation model:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The Driver produces action sequences.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The Simulator generates scenarios for training and testing.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The Critic evaluates driving quality and surfaces problems.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Large versions of each get distilled into smaller ones that run at the required volume. Two loops connect them:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>An inner loop applies reinforcement learning inside simulation, where scenarios can be generated and repeated cheaply.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>An outer loop begins with the Critic flagging suboptimal behaviour from real driving, turns improved alternatives into training data, verifies the fixes in simulation, and deploys only once the safety framework confirms the absence of unreasonable risk.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Waymo states that its fully autonomous mileage now far exceeds its manually driven data, and that no volume of simulation or test-driver operation reproduces the situations encountered when the system operates with no driver present [3].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Tesla’s data comes from a consumer fleet. The Vehicle Safety Report describes two telemetry paths [8]. On shifting to park, a vehicle transmits anonymised mileage broken down by control type and road classification. On detecting a major or minor collision, it transmits a separate packet tied to the vehicle. Tesla reports receiving 2.5 billion telemetry packages in the third quarter of 2025 alone. Tesla has also built an evaluation infrastructure from anonymised fleet clips assembled into test suites, alongside simulation producing sensor data for automated testing [6]. Training runs on Cortex 1, listed at over 100,000 H100-equivalent GPUs in production, and Cortex 2 at over 130,000 in early ramp.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The same question recurs at every stage of an autonomous driving process.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>How much gets determined in advance and written into a form that can be examined, and how much gets computed during the drive by a model whose internal state stays out of reach?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each stage poses one version of it:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Sensing asks whether distance arrives as a measurement or as a derived value</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Representation asks whether the description of the world stays inspectable</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Prediction asks how many futures the system carries at once</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Planning asks what verifies a trajectory before execution</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Validation asks what kind of safety claim the resulting evidence can support</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Training asks which miles improve the system</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Waymo sits further toward written-down knowledge at most stages. This involves per-city preparation and purpose-built hardware. Tesla sits further toward computed knowledge. Both positions have merit, and only the future will tell which approach becomes more dominant or do things fall somewhere in the middle.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: item.title: Compression is prediction
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Compression is prediction

Annie Sexton

19 minutes by Annie Sexton Compression works by finding patterns in data and encoding them more efficiently, and better predictions about what comes next lead to better compression. Language models like GPT work the same way: they predict the next word based on context, which is exactly what a compression model does. A 2023 DeepMind paper confirmed this link, showing the two are mathematically equivalent. The main reason we don't use LLMs for everyday compression is cost — they are far too large and slow for practical use. Cloud vector databases were priced for humans. AI agents just
item.description: Compression is prediction

item.title: Improving heuristics
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Improving heuristics

Amit Patel

13 minutes by Amit Patel Placing "landmark" nodes on a map can make A* run faster without changing the algorithm itself. Before each search, Amit suggests running Dijkstra's from each landmark and storing the costs. Then use the triangle inequality to get a tighter lower bound on path length, replacing the standard distance heuristic. Placing more landmarks near map edges or common paths means fewer nodes are explored, though the best placement depends on your specific game and map layout.
item.description: Improving heuristics

item.title: A deep (and fuzzy) dive into search
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
A deep (and fuzzy) dive into search

Andrey Abramov

15 minutes by Andrey Abramov Fuzzy search helps search engines find results even when words contain typos or extra characters. Andrey explains two approaches used by SereneDB: Levenshtein automata and n-gram similarity. Levenshtein is useful for precise typo matching, while n-grams work better with longer text and partial matches. SereneDB combines these techniques to make fuzzy search practical and flexible.
item.description: A deep (and fuzzy) dive into search

item.title: Email encryption
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Email encryption

J. B. Crawford

32 minutes by J. B. Crawford Email was invented in many places at once, and its security was never a priority. Two main encryption standards emerged: PGP, which is open and decentralized but notoriously hard to use, and S/MIME, which works well inside organizations with shared infrastructure but struggles across them. In practice, most email today is encrypted in transit between servers, which solves many real threats even without full end-to-end encryption. The core problem is that strong encryption requires key distribution, and no universal solution for that has ever taken hold.
item.description: Email encryption

item.title: A shell exclamation mark is not for yelling
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
A shell exclamation mark is not for yelling

Filip Roséen

7 minutes by Filip Roséen Filip introduces shell event designators, a powerful but often overlooked way to reuse and modify previous commands. He explains useful shortcuts such as !!, !$, and !ssh, along with word and path modifiers. Filip also covers the POSIX fc command, safer ways to use these features, and when alternatives like Ctrl-R may be better. And the most popular article from the last issue was:

item.title: Passkeys in ASP.NET Core 10
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Passkeys in ASP.NET Core 10

Adrian Bailador

ASP.NET Core Identity in .NET 10 ships built-in WebAuthn/FIDO2 passkey support. Here's how registration and sign-in actually work under the hood, what MakePasskeyCreationOptionsAsync and PasskeySignInAsync do for you, and where the implementation deliberately stops short of a full WebAuthn library.
item.description: Passkeys in ASP.NET Core 10

item.title: REST API security best practices in ASP.NET Core
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
REST API security best practices in ASP.NET Core

Anton Martyniuk

Building secure ASP.NET Core APIs comes down to consistent habits across the whole codebase. Anton covers 18 practices, from enforcing HTTPS and validating JWT tokens properly to preventing SQL injection with EF Core and capping request sizes. Key themes include treating all input as hostile, using policies for authorization, storing secrets outside source control, and keeping dependencies patched. No single fix is enough, but starting with HTTPS, token validation, and input handling closes the biggest gaps fast.
item.description: REST API security best practices in ASP.NET Core

item.title: Cache invalidation in .NET
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Cache invalidation in .NET

Yohan Malshika

Caching speeds up apps but causes problems when data changes. Cache invalidation solves this by removing or updating stale cache entries after database changes. The Cache-Aside pattern handles this well: read from cache first, and after any update or delete, remove the related cache entry so the next request fetches fresh data. Adding a TTL gives extra protection, but explicit invalidation is still needed when accuracy matters.
item.description: Cache invalidation in .NET

item.title: The role of ActivitySource in OpenTelemetry for .NET
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
The role of ActivitySource in OpenTelemetry for .NET

Bart Wullems

ActivitySource is the entry point into .NET's native tracing story, and OpenTelemetry is just one listener on top of it. The name is the contract; get that right, register it with AddSource, and you can create as many instances of it as your codebase's structure naturally calls for. Don't let the fear of "duplicate instances" push you into DI ceremony you don't need.
item.description: The role of ActivitySource in OpenTelemetry for .NET

item.title: EF Core interceptors: The complete guide
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
EF Core interceptors: The complete guide

Mukesh Murugan

EF Core interceptors act as middleware for database calls, letting you observe, modify, or cancel operations like saving changes or running SQL without touching the calling code. The two most useful types are ISaveChangesInterceptor for audit fields and soft deletes, and IDbCommandInterceptor for SQL-level work like logging slow queries. To inject a scoped service like the current user, register the interceptor as scoped and resolve it through the AddDbContext service provider overload. 0;"><span><span>A forward proxy sits next to the client. Your laptop sends a request, the proxy forwards it out, and the destination never sees your real IP. Corporate networks use this to enforce policy, block sites, and cache traffic.</span><br><br><span>A reverse proxy sits next to the server. The client has no idea how many machines are behind it. The proxy decides who handles the request, terminates TLS, and keeps your backend off the public internet. NGINX and HAProxy are commonly used here, typically paired with a load balancer in front.</span><br><br><span>An API gateway is a reverse proxy that does more than route traffic. It also handles auth, rate limits, API keys, versioning, and request shaping. Without it, each microservice has to implement its own version of validation, throttling logic, and request logging.</span><br><br><span>A forward proxy represents the client, a reverse proxy represents the server, and an API gateway is what you add when ten services need the same authentication and rate limiting rules applied consistently.</span><br><br><span>In most real systems, all three are running at different layers. The forward proxy filters outbound traffic, the reverse proxy fronts the application servers, and the API gateway sits in front of your APIs to enforce policies before requests reach them.</span><br><br><span>Over to you: What's your proxy + gateway combo? Always interesting to see what teams pair together.</span></span></p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;font-size: Meta is now offering large equity retainers to keep these folks, and it doesn’t seem to be working.</span></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><em><strong><span>Grok Bot: the “OpenClaw moment” for managed AI agents? </span></strong><span>The Cursor team built and released a generic AI harness that feels like the “Codex experience, but for knowledge work.” I tried it out, automated a lot of my daily workflows, and am a massive fan. More AI vendors will surely copy this harness.</span></em></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Apologies for this week’s The Pulse arriving a day later than usual – our family got a puppy this week – who is beyond adorable –, but has kept me up a few nights, indirectly delaying this week’s The Pulse. We’re getting into a rhythm, so things should be back to normal, looking ahead.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>1. Meta unable to stop the “resignation-wave” it triggered?</span></h2><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Two months ago, I </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2daf997f-f3e0-452d-b560-8cf3886669b1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>covered</span></a><span> how Meta seemingly deliberately started destroying its once-standout engineering organization. The company did 10% layoffs at a time when revenue and profits hit an all-time high, and reassigned about 20-30% of software engineers to data labeling with basically no notice.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The result was that a good chunk of software engineers at Meta – even those not reassigned – were starting to interview elsewhere:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table visualised. Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2daf997f-f3e0-452d-b560-8cf3886669b1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>Why is Meta destroying its engineering organization?</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I said – and still maintain – that the layoffs were an unenforced, self-inflicted error on Meta’s part. Coupled with forced reassignment, they struck disaster. And I’ve now gathered new details that confirm that Meta is bleeding top engineering and product management talent:</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Some layoffs reversed, in the 11th hour</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the UK, mass layoffs require a notification to those </span><em><span>potentially</span></em><span> affected, before the cuts can happen. A few weeks after this notification, a good chunk of folks were “un-notified,” I confirmed. But those on notice had already started to look for jobs, obviously.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Retainer equity grants offered to IC6+ engineers resigning</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Meta started to offer large retainer equity grants to those resigning and leaving for Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI: a practice not done before. Talking with long-time Meta engineers, Meta simply didn't make counteroffers or negotiate when an engineer handed in their resignation. But this practice has been abandoned. Here’s a story of a senior, long-tenured engineer I confirmed to have happened:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>This dev was force-reassigned to one of the AI data labeling teams</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>They thought “oh no, this is not what I want to do” and started to interview</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Got a Google offer, but compensation was below their current one. Google basically lowballed them.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Decided to leave anyway. Told their new manager they are resigning.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>New manager asked for some time, then presented a large, one-off, retainer equity grant, vesting over 3 years</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The engineer went back to Google, telling the company unfortunately, they are a key engineer and showed them the retainer amount Meta is paying for them to stay</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Google upped their offer, out-bidding Meta’s retainer offer</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The engineer who was desperate to leave – even for lower compensation! – was thrilled, and happily left for Google.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Retainer equity seems to be offered for most IC6 engineers who resigned in the last few weeks. </span></strong><span>I talked with seven such people, who were all IC6 (staff-level engineer) and IC7 (principal-level engineers), who shared more details. They are not aware of IC4 (mid-level engineer) or IC5 (senior-level engineers) getting such offers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Retainer equity offered is $400K to $1M+</span></strong><span>, and vests over 3 years, for the folks who got these offers. The $1M+ offers were all for engineers with Anthropic or OpenAI offers, and I confirmed a $400K and a $600K grant for engineers with an offer for other, smaller AI startups.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A current Meta engineer who is interviewing asked me if these folks needed to present their offer letter to get a counteroffer. I asked two of these folks with counteroffers, and neither had to do so, but they both indicated they were handing in their resignation. Upon receiving this notification, their director, together with HR, offered a discretionary retainer equity, should they stay.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Anthropic and OpenAI on a hiring spree from Meta</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Anthropic and OpenAI seem to be on a hiring spree, signing Meta engineers that Meta wants to retain now that it is too late! I have confirmed that three engineers who received an offer from Anthropic were also offered large, $1M+ equity grants (vesting over 4 years) as counter-offers to stay. Two out of the three rejected it and joined Anthropic, and the third one initially accepted the offer and then still left for Anthropic a month later, forfeiting this grant.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI is having similar success, and the two AI labs seem to be the main destination for now ex-Meta engineers to bounce to. It makes sense: these companies can match Meta’s total compensation, and although neither OpenAI nor Anthropic is publicly traded, both companies organize secondary equity sales, and their respective IPOs are likely to happen in 3-12 months’ time.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>AI startups also successful in hiring infra experts from Meta</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I had an in-depth discussion with another long-tenured AI infra engineer at Meta, who was considering whether to stay, or to go. This person wrote up their situation, and shared it with me, writing:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“With the current situation at Meta (layoffs, forced drafting to do AI work, general sense of disruption at work, low moarale, and almost zero productivity across teams, plus multiple reorgs) I started to look around, on the market, a few weeks before the 20 May layoffs. I figured I have a 50% chance of being let go.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I did not get laid off, but I got offers from startups, and one from a high-growth AI startup I like, and also an offer from Google.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now, the pros to staying a Meta:</span></p><ul style="margin-left: 20px;margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Context, relationships</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Scale that few others have</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Big Tech perks, relatively “chill” WLB in terms of oncall</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>High TC</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The cons:</span></p><ul style="margin-left: 20px;margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Terrible morale, hard to “move” work through mostly unmotivated teams all around me</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Re-orgs continue, I have very low confidence in middle management (Directors, VPs) to navigate this churn</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Further layoffs are likely: it’s clear that there’s more bloat, surely Zuck will do another round in 2027. And no one is safe during a layoff</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>A ‘doom loop’ for anyone who stays</span></strong><span>: low morale → unmoitivated bith highly compensated engineers → a bloated organization that moves slow”</span></p></li></ul></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>After a new reorg, this engineer got a supportive manager, who made it clear they would help them thrive inside of Meta. So the engineer rejected both the AI startup’s offer and that of Google, deciding to stay… but only for a month!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The AI startup’s founder spent more time with this engineer, increased the equity in the package significantly, and convinced this engineer that at the startup they </span><em><span>matter </span></em><span>as a person, while at Meta they would be doing soulless work, worrying about the next layoff, probably early 2027.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So this engineer also handed in their resignation. And it all started with the layoffs: the engineer assumed there was a 50% chance of being let go and wanted more career stability!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Those deciding to not resign: stay for the money?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are engineers staying – at least until the end of the year. Another engineer I talked to decided to quit Meta with morale so low, and start his own thing. Management convinced him to stay until the end of the year, hinting at large equity refreshers being handed out around January, which could be in the $1M+ range for this specific engineer.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>A “mercenary” culture at Meta?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I wonder if Meta made a massive mistake by treating engineers as “commodities” and turning their culture into a “mercenary” one. Between March and June, Meta treated engineers as replaceable commodities that could be thrown out or moved between teams, while stripping them of any autonomy. The reassignments to AI labeling were not explained, nor were managers or individuals asked about preferences: from above, someone said that </span><em><span>Alice</span></em><span> and </span><em><span>Bob</span></em><span>, starting on Monday, are no longer with the team, but are training up Meta AI. Never mind that these were the two most experienced engineers on the team, or that </span><em><span>Bob</span></em><span> was the team’s infra expert, and </span><em><span>Alice</span></em><span> the “fixer” engineer on the team.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And all this damage was done, for what? It was to allow Meta to restart its AI coding model development efforts, and release </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2658ec7e-344b-4e2a-a9e1-cb39f2e8d5dd?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Meta Muse Spark</span></a><span>: an AI model that is currently the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/40429bac-9bd8-4e74-854f-7b40117233ae?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>7th most capable</span></a><span> AI model as per Artificial Intelligence Analysis, tied with Grok 4.5. Credit where it’s due: with this model, Meta is now well ahead of Google’s Gemini in capability.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With the damage done, there is little motivation for anyone to stay at Meta – unless they are on a visa, or if it’s about the money. You can have an OK engineering culture with a team who is mostly interested in making more money than what they would elsewhere: but this is more of a mercenary culture, and companies run by mercenaries are more easily out-executed by teams where people believe in the mission of the company.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>If you work at a company that would love to hire from Meta: now is (still) your opening!</span></strong><span> So go for it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And if you’re at Meta: you are </span><em><span>so</span></em><span> in-demand, outside of the company, at places where engineering is still treated as a profit center. As Ryan Nystrom, currently building AI at Notion, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/28cf2ef7-56b6-410c-aef7-a450032a6565?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>put it:</span></a></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Meta friends: the industry is exhilarating right now. Get out. Go build something. The handcuffs are an illusion.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’m having the time of my life at Notion. Come, and have fun again.”</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>2. Grok Bot: the “OpenClaw moment” for managed AI agents?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>AI agents are already excellent for coding work, and apps like the Claude Cowork desktop app, the Codex desktop app are </span><em><span>okay </span></em><span>at using your own computer for more complex tasks. For example, a few weeks ago, I asked Claude Cowork to help with my business accounting: log into my bank (Revolut), download statements, match them up against invoices filed, and download missing invoices. Cowork took over my browser and did </span><em><span>some</span></em><span> of this, but in the end, I just took over and finished it manually, because it kept getting confused.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In general, I did not find any tool that could speed up my “mindless administrative work of clicking here then here then there then saving this file, then uploading it…”. Until yesterday, that is, when I tried out Grok Bot, a new tool from SpaceX.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Now, before I continue: I have zero affiliation with SpaceX or Grok, and if anything, I have quite the reservations about anything named “Grok”, given how one month ago, Grok CLI </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b079fd34-9c17-4d4b-b443-d14663164d1d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>uploaded sensitive .env files</span></a><span>, secretly, to the cloud. I’m talking about this tool because the UX it has invented works better than anything before, and I expect many more tools to follow this UX pattern and gain rapid adoption.</span></em></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>OpenClaw, but without needing to set up anything</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The interface of Grok Bot is familiar to all of the other GUI-based AI harnesses (like Codex / ChatGPT, Claude Cowork). Who knows, but probably so!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, we’re stuck in this world where, when APIs with granular control and more secure access do not support certain things, you don’t have much choice but to automate a web-based workflow rather than end-to-end automation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In my case, I took a calculated risk, signed in the bot to my support and contact email, and the agent now took over to do work that would have been impossible via API. And it found emails in spam that were mislabelled.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This felt magical!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Automating “grunt” workflows</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Another weekly workflow has to do with archiving my podcast recordings. My video production team prepares a several GB-large file with several videos, on their Dropbox account. I want to save this to our team Dropbox account. The flow is this:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>I get a Slack message with a Dropbox link for the podcast video assets</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>I open it, click “copy to Dropbox”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Once it’s copied to Dropbox, it’s copied to the wrong place: by default it chooses my personal Dropbox.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>I move the files to the team folder, into a specific structure with numbering, by the year published, etc</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>This whole thing takes about 2-3 minutes… but I have to do it every week!</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I automated this whole process in a matter of a few minutes by describing the above workflow to Grok Bot.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>First, I asked it to set up connectors by connecting to Slack and Dropbox. (This is meta, but it’s pretty amazing that with an “AI-native” tool like this you can ask the tool to do stuff in its own app, so you don’t even need to learn yet another new UI!)</span></p><div
