style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In a matter of minutes, I had my workflow to block and block PR-like emails set up, and set up to run three times a week. This is how </span><em><span>easy</span></em><span> this should be – and it was the first tool where I felt that the tool doesn’t get in the way of helping automate my workflow: instead, it helps with it.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Verbal expression >> UI connectors for casual workflows</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One reason no-code and “visual coding” tools never got mainstream adoption is that they become difficult to manage when you do anything moderately complex. They also take effort to learn, and have a bunch of limitations that you only discover as you go.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In contrast, a lot of the “everyday” work can be described with a few sentences. For example, this spam filtering and blocking exercise is a sentence: even if we could build a massive state machine to get a similar result!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Grok Bot has lots of issues, but it shows where “general agents” are heading</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Grok bot it not without its flaws. The biggest ones are:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Permissions system is nonexistent. </span></strong><span>There’s a very basic permissions systems with the plugins/connectors, but nothing similar to how Codex or Claude Code asks for permissions before doing any kinds of operations.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Security. </span></strong><span>How secure is this setup? How easy is it for webpages to trick the AI to give out sensitive secrets, keys, session tokens it has? I don’t know: and I assume there are lots of risks here.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Auditing</span></strong><span>. There’s no easy way to review what the agent has done: especially around what “user actions” it did (e.g. send an email, initiate a payment, and so on)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Privacy: </span></strong><span>how can I block the bot from accessing very sensitive data like passwords, credit card numbers, 2FA restore codes? There currently seems to be no way of doing so.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Transparency:</span></strong><span> what if the developer sneaks malicious code into Grok Bot, how would I or anyone else know? What if they make an update that starts uploading all my private files to their cloud, like Grok CLI did? Also no answer.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Until all the above are solved, Grok Bot is unlikely to be secure enough for enterprise usage. However, the UX and workflow paradigm this tool built is a massive step up from existing tools, and I expect vendors like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google to copy this approach and offer similar harnesses, perhaps with better security / auditing / transparency promises.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the meantime, I’d suggest using Grok Bot at your own risk, and connect it to systems that do not have overly sensitive data stored in them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The kind of “general AI harnesses” that will go mainstream will be similar to Grok Bot – I’m pretty certain of this. </span></strong><span>This kind of UX is so intuitive, and the models have gotten good enough to interpret vague instructions. I’m sure there will be a need for more specialized harnesses with more sophisticated UI, but for broadly general administrative and general knowledge work, this kind of user experience works amazingly well.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><em><span>Do leave a comment if you’ve tried out this tool, or another similar one, and what part of your daily workflow it’s made easier.</span></em></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>This post is only for paying subscribers of </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIxMTIwMjE0OSwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3ODY3MjY4NTksImV4cCI6MjEwMjMwMjg1OSwiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.IVnL2Fpd3o8fuuFkkPkfkHJhGjTXut55UiC-OKHBRGU?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. item.title: Landing The Plane
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Landing The Plane

James Stanier

“If starting a project is like takeoff, finishing it is like landing, demanding a completely different kind of skill and attention, and it’s where most of the risk accrues. After all, the hardest part of flying a plane is landing it. This article is about why endings are so hard, what goes wrong when you don’t manage them deliberately, and how to land your projects well.”

#Management Productivity
item.description: Landing The Plane

item.title: The Same Side Of The Table
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Same Side Of The Table

“The cardinal rule of meetings with your direct reports is that you are always on the same side of the table. From the moment you walk in to the moment you leave, every single thing that your team does is a reflection and extension of you.”

#Leadership Management
item.description: The Same Side Of The Table

item.title: Advice So Common You Think You Can Skip It
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Advice So Common You Think You Can Skip It

Steve Huynh

“There is a whole class of advice that gets repeated so often it stops registering with us. Somewhere along the way, we decide that anything this common must be for beginners, so we’re allowed to skip it. We nod, we say “Yeah, yeah, yeah,” and then we go looking for the real advice. You can spot this sort of advice by noticing (a) how fast you agree with it and (b) how rarely you do it.”

#CareerGrowth
item.description: Advice So Common You Think You Can Skip It

item.title: Control And Complexity: Tension In Systems Design
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Control And Complexity: Tension In Systems Design

Fred Hebert

“The adoption of LLMs in software development has led countless organizations to rapidly change their practices and structures. Old methods are questioned, replaced, and repurposed as the economics around creating new code get shaken up. Because humans and LLMs aren’t interchangeable, the dynamics in play are also very different. Systems are systems, and so regardless of what is changing, there are known patterns on which we can draw to provide some guidance and warnings.”

#Architecture AI
item.description: Control And Complexity: Tension In Systems Design

item.title: A Harness For Every Task: Dynamic Workflows In Claude Code
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
A Harness For Every Task: Dynamic Workflows In Claude Code

Thariq Shihipar

“Workflows allow you to dynamically create harnesses that enable Claude to solve all of those problems and more natively inside of Claude Code. You can also share and re-use these workflows with others. In this article, I’ll cover my initial workflows experiences and learnings so you can take full advantage.”

#AI Guide DevEx
item.description: A Harness For Every Task: Dynamic Workflows In Claude Code

Software Engineering At A Proprietary Trading Company: Optiver

Gergely Orosz

“Building better AI models getting more focus than lower latency, owning the full stack from applications to building custom hardware, very different incentives to most tech companies in play, and more.”

#DeepDive IndustryTrends
item.description: Software Engineering At A Proprietary Trading Company: Optiver

item.title: Write For People
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Write For People

Vicki Boykis

“We should strive for simplicity. If we can’t, it could be because we don’t understand the problem ourselves yet enough to compress it. That’s cool. Understanding things is hard. Naming things is hard, for the same reason. But it should be a little harder. Like 10% harder. We should be more tired than the model, or at least a little less verbose.”

#AI Communication
item.description: Write For People

break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>In a service-based architecture, a single product screen showing a user profile, that user’s five most recent orders, the delivery status of each order, and a short list of recommendations requires data from four separate services. Each service stores only its own data, so none of the four services returns the full set on its own. In other words, the caller issues four separate calls, and merges the resulting four responses in the structure needed for the user interface. This merging step is API composition, and it exists in every system where data is split across more than one service.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The code that performs this merging can run in several places. It can run inside the mobile application, on a server in the datacenter, at a CDN edge location, or inside one of the four services. Putting a server between the mobile application and the four services adds a network hop, which sounds like it should cost extra time. However, it usually reduces total load time instead, because a round trip between a phone and a server on a weak mobile connection can take a few hundred milliseconds, while a round trip between two services inside the same datacenter takes a fraction of a millisecond. To put it simply, trading four expensive round trips for one expensive round trip plus four cheap ones is often a large net saving.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, latency is only the first tradeoff. The place where the merge operation runs also determines what happens when one of the four services is unavailable, how much of the response can be cached, and which team has to approve a change before the screen ships.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we are going to dive deep into the area of the API composition problem and the patterns associated with it. Here’s what we will cover:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The API composition problem</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Client-side composition</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 under-fetching</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: This take is from one of my favorite voices in software reliability and observability: Charity Majors, CTO and cofounder of Honeycomb, co-author of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/210bc125-edd4-4411-8e31-544e55064ae8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Observability Engineering</span></a><span>. (Note: the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/210bc125-edd4-4411-8e31-544e55064ae8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>second edition of Observability Engineering</span></a><span> is out, and it’s pretty much a full rewrite of the book, I recommend grabbing it if you’re building reliable systems)</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this episode, I sat down with Charity to discuss how her thinking on AI has evolved, why she believes it is becoming a foundational part of software engineering, and what that means for how teams build, review, and ship software.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We explore how AI is changing the economics of code generation, why reliability and verification are increasingly the bottlenecks, and why the rise of non-deterministic systems requires more engineering discipline. Charity shares her views on code reviews, observability, DevOps, leadership, and why both AI skeptics and enthusiasts are getting important things right.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);">Takeaways from the conversation with Charity</h3><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/cf81be0d-0573-4bdc-a878-6ed2d8b91fe4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/HC8T1OlgYi0" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here are 13 parts I found especially interesting, talking with Charity:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>1. In March 2025, Charity told the audience at SREcon to try vibe coding, and back then, the response was grumbling.</span></strong><span> Charity’s point was that people who are skeptical of AI should still learn to use it, because you can complain better if you’ve learned it. At this time, Charity still saw AI having a bigger impact than a new programming language, but was skeptical that it would have a generational impact.​</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>2. Charity’s turning point in seeing AI as a generational change was in November 2025. </span></strong><span>This was due to Opus 4.5, but Charity argues that the coding harness (Claude Code) made the bigger difference. Because thanks to Claude Code, harnesses went from being more of a shell script to serious infrastructure.​</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>3. The impact of AI on the industry in 2025 was similar to the impact of the cloud in 2010. </span></strong><span>Looking back, Charity is comfortable saying this: in 2010, it became clear that cloud computing was certainly going mainstream and would change the infra-layer. After 2025, it’s also clear that AI will have a similar impact on the infrastructure of building software.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>4. Engineers who were skeptical of AI up to 2025: they had good reason to be so.</span></strong><span> This was because we’ve seen plenty of technologies and innovations in the past that all promised to transform the software industry, but later fell short. Examples include COBOL (a technology promising that programmers would no longer be needed to create software), neural nets, no-code and low-code tools.​</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>5. The question engineers need to answer: what would it take for you to be fully comfortable shipping code you have not read? </span></strong><span>Charity believes it is a “when” and not an “if” that professional software engineers will ship code they never looked at – and thus do not understand – to production. Engineering is building the systems that validate this code, and allow shipping with full confidence.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>6. AI could have the software industry go through the “pets” to “cattle” change that compute infra went through in the 2010s. </span></strong><span>Up to now, writing software from scratch was far more expensive than editing existing software. But now, generating hundreds of variants of a function can be done faster than how long it would take you to hand-write it once.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Charity believes that we might be at the beginning of the transition from “pets” to “cattle” that happened at the hardware infrastructure layer. Before the 2010s, configuring and repairing individual servers was commonly done. But with tools like Terraform and Kubernetes, individual servers having issues are no longer fixed up: they are re-created instead. Charity thinks the same might happen with code, sooner rather than later. When there’s an issue with the code, generate new code that solves it, and is verifyably correct.​</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>7. Her contrarian take: code review is overrated, and the least valuable part of what humans add to software engineering. </span></strong><span>Charity says that humans are good at conversations and deciding what to build, not reading code to check for correctness, syntax and bugs.​</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>8. Charity’s verdict of 20 years of DevOps: it failed. </span></strong><span>The DevOps feedback was about trying to create a feedback loop that connected people writing the code to the code running in production. She thinks that the “ops people: learn to code!” wave worked, but the “software engineers: understand your code in production” failed,  to this day.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>9. Non-deterministic systems require more engineering discipline versus before. </span></strong><span>With code written by AI, we’re reducing the trust in the code (because we no longer wrote it), so we need to increase trust at the other part of the development process. Specifically, at validation: with things like tests, evals, and conformance testing.​</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>10. Charity’s career advice for engineering directors: run towards the waves, and get AI on your resume, immediately. </span></strong><span>It’s an anxious time to work in tech, thanks to all the change, driven by AI. Charity reminds us that anxiety and excitement are physiologically almost the same, but the difference is agency. When you have no agency, you’re more likely to get anxious, and when you do, you’re more likely to get excited.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So her advice to anxious engineering directors: consider going back to IC work, where you’ll have far more agency. IC work is well-respected, getting back to it has never been easier, but the window to do so is closing. As she put it:​</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The next time you’ll have a job interview, you’ll be filtered out if you don’t have AI experience.”​</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>11. On AI fatigue: take back control with small acts! </span></strong><span>We talked about various types of AI fatigue: reviewing AI slop, getting tired of the AI hype, and getting worn down by “doom trolling” by AI CEOs. Charity finds small acts of taking control back in your work from AI tools help. For example, none of the Honeycomb team uses AI on Wednesdays.​</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>12. Charity would like to see both the “AI-pilled” and the “anti-AI” camps tell the stories better. </span></strong><span>As she put it:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“There are some really incredible things happening in software right now, for example, with rewrites and with automating away toil. Not a single person that I’ve talked to would give up using AI.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But half of the people are seeing the </span><em><span>wins,</span></em><span> and they’re not connecting it to the </span><em><span>cost</span></em><span>, which makes them think that their coworkers are just afraid of getting automated out of existence.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So that’s my beg to everyone who listens to this: tell the whole story! Talk about the costs as well. We’re all in it together.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>13. Charity’s rule on AI writing: do not send any message/email to a human that you yourself have not read in full. </span></strong><span>She also says that it would take them longer to read whatever you send than it took you to produce it: it’s probably slop!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The mechanics start with where the code runs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>GitHub’s coding agent operates in its own ephemeral development environment, which is a temporary workspace that exists only for that task. It is powered by GitHub Actions, the same automation system that runs tests and builds on the platform [1][2]. In practice, you assign a task to the agent the way you would open a ticket. The agent reads through the repository, edits files, runs the tests and linters (tools that check code for problems), and opens a draft pull request for a person to review [1]. Each cloud run happens in a fully isolated, single-use Linux environment hosted by GitHub. Every new task starts from a clean workspace [4]. The review step stays human, which keeps the existing quality gate intact.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram Reviewing a colleague’s branch is not so different from reviewing an agent’s branch.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Routing to other companies’ models is a deliberate decision. GitHub is positioning the workflow, the execution environment, and the governance layer as the durable product, and treating the underlying model as a swappable component.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let us now look at how Vercel developed its architecture around what happens after the code exists. This is somewhere between a working demo and production-ready software.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Production</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Vercel starts from a different premise where code generation is assumed, and the design deals with carrying the generated code into production. This is the stage where most enterprise software work actually happens, because it involves existing applications rather than fresh prototypes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The rebuilt version of v0, Vercel’s generation product, runs on a sandbox. It is an isolated space for executing code that imports a real GitHub repository and automatically pulls in the project’s environment variables and configuration. Every prompt produces code that fits the actual application and lives in the repository itself [5].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A Git panel handles the workflow around it. You create a branch for each chat, open a pull request against the main branch, and deploy when it merges. This means a product manager or a designer can ship through the same review process an engineer uses [5].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Vercel’s rationale about this approach is that AI-assisted building is already happening inside companies, and it has produced real failures. Incidents have been reported, such as credentials pasted into prompts, private data reaching the public internet, and deleted databases, often with the audit trail left empty [5]. Therefore, wrapping code generation in real deployment controls is the right response.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table workflow is the execution layer. Every sandbox runs inside a Firecracker microVM, a lightweight virtual machine that isolates untrusted code. The reason for this isolation is that the code an AI wrote is code you have yet to review. Therefore, running it needs a boundary strong enough to contain mistakes. A microVM provides that strong boundary.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The billing model depends on how agents actually run. Vercel’s Fluid compute lets several requests share one running instance, with one using the processor while another waits on input or output. It charges for active processor time while treating wait time as free [6][7]. Agentic workloads spend much of their time waiting on a model to respond, so this pricing matches the real work being done.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: with a frustration many developers face in their careers. The thing that worked in a demo behaves differently in production. However, Vercel’s design tries to close that gap by making the preview a real deployment from the start.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Nevertheless, strong isolation carries a cost per unit of compute. There is an open question about whether the heaviest workloads eventually move to cheaper execution options elsewhere. Vercel’s wager is that a single, convenient platform keeps them in place.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To summarize, GitHub owns the workflow, and Vercel owns the route to production. Both of them still depend on one assumption that Replit chose to attack directly. Let us look at that now.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Verification</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Replit concentrated its work on whether autonomously generated code genuinely works using a verification loop built into the agent itself.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Replit’s Agent 3 runs what the company calls a reflection loop. The agent generates code, runs it, tests the result, and repairs failures, repeating that cycle until the tests pass [8]. This loop is reliable because of how the testing is done. Replit built a REPL-based verification system that runs code immediately and pairs that execution with a real browser it drives automatically, so it can click buttons, submit forms, and check data the way a user would [9].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The specific problem this approach targets has a memorable name inside Replit: the Potemkin interface. It is basically a feature that looks complete on screen yet fails the moment it is used [9]. Catching that class of error is what allows the agent to run on its own for more than 200 minutes at a stretch, a large increase over the roughly 20 minutes of its predecessor [8][9].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The verification runs as its own process.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A testing subagent follows a simple cycle of taking an action, observing the result, and repeating. When it finishes, it returns a summary to the main agent describing what works and what broke [9]. This multi-hundred-step testing costs a median of roughly twenty cents per session and runs several times faster and more cheaply than relying on general-purpose computer-use models [9].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: shipped a feature that looked finished and later broke understands the problem here. Replit is trying to automate the check that catches exactly that, so that the automation can be trusted.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A verification loop reduces the risk substantially. Some failures still surface only under conditions a single test session might miss, which keeps this a pretty hard problem even with a capable tester in place.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Interoperability</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Every architecture we have looked at assumes its agent can reach tools and data that live outside the model, and doing that cleanly requires a common method. That method is the Model Context Protocol, usually shortened to MCP.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Before a standard like this existed, connecting several AI applications to several external tools meant writing a separate custom integration for each pairing. In this approach, the number of integrations grew quickly as both sides multiplied. Anthropic introduced MCP to replace those fragmented, one-off connections with a single protocol, so each application and each tool implements the standard once and then works with everything else without additional changes [10].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A host, which is the AI application such as an IDE or a chat client, creates one or more clients, and each client connects to a server that exposes some capability [11]. A server offers three kinds of capability:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Tools, which the model can call to take an action, such as creating a record or running a query.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Resources, which supply context data the model can read, such as a file or a database schema.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Prompts, which provide reusable instruction templates.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The whole exchange runs over a defined message format across either a local or a remote connection. The effect is that a tool provider builds one MCP server and every compliant agent can use it [11].</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" the earliest developer tools to integrate MCP [10], GitHub added an MCP registry to VS Code where a server can be enabled with a single click [3], and Stripe runs an official MCP server for its payment operations [12].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Going deeper, MCP also standardizes how agents reach existing APIs rather than replacing those APIs. A single shared entry point also concentrates security in one place. That makes careful control over which servers an agent may use an important part of any real deployment.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Tradeoffs</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each of these architectures and approaches has trade-offs:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>GitHub gains breadth and governance by routing to many vendors’ models. But the cost is that it owns the surface rather than the intelligence underneath. Whether a coordination and governance layer stays valuable as models and agents keep changing is an open question.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Vercel gains strong isolation by running generated code inside microVMs, and that isolation carries a cost per unit of compute. There is a question about whether the heaviest workloads eventually move to cheaper execution elsewhere</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Replit gains long stretches of autonomy through its verification loop, and the more work an agent does on its own, the more weight rests on that verification being right. The Potemkin problem (code that looks complete yet fails when used) stays difficult even with a capable tester, because some failures appear only in situations a test session might miss.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>MCP gains a clean, reusable way to connect agents and tools, and a shared standard also concentrates risk into a common entry point. When many agents reach many tools through one protocol, controlling which servers an agent may use, and their permission levels, becomes a central problem rather than a detail.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Understanding these costs is what separates picking one of these tools from understanding why it was built the way it was.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The pattern across all three companies is the same. Code generation became cheap, so the value moved into the engineering that surrounds it. Each company placed its bet on a different piece of that surrounding work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>GitHub bet on orchestration, building a control layer that runs and governs many agents inside the pull request workflow developers already use.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Vercel bet on production, wrapping generated code in real deployments and running it inside isolated microVMs built for untrusted code.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Lastly, Replit bet on verification, driving a real browser in a self-testing loop so an agent can work on its own for hours and still be checked.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Underneath all three, MCP provides the common protocol that lets any agent reach any tool, which is why every one of these platforms now supports it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>References:</span></strong></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: We resume with a detailed deepdive about the trading industry, and interesting engineering challenges that come when working at a company that has no external customers, but where a single, unfortunate enough software bug could wipe out the whole company.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In tech recruitment, proprietary trading companies have a particularly high bar and typically offer compensation on a par with, or even exceeding, Big Tech; right at the top of the market. That’s because for these market makers, success is all about gaining a competitive edge over rivals. Such competitive advantages today includes software that is superior to that at their competitors.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Software engineers tend to know little about trading companies – and this piece aims to change that. </span></strong><span>Trading companies build bespoke hardware stacks and have larger platform engineering teams than most workplaces. For software engineers, it’s a lucrative niche in terms of compensation, full-stack (hardware to software) work and for engineering challenges, and so we decided to go deeper in this interesting area.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In order to find out more, The Pragmatic Engineer sat down with a leading proprietary trading firm, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a54337e3-640a-47cd-8526-f959513cac8f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Optiver</span></a><span>. Headquartered in Amsterdam, they also have a large engineering presence in the US and globally. We met engineers and engineering leaders to learn in depth how engineering works in a modern trading business, with contributions from:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c5e67c46-5517-4dd1-9ead-ff64ba7a9b4e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Alex Itkin</span></a><span>: CTO, Optiver US</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aa3ffade-82e8-4ac1-a18e-b017e2ad5188?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Pat Cooney</span></a><span>: Head of Global Platform Engineering</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/607c5eba-d150-4733-8ebd-e74ff95f3445?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>David Gross</span></a><span>: Technology Lead, Options</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Thanks to everyone at Optiver for taking part in this report which lifts the lid on how software engineering is done when even nanoseconds can count. In this article, we look into a software engineering environment that’s distinct from what you expect at most startups and Big Tech. For example:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>No external customers. </span></strong><span>Usually, companies have consumer customers (B2C), business customers (B2B), or both. But not trading houses like Optiver, where their own business is </span><em><span>the</span></em><span> customer. This is a different reality: there’s no external deadlines and related pressures, but personal motivation to improve is highly valued.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Latency: “enemy number one”. </span></strong><span>Nearly every major engineering decision at Optiver is made in the interest of minimizing latency – the amount of time between a request and response. This approach is present across the software stack and in kernel-level work. It’s why Optiver manufactures its own hardware.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Today, latency is the floor, and AI models are becoming a differentiator. </span></strong><span>Gone are the days of having lower latency than the competition allowing for arbitrage opportunities to make risk-free profits. Instead, information models are becoming a differentiator: slow models with a fast trigger sending signals to execute trades, and fast models running at the edge of the network making trade decisions realtime.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Haunted by a bug that nearly killed a business.</span></strong><span> Among trading houses, there’s a cautionary tale of when a peer company, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f1acf5f4-8042-4504-8127-e843823135ed?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Knight Capital</span></a><span>, nearly went bankrupt after a single bug in a high-frequency trading system triggered a $440M loss.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Different incentives. </span></strong><span>The business is incentivized to move very fast, but with a high premium on caution in order to avert potential financial disasters on the market. This cautious attitude to risk in concert with chasing speed feels pretty distinct in tech.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: source</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Based on whose money is being traded, there are three main capital sources:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Investment banks </span></strong><span>serve corporate and institutional clients by raising capital, advising on deals, and executing trades on their behalf. Examples: Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Hedge funds </span></strong><span>raise money from external investors and trade it on their behalf, charging management & performance fees. Examples: Citadel, Millennium, Two Sigma, Bridgewater.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Proprietary trading firms</span></strong><span> trade only their own capital, with no clients or external funding. Examples: Optiver, Jane Street, Jump Trading, DRW, Hudson River Trading.</span></p></li></ol><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Trading eras</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver’s CTO US Alex Itkin pictures the evolution of trading as having unfolded across four eras to date:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Pre-electronic (pre-1990s).</span></strong><span> Trading was done face-to-face on noisy trading floors and by phone. Prices were shared on reels of ticker tape and printed in newspapers. Investors contacted brokers to place orders.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>First wave of electronification (early/mid 1990s).</span></strong><span> Financial markets moved onto computer screens but orders were still entered manually.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Automated trading (late 1990s to ~2015).</span></strong><span> Computers did the same as human traders, but faster and at scale. This was the “mechanical” automation era of building automated workflows without data-driven decision-making.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Quantitative trading (~2015 to present).</span></strong><span> Data-driven decision-making with machine learning models and inference compute, with human decision-making in some key areas.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Each era “weeded” the market. </span></strong><span>Some companies excelled at automated trading but never made the leap to quantitative trading. According to Itkin, competition has got tougher over time, while the number of serious players has decreased. Today, there are only a handful of really big firms, and one reason for this is cost: investment in research clusters – which serious prop shops all do – requires hundreds of millions of dollars.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Optiver at a glance</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver turned 40 years old in March 2026, launching in 1986 at the European Options Exchange. Today, the company has:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>~2,200</span></strong><span> employees</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>~950</span></strong><span> engineers and ~1,000 traders and researchers</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>11</span></strong><span> </span><strong><span>offices</span></strong><span>: Amsterdam (HQ), Chicago (US HQ), Austin, New York (2025), London, Sydney, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Singapore, Taipei, and Mumbai.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>10M+</span></strong><span> trades executed per day, across 100 exchanges</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>€4.5B </span></strong><span>($5.1B) in trading income, and €1.7B ($1.95B) profit, as per </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/16a78e44-1c77-453d-8acd-2f0c33558a88?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>2025 financial results</span></a></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver is a mix of:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Market maker</span></strong><span>: providing liquidity on exchanges by quoting ‘buy’ and ‘sell’ prices of financial products and earning the spread between the two.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>High-frequency trader:</span></strong><span> executing automated trading strategies at very low latency</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>High-Frequency Trading (HFT)</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>High-frequency trading involves placing high volumes of orders at lightning speed in an effort to take advantage of extremely rapid market movements. In this domain, speed is the biggest advantage, and achieving it obviously involves high-performance computing. The basic trading loop is run millions of times a day. It’s made up of three steps:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Watch</span></strong><span> the market for new information like price changes</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Decide</span></strong><span> what the information means and the right trade to make</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Send</span></strong><span> a trade to the exchange before competitors do</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In trading, timing is everything, and for some types of trade even nanoseconds count. Optiver’s fastest trading system operates in the realm of sub-nanosecond, where measurement noise becomes a challenge in itself. Software, hardware, and physics are all involved, along with microwave and shortwave links between data centers, and custom-manufactured chips.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>We go deep into this in the “Hardware Engineering” section below.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>However, in this niche, even ultra-low latency is no longer a competitive moat in itself</span></strong><span>. As competitors have squeezed performance out of their systems, focus has shifted towards fine-tuning of trading strategies. Today, Optiver invests substantially more in building better models than it does in lowering latencies.</span><em><span> More on this in the “Network and physical infrastructure” </span></em><span>section below.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>HFT evolves faster than other industries. </span></strong><span>Profitable strategies don’t last long, opportunities are fleeting, and innovation is a constant. In this environment, a tool like AI is relatively straightforward to implement because trading houses like Optiver are well used to change in their daily business environment. </span><em><span>More on this topic in the ‘Optiver & AI’ section.</span></em></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Plenty of ML & math</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There’s a big role for machine learning (ML) and mathematics in quantitative trading. A good chunk of Optiver’s business is the buying and selling of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4f7a446d-b8be-430d-b2c8-d341b88d2c28?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>options</span></a><span>, and the pricing of these rests on mathematical theorems like the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/81712d80-043b-4ed5-90e0-431af2ccb4c1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Black-Scholes model</span></a><span>. Traders, quants, and even software engineers building option-pricing strategies must understand the math of this problem space.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Over time, machine learning is becoming more important than math models, but it’s worth keeping in mind that trading is not purely an ML pursuit.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>AI infra providers are heavily involved. </span></strong><span>NVIDIA, Groq, and Cerebras are actively courting trading firms, due to how much money they spend on GPUs. For example, see Hudson River Trading </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e6a8dc2a-18e5-42dc-8493-94019adaaf57?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>discussing</span></a><span> Blackwell deployments at NVIDIA’s GTC conference, or Jump Trading being among the first </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fa72aacd-b1a5-4161-ab5f-fa8a2df5208f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>to deploy</span></a><span> next-gen Vera Rubin systems. HFT companies have very clear monetization paths for GPUs and spend large sums on hardware, hence why NVIDIA and other suppliers are keen to partner with them.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>AI labs poach trading talent</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One new trend is AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI recruiting from prop shops, defying the assumption that AI labs mostly recruit from Big Tech. There are a few reasons why AI labs seek out talent from the trading world:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Infra expertise.</span></strong><span> Prop shops like Optiver have spent decades operating their own data centers and deploying on-prem hardware at co-location facilities.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Custom, high-performance hardware. </span></strong><span>Prop shops also often build their own hardware and their kernel stacks achieve very low latencies. That’s a talent AI labs seek!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Skillsets. </span></strong><span>The highest-paying destinations for CS majors out of standout colleges are often prop shops, paying top-of-market compensation for standout talent. </span><em><span>Outside of select colleges prop shops recruit from, however, there tends to be little awareness about these companies for new grads, or across the industry.</span></em></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>2. Engineering organization</span></h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Two eras of Optiver tech</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver’s history can be seen as two distinct ages:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Regional systems (“unblock yourself”: 1986-2020):</span></strong><span> internal systems and platforms were built to serve local needs, such as building support for a market. Systems built exclusively for the US, Europe, or Asia were common.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Global platforms (“build for the whole company”: 2020-present): </span></strong><span>Optiver recently started to build new systems to work globally across their platform. This global focus is also why the company is investing a lot more in its platform engineering arm. A globalization push started around 2023, and its momentum has been growing.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The benefit of the old “unblock yourself” approach of local teams building whatever they needed, was that it enabled them to move fast and not get held up by dependencies. But this became problematic because of fragmentation and duplication, and the downsides became more visible over time:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Fragmentation: different teams use different technologies, frameworks, and infrastructure</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Duplication: teams in different parts of the business independently build the same or very similar services</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The career trajectory of Pat Cooney, Optiver’s head of platform engineering, mirrors the shift to a global platform: he was the CTO of Optiver in Europe in the mid-2010s when the business was split by region, and was appointed head of platform engineering in 2025 when that approach was replaced.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver’s approach to continuous integration (CI) has also evolved. Previously, the company had several regional CI services, but from 2025, it started to rebuild its CI system with two new goals:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Build for scale: </span></strong><span>create a CI system built to scale across regions and stand the test of time</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Use from any region: </span></strong><span>standardize deployment pipelines, so that code built in one location can run anywhere without friction</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>How roles work together</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At Optiver, there are three main areas for tech roles:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Engineering</span></strong><span>: build and own the full trading-platform stack</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Research</span></strong><span>: quantitative scientists who build models and predictive signals to create and improve trading algorithms. Typically, their background is in math, physics, economics, and statistics</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Trading</span></strong><span>: quantitative traders who watch live markets, adjust trading system parameters in response to conditions, and build tools to automate decisions</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>In reality, the boundaries between these areas are porous. </span></strong><span>Yes, people do the job they were hired for, but it’s common to also see researchers roll up their sleeves and take part in implementing a trading strategy, or software engineers conducting research.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height:
