task</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Cross-functional collaboration between roles is very common. </span></strong><span>For example, when developing market signals and associated trading strategies, it’s normal for engineers, researchers, and traders to collaborate on most, if not all, projects.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>End-to-end ownership, plus autonomy, is a given. </span></strong><span>Engineers have autonomy in how they get things done, and they own and solve problems from the ideas stage through to implementation. There is a limited amount of guidance for trading, and it’s down to engineers to find the right solution.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In many ways, this approach to software engineering is pretty similar to startups’: software engineers get limited guidance and lots of autonomy. In order to succeed at tech startups, engineers typically need to understand the business, as well as being excellent at building production-ready software. It’s the same at Optiver, where understanding the business means understanding markets.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Platform engineering</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Before Optiver’s globalized platform efforts started seriously in ~2023, regions duplicated effort:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Multiple implementations of identical core logic</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Each region had its own systems, frameworks, and infrastructure</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Local teams built whatever they needed in an “unblock yourself” culture</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But that’s all changed. An obvious sign of global platform efforts is the appointment of Optiver’s first global CTO, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/78a3c513-f922-4e8c-b082-d1185df2754b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Lance Braunstein</span></a><span>, who joined with a mandate to scale the platform.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Roughly 30-40% of Optiver’s 950 engineers work on the platform. </span></strong><span>In contrast, a more typical ratio at other large tech companies is for 15-20% of engineers to be dedicated to platform work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Prior to the global platform, there was a lot more tolerance of development experience friction; new engineers could spend weeks checking out the codebase and getting their build system to work. This mindset has changed, with the platform team stressing user empathy and reducing friction on engineers’ journeys, like by setting up build pipelines for their software.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Now, the platform is beginning to reimagine itself as built for AI.</span></strong><span> As agents proliferate at Optiver, users are both humans and automated systems. The goal of this shift is to empower people to decompose work into workstreams and orchestrate agents. Two projects were launched earlier this year by the platform team for agentic work:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>AI gateway</span></strong><span>: gives Optiver engineers access to models</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ba0ba164-bef8-4fba-9df6-419d3c70fbd1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>MCP</span></a><span> hosting platform:</span></strong><span> makes it easy for engineers to access internal systems and tools via agents</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>How trading teams are organized</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Trading teams at Optiver have three roles:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Traders decide strategy and make risk decisions</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Researchers and quantitative analysts (“quants”) build hypotheses, pricing models, and run evaluations</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Engineers build production systems</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In practice, these roles overlap. This was true before the AI era, but it seems to be accelerating with AI adoption. Most traders and quants have STEM backgrounds without recent production coding experience. AI enables quantitatively-minded people to automate workflows with agents and to implement strategies.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Trading teams are organized by asset class and strategy.</span></strong><span> For example (asset classes in </span><em><span>italic</span></em><span>):</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A large team is focused on a broad area like </span><em><span>options</span></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A team focused on </span><em><span>cash markets</span></em><span> and building strategies for exchange-traded funds (ETF) and stocks.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A team focused on machine learning (ML) and trading in the </span><em><span>cash market</span></em><span>.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Within larger teams, there are horizontal and vertical sub-teams. </span></strong><span>Horizontal teams take on challenges that impact any trading desk; for example, pricing is a horizontal team as the underlying mechanism is the same whether a soybean or an index fund being priced.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Vertical teams are similar to “tiger teams”, accelerators, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/27f55e3d-e685-45cd-af9e-13afd93ec238?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>program teams</span></a><span> at other companies. They focus on short-term goals attached to a few different desks in a location like the US, Amsterdam, Mumbai or Sydney.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each team has a trading or research lead and a tech lead, who identify work for the team to do. The overall direction is set by a partnership structure, similar to an investment bank, but partners are not necessarily in charge of teams. At Optiver, partners are collections of senior people responsible for overall strategy.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Regardless of asset class or vertical, every trading team builds a version of a trading loop with four components.</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Retrieval of market-related information</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Collecting signals to work out which trades to execute</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Execution of strategies (sending orders to market)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Intervention via a feedback loop, enabling a trader to monitor the system.</span></p></li></ol><div 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>“Build and own” culture</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver runs on an ownership culture, with the principle that the best engineers take work personally and care deeply about Optiver’s systems, decisions, and outcomes. Leaders want engineers to treat their projects as if they were CEOs of a company, and be responsible for design, build, rollout, shipping, or support. There is no notion of throwing work over the wall to a QA team.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver’s ownership model:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Traders and engineers define problems together.</span></strong><span> Engineers design, build, test, deploy, and monitor a solution. There are hundreds of production changes daily</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Design reviews for architectural decision-making.</span></strong><span> When an engineer has a project that entails architectural change to the stack, the engineer is responsible for bringing multiple options with the pros and cons to the team for consultation. The goal is to share information and knowledge, and to make decisions</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver pushes new hires and interns to develop ownership. From day one, engineers have something they own and are assigned a real project with mentoring support. Production code changes are an expectation for new hires. Within a year, a new hire becomes the experienced person in their domain, ramping up the next engineer. This is explicitly emphasized in Optiver’s onboarding materials:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Case study: the Options Org</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver started life with options trading. The word ‘Optiver’ is actually a Dutch portmanteau of “options” and “trader”, so it’s unsurprising that the options team is among the most developed parts of the operation, with engineers split across multiple locations. The organization is composed of both vertical and horizontal teams.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One of the technical systems for which the Options organization is responsible is the retreat system. When Optiver trades an option, that trade itself changes the price of the next quote on offer. The retreat system has to reprice the entire option surface (i.e., all options related to the one just traded). This is called a ‘retreat’.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the case of S&P options, the option surface can consist of thousands of options that have to be updated. Ten years ago, the retreat process took seconds; now, through optimizations at every level of the stack, it’s down to nanoseconds.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" high-level</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Retreat speed matters because everything changes as soon as a trade occurs: the original quote is stale and a trader needs to remove the bid from the exchange before anyone can exploit it. Faster firms can take advantage of others’ stale prices, leading to an adversarial market dynamic.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Horizontal vs vertical team structures</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Vertical teams work on specific tactical problems related to local trading desks with a focus on immediate impact. But they are not short-term or temporary teams, even if they work on short-term problems. They’re empowered to solve the most important current problems, end-to-end. On the other hand, horizontal teams serve most desks, and have longer time horizons because they work on cross-cutting problems like pricing, market connectivity, or auto-trading.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>3. Software tech stack</span></h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Basic trading loop & three-layer tech stack</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most trading software applications or services (aka “apps”) at Optiver can be simplified to the basic trading loop. Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>Signals</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is the information-gathering phase where services collect market data such as prices and order book information, and also run various data calculations, such as pricing algorithms and machine learning pipelines. These signals are made available to strategy applications/services which decide how to trade.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>Strategy</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A single trading strategy typically focuses on a particular class of assets and trades, and many different strategies run concurrently. The strategy sets what and how to trade, but doesn’t execute the trade; that’s the next step.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>All strategies are enveloped by a risk management system that can block trades and stop individual strategies. To be effective, it has a broader view of the combined risk level of multiple strategies.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Risk mechanisms can include human oversight, with traders tweaking strategy parameters, and also automated monitoring that checks if apps are outputting orders within expected parameters, regardless of what the algorithm wants. The latter approach is essential in low latency strategies where faster-than-human reaction speeds are needed.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>Execution</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The execution step involves executing trades on exchanges. There’s a hard ‘separation of concerns’ principle where execution steps are only permitted to execute the trade. No additional logic is meant to run there.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>Ultra low-latency loop</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In some market-making use cases where nanosecond-level latencies matter, much of this process may run within a single chip (FPGA or ASIC) where the strategy part can be </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0dfae088-9027-40a8-94b2-7c83df902f6f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>memoized</span></a><span> with precomputed responses for all expected input patterns. This is then burned into the hardware to minimize latency from when market information arrives until a trading order is issued.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>The tech stack’s three layers</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>All apps implementing the trading loop sit on top of a multi-layered internal platform:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Basic infrastructure layer</span></strong><span>: the stuff you’d see at most tech companies (CI/CD pipelines, k8s, Kafka, Postgres, etc), but they’re also customizing their stack. They run their own data centers, have custom hardware, custom Linux kernels, customized CI tooling, and databases.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Domain-specific infrastructure</span></strong><span> contains core trading-specific services such as trading data dictionaries, metadata on securities, and the trade booking system.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" href="https://substack.com/redirect/b0f37e4c-d4a6-47c9-a137-299ffecab994?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>VHDL</span></a></strong><span> and </span><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6e62a6a2-d85e-47d3-acda-a27d132e72f0?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>SystemVerilog</span></a></strong><span> for FPGA development.</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>CI/CD stack</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Much of the software that Optiver builds interacts with custom hardware, custom Linux kernels, and requires predictable compute performance for predictable results in performance tests. These are all constraints that the CI/CD stack has to operate within.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Optiver’s CI/CD runs on bare metal machines, </span></strong><span>with custom hardware installed, the right OS tweaks, and a well-understood performance profile. Interestingly, this means Optiver needs to plan capacity in advance for its CI/CD clusters in the same way as it plans capacity for production systems. This is tricky since AI-coding tools started boosting the number of builds an average engineer does in a day.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>They chose GitHub Actions as their CI Platform for the seamless development experience with GitHub. Unfortunately, Actions doesn’t provide overall, system-level metrics like queue times and utilizations, which are critical information for planning CI cluster capacity. Therefore, they had to build a bespoke observability layer over GitHub Actions pipelines with GitHub webhooks.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Data</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When it comes to databases and storage systems in general, Optiver is a big user of </span><strong><span>Kafka</span></strong><span>, </span><strong><span>Postgres</span></strong><span>, and </span><strong><span>Databricks</span></strong><span> (the company built its entire data platform around this).</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A few interesting details show the role of Postgres:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>They contributed </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4d8ea78e-a693-4ebb-870a-44543bf89b70?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>a new timestamp type</span></a><span> to Postgres, allowing timestamps to be expressed with nanosecond precision. Few Postgres applications care about nanosecond-level precision, and this wasn’t available “out of the box”.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>They built their own internal version of the NOTIFY - LISTEN mechanism called ‘PG Feed,’ based on Postgres’ write-ahead log. This is used for distributing high-fanout, latency-sensitive messages to clients like pricing and configuration data, whereas using something like Kafka may involve additional disk reads and writes, which imply unwanted latency.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver generally picks industry-standard tooling, but heavily tweaks it to fit their specific performance needs. Not many tech companies of this size tweak Postgres or GitHub Actions, let alone Linux kernels!</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>4. Hardware engineering, FPGAs and Silicon</span></h2><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>The hot path</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In high frequency trading, a “hot path” is a sequence of events in a trading application, starting with an external trigger to issue a market order, e.g., a change in price. The time spent on the hot path (the time from the external event until a responding order leaves the system) is called “trigger-to-order” or “hot path” latency.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here’s an explainer on what happens between a market event arriving, until the order leaves:</span></p><div The trigger time path is match inbound pattern (1) → emit pre-computed response (4)</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Everyone on the market sees the same thing, so being first to react is critical when opportunities arise. </span></strong><span>This is because those opportunities disappear once orders are made, since those orders change the conditions which created an opportunity in the first place</span><strong><span>.</span></strong><span> That’s why Optiver puts so much effort into minimizing hot path latency.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Depending on the different triggers and decisions, there are actually multiple latency-sensitive hot paths, such as:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Quote/requote - continually update prices shared with the market</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Aggress/take (trigger-to-order) - detect an opportunity and execute trade</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Retreat/reprice - After completing an order, reprice</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Cancel/pull - Cancel orders</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Latency progression</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Folks whom we talked with at Optiver say the firm hasn’t yet reached the physical limit of what’s possible. Below are two interesting presentations on this quest for lower latency:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f08026de-f700-48f6-ac96-6847b0826384?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>When a microsecond is an eternity</span></a><span> (2017) by software engineer Carl Cook</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cbb4c1a5-d7dc-402f-95f8-c7783b6b1ef9?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>When nanoseconds matter: </span></a><span>ultrafast trading in C++ (2024) by Optiver tech lead, David Gross</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Custom hardware is a logical step for optimizing latency at a trading firm like Optiver. Moving from microseconds to nanoseconds in latency requires improvements across hot paths. Here are some typical optimization steps:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>A “regular” C++ app.</span></strong><span> A trading application starts life as a regular C++ app that’s optimized until CPU context switching and the kernel’s network stack become the slowest or highest variance parts.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Pin CPU cores.</span></strong><span> To address CPU context switching, engineers at Optiver first pin CPU cores. Operating systems will typically run multiple programs on each CPU core. This means a program can be temporarily stopped and replaced by another program. This is not desirable for consistent high performance, so a CPU core is pinned exclusively to a specific trading program, preventing it from being interrupted by other programs.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Work with the network card, bypassing the kernel. </span></strong><span>To address performance variance in the networking stack, they bypass the kernel and work with the network card directly. Normally, when data arrives from the exchange, the kernel sits between the network card and the application, making networking safe and uniform to program against. This imposes a small “speed tax” (aka, it runs slower) that is well worth it for many applications, but is a cause of lag and performance variance for latency-sensitive use cases like Optiver’s. By taking the kernel out of the data path, they forgo the speed tax at the cost of dedicating a CPU core to the network card via CPU pinning.</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Custom Hardware: FPGAs</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Once CPU cores are pinned and the kernel is bypassed for networking, the next bottleneck is typically the operating system itself and the CPU command execution pipeline.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Burning application logic directly with FPGAs comes next. </span></strong><span>In 2012, Optiver started experimenting with field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), which are chips that can be rewired for a specific purpose. Custom trading logic is typically written in </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/040e5e7c-49d3-408e-b8db-34a51355c443?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Hardware description language</span></a><span> and then compiled into a chip-specific logical gate configuration that can be burned onto a chip. A nice property of FPGA chips is that they can easily be rewired as needed, which is very useful for iterating on the logic.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The logic is directly encoded in physical electronic gates, so FPGAs can do in a handful of clock cycles what takes a generic CPU tens or hundreds of cycles. Processing can also be massively parallelized by data flowing through separate physical gates. This makes FPGAs significantly faster than generic CPUs, despite running at clock speeds an order of magnitude slower (typically 100s of MHz vs 3-6 GHz for modern CPUs).</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>What is bit memoization & why does it matter?</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The logic implemented in an FPGA is a different implementation of essentially the same algorithm from the original C++ application. Many of these algorithms can be represented with a simple request/response table, so responses don’t require anything more than a lookup.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For each expected market pattern, engineers at Optiver precompute responses in advance. When a particular market pattern is received, the chip matches the pattern and emits the prepared bits. Here’s how:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Enumerate patterns</span></strong><span>: list inbound market patterns that might arise</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Precompute:</span></strong><span> prepare a response in advance for each potential market event, typically during the FPGA design phase</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Hold behind the gate:</span></strong><span> precomputed responses are held behind a fast gate</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Drop the gate</span></strong><span>: receive an event for which there’s a precomputed response, and release the prepared bits to the exchange</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This precomputation approach allows Optiver to reduce response times into nanosecond territory.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Custom hardware: silicon/ASIC</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>FPGAs operate at lower clock frequencies than custom chips, so a logical step towards lower latencies is to build custom silicon (</span><strong><span>ASIC</span></strong><span>: Application-Specific Integrated Circuit) where clock speeds operate in the GHz territory.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Optiver began exploring custom silicon design in 2019.</span></strong><span> Building and testing ASICs takes significantly longer than building FPGAs, and involves talking to manufacturers, adapting the design to work with a manufacturer’s process, verifying prototypes, etc.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This process takes months and once the chip is done, it can’t be modified without restarting the process. On the other hand, FPGA chips are similar to the compiling of code in terms of flexiblity: the configuration is simply uploaded into a chip which is ready to be used within minutes and can be reconfigured at will.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Hardware org: small teams & full-stack scope</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Teams working on hardware projects are not so different from those on software projects: they’re trading teams which understand the domain they’re building in, and own outcomes end-to-end.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Hardware teams are very small, typically 5-10 engineers. </span></strong><span>They include those doing FPGA and ASIC work. Given their size, they are also nimble; for example, in hardware, lead times of six months-or-more for custom manufacturing are not unusual. But within small and nimble teams working with traders, it is considerably faster.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Hardware teams own the hardware stack as well as the software they build on top of it. It’s a baseline expectation for FPGA engineers at Optiver to be comfortable working in C/C++ to write software on top.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>FPGA testing is part of CI. </span></strong><span>FPGAs are tested in the same way as software; they’re part of the CI pipeline and are run against the same automated tests as software. Hardware Description Language (</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/040e5e7c-49d3-408e-b8db-34a51355c443?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>HDL</span></a><span>) code is reviewed in the same way as regular source code is reviewed, and the same monitoring and alerting procedures apply.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>AMD hardware partnership</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>AMD is best known for providing CPUs and GPUs, and is also an FPGA and custom network interface cards (NICs) provider. Optiver is a customer and also a co-development partner of AMD.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>AMD is increasingly investing in industry-specific solutions, as per HFT</span></strong><span>. This is notable as AMD’s major competitor, Intel, does not have as many such partnerships. Kevin Sprague, Optiver’s Hardware Engineering Lead, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/69eb47a6-17b5-4874-9c67-18064de4a208?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>explains</span></a><span> the need to build custom hardware:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We operate on numerous global exchanges, each with different protocols, throttling rules and regulatory nuances. We also support various trading products and teams, such as D1 Futures, Single Stock Options (SSO), and Index, each with unique system requirements. Every product demands its own distinct approach and design tailored for the specific strategies of the team involved.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Managing this complexity means we can’t afford to rely on off-the-shelf solutions. We need tailored hardware that supports varied trading approaches while maintaining the speed and reliability our systems demand.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Building custom hardware is vital to reduce latency</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A common theme in most hardware engineering at Optiver is full ownership of all potential sources of latency; the company cares not only about peak performance, but also about latency variances. The logical step is to focus on network and physical infrastructure.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>5. Network & physical infrastructure</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Once the core trading logic is fully optimized and living in custom chips, the next biggest source of latency and latency variance is the network:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The network over which market information and market orders travel</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>All networking components, from when the order leaves the server’s network card, until it reaches the exchange endpoint</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Physical infrastructure</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver aims to own the whole physical networking stack, all the way to the exchange.</span><strong><span> </span></strong><span>This is the same principle that led to the building of FPGAs and ASICs: the company builds bespoke network hardware and cabling inside the data center in order to fully own all network infrastructure on the way to the exchange.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Link congestion is one reason to own a complete networking stack. </span></strong><span>When Optiver wants to move data from its data center to the exchange, the internet is not how this is done because it’s too unpredictable. Data traveling via the internet can follow routes with unpredictable latencies, and be delayed by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7a1e838e-f25d-46e9-b937-45002374291d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>networking congestion</span></a><span>, aka link congestion.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Dedicated fiber & wavelength leasing</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In order to circumvent network congestion, Optiver rolls out its own dedicated fiber, or rents dedicated slices of existing fiber. Multiple beams of light can travel through the same optical fiber without interference if they are at different wavelengths.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Optiver leases “wavelength” services. </span></strong><span>This means they get exclusive rights to a range of light wavelengths on a given cable, providing guaranteed bandwidth and latency.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Challenges of optical cable</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Even so, optical cables aren’t perfect; they can get cut off – and regularly do. The most common cause is construction work on land, but there are some notable cases of cables being cut by ship anchors and shark bites. Most damaged cables can be repaired in a day or two, but undersea repairs can take months.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Therefore, Optiver must ensure its redundant cable connections are as independent as possible. This means making sure they enter a landmass at different places, follow different routes, and, ideally, enter the data center building from different sides.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Optiver manages a network with around 75,000 km (46,000 miles) of fiber.</span></strong><span> These cables run along highways, powerlines, and even along the ocean floor. Management of this infrastructure is done from the Amsterdam office.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Radio</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Optiver also runs its own microwave radio network</span></strong><span>. Some parts of this network are rented from third parties. This might be surprising, until we learn a fun fact about radio vs optical latency: radio waves travel through air 30-40% faster than light travels through an optical cable. </span><em><span>This is because radio waves are a form of light traveling through air, as are optical signals traveling through glass: but glass slows the propagation of light. Radio through air travels roughly at 300,000 km/sec, and light through glass roughly at 200,000 km/sec.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On the other hand, microwaves are disrupted by snow and heavy rain, so they have to maintain a fiber connection for failover.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Shortwave radio is used to reduce latency across longer distances. </span></strong><span>Microwaves don’t travel far, so to cover longer distances, Optiver uses shortwave radio. This approach can shave off a few milliseconds of latency (compared to optical cables) over large distances. Similarly to microwaves, this comes with reliability and bandwidth caveats as radio waves can only carry limited bandwidth, so the optical cable network is still critical for bandwidth and failover reasons.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Data centers & co-locations</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The next step in reducing latency via infrastructure decisions is to place hardware as close as possible to the exchanges that Optiver is connected to. In nanosecond territory, cable lengths matter: in an optical cable, light travels about 20cm per nanosecond, so even a cable that’s a bit longer than necessary introduces latency.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Optiver runs 30-40 co-locations with various exchanges, </span></strong><span>and has servers as close as possible to electronic exchanges. Here’s a typical setup at an electronically traded exchange:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/fb2ebfbc-8ea5-400f-8193-b42d690dfc24?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>A typical exchange setup. Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/24f7c679-d243-44c0-83f8-05882593304d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>Optiver</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The exchange sends market data to all exchange participants using </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d2b78338-ff70-4ffd-8e6b-1475a5708bba?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>UDP multicast</span></a><span>, guaranteeing all members receive the information simultaneously. Traders like Optiver make their orders using TCP connections to the exchange.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>While each data center and co-location is technically self-contained and can run independently, many trading strategies require signals that aren’t locally available. For example, a trading strategy focused on ETFs in New York might need information about </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/40d466a6-dddc-43bd-bba0-cf9ecdda65cd?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>futures</span></a><span> traded in Chicago. Since that information is also latency-sensitive, you need a low-latency, guaranteed-performance connection to the data source in Chicago.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Part of why Optiver’s Platform team is such a large portion of the whole team is because they have teams managing all the details mentioned above. It is a huge undertaking to maintain almost a dozen proprietary data centers and 30-40 co-locations, while building customer hardware and cabling, planning and maintaining connections between these locations across multiple redundant links (fiber, radio).</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The business can manage this complexity with a fairly small team of a couple of hundred engineers by employing a high degree of specialization: they don’t need general purpose data centers and connections, and instead optimize for guaranteed throughput and low latency for their specific use cases.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is also exactly the type of skillset which AI labs value. Squeezing as much performance as possible from existing hardware, or rolling your own hardware to get even more performance has a similar impact on training and serving AI models as on high-frequency trading. This capability is considered an important source of competitive advantage, so the competition for talent is heated.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Models and AI now matter even more than latency</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most market-making strategies are latency-sensitive because they are all fundamentally an </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c674f81e-a8a2-49fe-8407-8aa41fc4675e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>arbitrage opportunity</span></a><span>, or suffer from being exploited by arbitrage traders if they don’t move their prices fast enough. That’s why Optiver has had to historically obsess over latency; if not, they would fall behind competitors.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>These days, latency is the </span></strong><em><strong><span>floor,</span></strong></em><strong><span> and the differentiator is models, including AI ones. </span></strong><span>Back in the early days, having lower latency than the competition allowed for arbitrage opportunities to make risk-free profit. But as most serious players now have low-latency market access, this advantage has gone. Today, low latency is a baseline, and it takes more to make consistently profitable trades.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As such, information models are becoming the differentiator. Alex Itkin says Optiver thinks of information models in two ways:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Slow model with a fast trigger: </span></strong><span>a more complex model – often AI – runs on a slower cadence, digesting rich data. This model identifies likely scenarios, which are then memorized. When a scenario happens, the model sends a signal to the system, </span><em><span>fast</span></em><span>, and a trade is made which should be profitable.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Fast model near the edge of the network. </span></strong><span>A simpler but fast model – which could also be an AI model – runs close to the decision point, e.g. very close to an exchange. It monitors signals in realtime, and acts immediately and with low latency when it identifies a profitable scenario. This model is often a </span><em><span>distilled</span></em><span> version of a more complex model, built to run fast inference on the edge.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Today, more work goes into model work than reducing latency. </span></strong><span>There is easily 20x more engineering work happening with models and data than in efforts to further reduce latency. After all, there are only so many ways to reduce latency – the speed of light limitation applies! – but there are far more ways to gain an advantage with slow models firing triggers, or fast models running close to the edge.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>6. Engineering practices</span></h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Risk versus speed</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In our research, we found two factors which strongly influence engineering culture at a company like Optiver:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Approach to risk and ownership</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Move-fast mindset</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Trading carries inherent risks, especially at Optiver’s scale; even a single mistake can bankrupt a business, as shown by the</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f1acf5f4-8042-4504-8127-e843823135ed?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span> Knight Capital incident</span></a><span>. That event was a turning point for the industry, which then started to significantly increase investment in risk management tooling.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“No risk without reward” is a mantra. </span></strong><span>This came up when we talked with engineering leaders for our research, and it has two important corollaries:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Risk awareness: do not take risks blindly; make them explicitly visible</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Payoff: there must be adequate reward for taking a risk</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Below is an excerpt from an onboarding talk at Optiver which illustrates this approach.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure Optiver</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As mentioned, software at Optiver exists for the purpose of making profitable trades, and teams are encouraged to maximize the value of their trades by taking whatever approach seems most promising.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Rapid experimentation is a day-to-day practice company-wide.</span></strong><span> Teams deploy hundreds of changes to production daily. Therefore, everyone is expected to own outcomes end-to-end,</span><strong><span> </span></strong><span>and work independently across different roles and areas, as needed. So, how does Optiver reconcile this extreme ownership and rapid experimentation culture with the high-stakes environment it operates in? The business frames it as a knowledge question: </span><strong><span>if a team has all the relevant information, it’s assumed they will make the right call.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This philosophy of trusting teams which have the right context can be tied to the risk-management approach: they make risks visible via knowledge sharing, testing, and monitoring setup.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Knowledge-sharing culture</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ensuring individuals and teams have the right information starts with onboarding.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Optiver hires many graduates, </span></strong><span>who go through an extensive onboarding program called Optiver Global Academy where, in addition to tech onboarding, they are also taught about trading and financial fundamentals. Those graduates are soon expected to start solving real trading problems in production. New joiners are expected to start pushing changes to production within days, and to help onboard new joiners within a year.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“Quant dev” is a popular role at the company. </span></strong><span>Engineers get a very specific combination of skills that are uncommon at other tech companies. They’re performance-obsessed engineers with a solid background in trading and financial modeling.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Design reviews and architecture decisions</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Knowledge sharing continues after onboarding is over, via weekly internal tech talks, and this is a vital part of the software development lifecycle. A notable example of this are design reviews. They help teams refine designs before they start building, and an extensive testing suite provides actionable feedback while building apps. Meanwhile, robust monitoring allows the team to detect when an app misbehaves, and to take production lessons forward to the next iteration of a design.</span></p><div
